The static property formAssociated should be equal to true. This property is used so the browser can feature detect, resolving the custom element is a form-associated custom element.

After declaring formAssociated, inspect the DOM again, and you’ll find the custom element has been added to the HTMLFormElement DOM node list and has an index of 0.

Even though the custom element is now eligible to participate in the form, we still need to give the element API consistent with a typical form control like HTMLInputElement. attachInternals is a method that was added to the HTMLElement spec for that purpose. A call to the attachInternals method grants access to methods on the ElementInternals interface for the custom element. ElementInternals gives a form control the ability to communicate value and validity with the form.

Before the closing bracket of the constructor, set this.internals equal to this.attachInternals().

Once you do that, TypeScript may throw two errors: Property 'attachInternals' does not exist on type 'TextInputComponent'. and Property 'internals' does not exist on type 'TextInputComponent'.. That’s because the type definitions exported from lib.dom.d.ts do not currently support ElementInternals interface. lib.dom.d.ts is where TypeScript stores all the type definitions related to DOM APIs. To fix this type discrepancy, a type definition is included in the project repository in the file /types/lib.elementInternals.d.ts. This static type definition will not be necessary when the TypeScript DOM library properly exports the type definition for ElementInternals.

Before the constructor, declare the type for a private property called internals and set the type to ElementInternals. Declare the type for the private property attachInternals as () => ElementInternals.

Setting formAssociated allows the browser to detect that the custom element is a form-associated custom element, while ElementInternals grants several methods to the prototype of the TextInputComponent class. These methods are needed for the custom element to communicate with the form. Inspect the contents of lib.elementInternals.d.ts to become familiar with the methods you’ll be working with throughout this chapter.

Handling Validation

Now the TextInputComponent can communicate with a form, we should expose some of the methods used during form validation on the component class. Validation state is stored on this.internals, which is both private and possibly not as intuitive for engineers to access validity state. If validity state were to remain on internals, it would mean TextInputComponent won’t behave like a typical form element which stores this state on the root of the Object. We don’t necessarily want developers to reference input.internals.validity when looping over a form’s inputs to check validity. Accessing validity state from input.validity is much more preferable.

Create methods on the component class that expose the methods on the ElementInternals interface used for validation. First, make a method called checkValidity that returns this.internals.checkValidity(). This method checks for any constraints that have been declared, and when the check fails for any of those constraints, triggers the browser to emit an invalid event, and then returns false.

reportValidity is very similar to checkValidity, except that it also sends any validationMessage to the user agent for display. Add the reportValidity method to the TextInputComponent class, and make sure it returns this.internals.reportValidity().

validity returns a ValidationState Object that includes properties that reflect common validation errors, such as tooShort, valueMissing, and patternMismatch. This property is read-only. ValidationState is updated on calls to setValidity and reportValidity. Add the validity getter to the class, and make sure it returns this.internals.validity.

The next validation-related getter named validationMessages returns messages associated with each invalid condition of the form control. Add the validationMessages getter to the class, and make sure it returns this.internals.validationMessages.

ElementInternals includes a method called setValidity that does most of the heavy lifting during form validation. This method takes three arguments: flags, message, and anchor:

  • flags is an Object with properties that correspond to the validation flags the browser can interpret
  • message allows the engineer to pass a custom human-readable string that can be used to display feedback for the end-user
  • anchor is set to the HTMLElement the engineer wishes to display the user feedback stored in message

Whenever validation is triggered on the form control, usually when the user changes the value or blurs the input, you can write logic that validates the current value of the form control against some condition.

Consider the scenario of the required form control. The user focuses the input, then immediately navigates away without entering text into the field, effectively blurring the input. You could write a condition like the following that checks if the value of the text input has any content and then triggers validation on the ElementInternals interface by setting a validation error with the key valueMissing equal to true and a human-readable message.

There is an important distinction between the first and second arguments of setValidity. The ValidityStateFlags on the Object in the first argument communicates to the user agent what is invalid, while the message composed from a String in the second argument provides user feedback for the user to acknowledge the error and take action. The message Error: This field is required, Please type in a value. notifies the user there is a problem, prompting them to type something into the text field as a solution.

Two questions arise from the above example. Where does validation logic like the above belong in source code? How do you get the message to display in UI? For now, let’s tackle the answer to this first question. Later in this chapter, we’ll dive into the second.

Where does validation logic belong in the source code?

The context of the TextInputComponent provides a convenient place to listen for events on the HTMLInputElement and provide a callback to validate the form control. Suppose somewhere in the component, you listened for the blur event on the input and triggered validation on a method called onValidate.

In the onValidate callback, you could check if the element has a required attribute and the validity of the input. When the condition returns false, call setValidity with the valueMissing flag because it matches this use-case and viable user feedback in the second argument.

This pattern seems like it would work but has some limitations. With the conditions hard-coded in the component itself, developers using the component can’t override them. In other words, validation isn’t configurable based on different use-cases. This is especially important considering that one of the properties on ValidityStateFlags is customError. Developers can call setValidity with a completely custom validation error that isn’t covered by the available flags. How would you support dynamic use-cases when the conditions are hard-coded?

One solution is to put the conditions elsewhere, like the application logic as opposed to the component logic. That way, developers using the component have full control over the validations of each form control. The component no longer prescribes validation, but the component could still handle calls to setValidity. Let’s explore how this could be architected by establishing a pattern for validations that are declared in the story, then passed to the component by setting a property on the component.

Sketching the Validator type definition

Start by sketching out the API for how engineers would handle each validation in application logic. Make a new file at packages/component/src/input/validator.ts.

Define the type definition for an interface called Validator here and export the new type from the file so it can be used elsewhere.

Validator is an Object so that the API can possibly expand over time. For now, Validator contains one property: validations. A single form control could have multiple validations, so validations is an Array of Object. Each Object specifies the flag(s) from ValidityStateFlags associated with the validation on the flag property. A human-readable message is set on the message property. Both flag and message can be passed directly to setValidity. The third property called condition is equal to a function that takes an element as an argument and returns a boolean. We should assume the element passed into the first argument is the form control we’re validating against.

Mocking the Validators in Storybook

In TextInput.stories.js, declare a new const named validators. Make validators equal to an Object with a property username, which is equal to another Object, the Validator.

The username Validator should have a property named validations that is equal to an Array. Specify the Objects in this Array for the input used to enter a username. The validation below tests if the input required property is truthy and the value has length.

For validation to work, you’ll need to store it on the component instance. To do that, give the in-textinput a new attribute called name and set the name attribute to username.

When you query for DOM here in the template function, you’ll find that the in-textinput isn’t available yet. That’s because LitHTML html function has to compile the template, so any queries have to be made behind a call to setTimeout. Using setTimeout, query for the custom element and set a property called $validator on the element, making it equal to validators["username"]. Setting properties like this on a custom element is one way for application logic to communicate with the component.

Uptaking the Validators in TextInput

Back in TextInput.ts, you’ll need to make some changes to uptake the validations. Import Validator from validator.ts, and declare a new $validator property on the class, making sure it’s public and type defined as Validator.

Declare a new getter on the class called $input and return the embedded HTMLInputElement.

Source of truth

Before we move forward, there is an important distinction to make between the custom element and the input. The form-associated custom element is where communication happens between the component and the form, while the input is where all user interaction typically takes place. When a user clicks the input or navigates there via the keyboard, focusing it, they are interacting with the input, not the custom element.

This poses a problem. Where is the source of truth for component state? So far, you’ve exposed methods on the class that suggests the source of truth is derived from properties and attributes on the custom element, but if you were to set a required attribute on the custom element, how does the input interpret this change to the required state? Conversely, when the input value updates, how does the custom element report the value to the outside world?

Part of the problem is that form controls usually expose getters that expose the state of required, disabled, the value, and so on, except the only stable way to set the state on the form control is via attributes. To make a HTMLInputElement required, for instance, you have to set the required attribute on the input.

When developing reusable UI components, the outward-facing API of the component matters. If we expose the component state only through getters and setters, it would be awkward for engineers used to setting attributes on form controls to set state. Consider a problem we’ve already introduced concerning the design of the Validator. In the condition declared in TextInput.stories.js, the first argument input checks if the input has a property required and validates if the input has a value by assessing input.value.length. But what is input? Is input referencing the TextInputComponent or the embedded HTMLInputElement?

One solution is to treat the HTMLInputElement as the single source of truth for component state and essentially use TextInputComponent as a pass-thru, exposing properties of the HTMLInputElement with getters on the component class and using setters that change the state of the HTMLInputElement. That way, TextInputComponent exposes an outward-facing API. Let’s see how this works in action. To achieve this we need a way to set attributes on in-textinput and have the component react to changes to those attributes, similar to how a typical input element behaves.

Listening for attribute changes

Luckily, custom elements provide an API for observing changes to attributes and reacting to those changes. Every custom element has access to a static getter called observedAttributes. Using observedAttributes, you can establish which attributes the component listens to for changes. For performance sake, you have to whitelist each attribute that should be observed.

Just below the constructor in the TextInputComponent class, declare the observedAttributes getter. observedAttributes returns an Array of String, each String corresponding to the name of the attribute that should be observed. Add required and value to the Array. You’re declaring observedAttributes so that developers can set the value and required attributes on TextInputComponent because those are the properties the condition in the Validator is referencing to validate whether or not the field has value. You’ll add more attributes that should be observed later, but for now, required and value should suffice.

After declaring which attributes should be observed, a second method named attributeChangedCallback handles attribute changes. attributeChangedCallback is another method available to all custom elements that must be used in conjunction with observedAttributes.

attributeChangedCallback has three arguments, name, previousValue, and currentValue that pass the name of the changed attribute, the previous value of the attribute, and the current value of the attribute, respectively. For the sake of brevity, we’ll call these arguments name, prev, and next. You could strictly type define the arguments and what the method returns, but for now we’ll ignore the types for this method. prev and next could have many different types, so type defining these attributes anything other than any can become tricky. name will most certainly always be of type string.

Looking at the attributeChangedCallback, it appears we need a way to do something based on the value of name passed through the first argument of attributeChangedCallback. A typical convention is to use a switch statement.

Add the switch to attributeChangedCallback, passing in the name. Set up case for value and required. If you try to set this.value and this.required based on the value of next, you’ll be prompted with errors the value and required properties do not exist, so let’s add them. When you are finished attributeChangedCallback should appear like the example below.

Using getters and setters to communicate state

Existing form controls like HTMLInputElement and HTMLTextAreaElement set their own state through attributes, and in some cases, properties. value and disabled can reliably be set through properties on HTMLInputElement, but there is no equivalent setter for required; required state must be set through an attribute. In this section, you’ll wrangle these odd behaviors by adding getters and setters to TextInputComponent class.

Earlier, we tried to set value in the attributeChangedCallback, but it failed because there currently isn’t a value setter, so let’s add one. A setter method in JavaScript starts with the set keyboard, followed by the name of the method: value. The first argument of this method is the value that should be set. The setter passes the value argument to the HTMLInputElement by setting that element’s value property.

To allow the Validator access to the current value of the HTMLInputElement, make a getter on the TextInputComponent class. Getters in JavaScript start with the get keyword, followed by the method name: value. There’s no arguments here, but you can set the return value as string, then in the curly brackets of the method, return the HTMLInputElement current value state: this.$input.value.

Repeat the same process for getters and setters for the required state, although this time, you’ll have to set state of the HTMLInputElement by setting its required attribute. When passing the required state from the TextInputComponent attribute through attributesChangedCallback, the type of the required state will be string, because that’s usually the type of anything passed through attributes. This is a problem because when coding the getter for required, you can reliably access the required state of the HTMLInputElement through the required property, which returns the required value with the type boolean.

Add the required getter to TextInputComponent.

In TypeScript, getter and setter types must match, so the setter has to accept both a string and boolean in the first argument. Code the required setter, adding conditions that check the value and either call setAttribute or removeAttribute on the HTMLInputElement.

Once you’ve completed the value and required getters and setters, return to TextInput.stories.js and add the required attribute to in-textinput in the story template.

You’d expect to see a required attribute set on the HTMLInputElement. However, if you use Dev Tools to observe the changes in DOM, you’ll notice the required attribute is still missing.

This is something we need to fix since TextInputComponent relies on the state of HTMLInputElement, but what is the problem?

Passing attribute values to children

It’s likely the HTMLInputElement hasn’t received a call to setAttribute because it doesn’t exist yet. Remember, the HTMLInputElement is encapsulated by Shadow DOM. When TextInputComponent instantiates, attributeChangedCallback fires almost immediately, but the browser hasn’t yet fully parsed all the nodes in the ShadowDOM.

To handle situations like this, custom elements include another lifecycle method named connectedCallback that runs when the custom element is added to DOM. connectedCallback offers a space where you can reliably query DOM nodes in the custom element ShadowRoot.

So, what does this mean for setting attributes reliably when you need to pass the value of the attribute from parent to child node? This means you need to store the values of the attribute somehow and defer setting the child node’s attributes to connectedCallback. Eventually, you’re going to handle many more different attributes in attributeChangedCallback, so create a new property on the TextInputComponent class called $attr and make it equal to an empty Object.

In the first line of attributeChangedCallback, set properties on this.$attr with whatever passes through the callback.

Before or after the declaration of attributeChangedCallback in TextInputComponent, make a new method called connectedCallback.

Inside the method implementation, loop over the properties on this.$attr and call setAttribute on the HTMLInputElement for every attribute currently stored in the $attr Object.

Inspect the DOM again in Storybook and notice the required attribute is now properly set on HTMLInputElement.

In this section, you learned about connectedCallback, a method that fires whenever the custom element is added to DOM. Combined with attributeChangedCallback, you developed a means to pass the values of attributes from parent to child whenever the custom element is instantiated, while getters and setters declared on the TextInputComponent class handle changing the value whenever it changes during the lifespan of the component. connectedCallback and attributeChangedCallback are lifecycle methods available on all custom elements. Later in this chapter, you’ll learn about lifecycle methods available only to form-associated custom elements.

Handling validation and child events

Since TextInputComponent can reliably handle state for required and value, we can finish setting up the Validator. To progress, we should consider when validation occurs and clarify some expectations around validation.

  • Validation only happens client-side in this application, which is why we need a robust client-based API for validating form controls.
  • Validation should happen on blur, i.e., when the user navigates away from the form control, not while the user is interacting with the form control.
  • Validation should occur when the component initializes. Otherwise, if the user submits the form without interacting with a form control, the form will be valid and allow submission.

Form controls need to register themselves with their parent HTMLFormElement in the connectedCallback so that the form can start from an invalid state where applicable. We don’t necessarily want to show the UI in an invalid state on initialization, though; any visible user feedback should only display after the form control is blurred in an invalid state. These are not necessarily recommendations for how validation should be handled in every application, but the above describes how the application we’re building behaves.

To get started wiring up validation in TextInputComponent, add a new method to the class named onValidate. This method takes an argument showError, a boolean that determines whether or not to display user feedback upon validation.

We could put all the logic here for validation, but other form controls would have to duplicate the code. To keep the implementation DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself), export a new function from validator.ts named validate. This function takes two arguments:

  • elem refers to the form control
  • showError is the option we’re going to pass from onValidate in TextInputComponent that either shows or hides user feedback

Import validate in TextInput.ts and call the function in the onValidate method, passing this into the first argument and showError in the second argument. this, in this context, means the instance of TextInputComponent.

Per the component requirements, onValidate needs to run on load and after the user navigates away from the form control, on blur. In the connectedCallback, call onValidate passing in false as the first argument. This means error messaging won’t be shown initially, but validity state can still be passed to the form element. Add an event handler for the onblur event on the input element, this time calling onValidate with the first argument set to true so validation messages can display properly.

That’s it for now in TextInputComponent. You’ll return later, but now, let’s focus on handling validation in the reusable validate function in validator.ts.

Changing validation state

Before you add logic to the validate function, consider the algorithm you’ll have to write. Looking back at the implementation in TextInput.stories.js, a property called $validator is set on the element. $validator is equal to an Object that has a property called validations: a Validator Array that you declared earlier.

In the validate function, you’ll need to check if $validator exists, and if it doesn’t, short-circuit the function so that the rest of the logic doesn’t run. Another good check is to make sure validations exists on the $validator Object. This conditional is mainly for instances of the component where validation is not necessary or to prevent errors when developers are implementing other form controls that expose a similar API as TextInputComponent or haven’t declared the validations yet in application source code.

Since the Validator supports many validations, the Array has to be looped over to check if each condition returns true. condition is a function that takes a single argument, the element currently being validated: elem. Call forEach on elem.$validator.validations, and use the callback to loop over each validation in the Array.

When the condition returns true, make a call to setValidity, passing in the flag and message declared on validator to notify the form of an invalid form control.

That takes care of invalid form controls, but how do you notify the form when the form control is valid? You’d need a way to check that no validations met the condition in the forEach. One way to handle this is to populate an Array with validations that meet the condition. Since forEach is blocking, you can check the length of the Array after the loop. If the Array is empty, call setValidity with an empty Object to notify the form that this form control is valid.

Make a new Array named activeValidators, and make it equal to an empty Array.

In the forEach, call push on activeValidators whenever a condition returns truthy to populate the Array. After the forEach, use another if statement to check the length of the activeValidators Array. When the length is falsey, call setValidity with an empty Object. The absence of any flags on the first argument of setValidity tells the HTMLFormElement this form control is valid.

To test these changes, you’ll need a way to listen for changes in validation state and mock an event listener in Storybook. HTMLFormElement doesn’t provide hooks into listening for validation state changes, even though under the hood ValidityStateFlags state is changing whenever setValidity is called. To solve this problem, you can make a CustomEvent that bubbles up to the HTMLFormElement. Then you can listen to validation changes on the form and mock the event listener in Storybook.

At the very end of the validate function, dispatch a CustomEvent with the name validate, setting the option bubbles to true so the event bubbles up to the HTMLFormElement.

Storybook renders Web Components with LitHTML by default. That’s why the template in TextInput.stories.js calls the html function exported from the lit-html package. html has some hidden powers we can tap into when mocking the template, specifically the ability to listen for events using a template syntax where you can also pass in an event listener callback.

Before you can attach the callback in TextInput.stories.js, you have to declare the callback function via Storybook. Locate the place where Primary is declared, and immediately after it, set the Primary.args to an Object. Pass in the validators you mocked earlier as one property on the args Object, then declare a property called onValidate.

In the onValidate callback, query for the TextInputComponent using document.querySelector with the attribute you added earlier: [name="username"] , and using an if statement, check the validity.valid. When valid is falsey, log "INVALID"; otherwise, log "VALID".

Inject onValidate and validations into PrimaryTemplate. Any property on args can be injected like this into the template in Storybook.

Bind the validate event to the callback using LitHTML @ attribute syntax. The @ automatically binds an event listener on the form element, passing in onValidate as the callback function typically set on addEventListener. @ is one of LitHTML features and not part of the Web Components specifications.

In Storybook, click on the input and type the Tab key on the keyboard. Observe in the Dev Tools console that INVALID is logged. Focus the input again, and type something into the form control. After blurring the input again observe VALID is logged. If you do not see any feedback in the Dev Tools Console, ensure the JavaScript context is set to the storybook-preview-iframe.

While you still have to provide visual feedback for the end-user, you’ve hooked up everything needed to start validating TextInputComponent against user input. validator was declared in a separate file because we are anticipating reusing this function in other form controls. Abstracting the declaration of each Validator to TextInput.stories.js simulates real-world usage of the validations. Storybook is providing an environment were you mock components similar to how they would be used in an application. Much later in Part Three of this book, you’ll declare validators for username and password fields in the application in the same way. In this section you also wired up an event listener to trigger validation on blur of the input element. The validator function also dispatches an event to the nearest HTMLFormElement to notify it of the custom element’s validity. The form-associated custom element is beginning to participate in the HTML form.

User feedback

Now that you have a test bed where validation state can be verified during development, it’s a good time to handle user feedback. According to the mockups in Figma, whenever there is an error associated with a form control:

  • The input border should change color to a shade of red
  • Messages that instruct the user how to validate the form control are displayed below the input

So far in the validate function, you’ve called setValidity whenever the user blurs the form control. Perhaps this is also a good place to handle user feedback. However, since validate is a reusable function that could be used in other components, it means any elements referenced here must be found in all of those custom elements. In TextInputComponent template, two elements are used to provide user feedback: the input (elem.$input) and a div with the class message.

In validator.ts, declare a new const named messageElem. Use querySelector to target the div with the class message in the ShadowRoot of the element.

To prevent errors when a form control doesn’t include this element, be sure to check if messageElement is truthy. Whenever validate is called, empty the messageElement of content by setting the innerHTML to an empty string. This is necessary because existing messages could have accumulated in the element, and in the case of the form control being valid, we need a way to clear them.

In the forEach, whenever validator.condition(elem) is truthy, include some logic to show the error state when the second argument showError is true. Again, check for the elements before interacting with them. Add a class to the input named error and create a new div, set its content to whatever is in validator.message, and call appendChild on the messageElem to append the message.

When the form control is valid, remove the error class from the input element and reset the content of messageElem by setting the innerHTML to an empty string. This has the effect of clearing the error state.

Test out the changes in Storybook. Click on the input and immediately blur, either by clicking outside the input or pressing Tab on the keyboard. You should notice the message “Error: Required” below the input. Focus the input, and this time enter a value, and then blur the input, causing the message to disappear. Repeat this process, inspecting the DOM in Dev Tools to ensure that the error class is added and removed from DOM at the appropriate times.

Pretty soon, you’ll style the input with CSS like the mockup in Figma, and the look and feel will get a substantial improvement. Before you engage in styling, there’s one more state you’ll need to handle in TextInputComponent whenever the input is disabled.

Handling Disabled State

Form controls can be disabled by setting the disabled attribute on the element, or when the element is a descendant of a <fieldset>, it should inherit its disabled state. Form-associated custom elements include a lifecycle hook for this specific use-case called formDisabledCallback. Whenever TextInputComponent is a child to a disabled fieldset in DOM, this callback will be activated. Whenever formDisabledCallback is called, the first argument contains the disabled state. Pass this state to the TextInputComponent.

TypeScript should throw an error because you haven’t yet established a setter for the TextInputComponent called disabled. This setter looks a lot like required from before, syncing the child input element with the current value of the disabled attribute on the instance of TextInputComponent.

Declare a getter that returns the disabled state from the HTMLInputElement.

Add the disabled attribute to the observedAttributes Array, and then include a case in the switch statement found in attributeChangedCallback that calls the disabled setter whenever the disabled attribute changes on TextInputComponent, making sure to also add the disabled to the Array returned in observedAttributes.

That’s all there is to giving TextInputComponent a disabled state. When a developer sets the disabled attribute on TextInputComponent, the disabled setter will update the HTMLInputElement disabled state. Developers can read the disabled state with the disabled getter. Whenever a parent fieldset is disabled, the TextInputComponent will use the formDisabledCallback to set the disabled state of the component via the setter.

Make stories

So far, you’ve developed the TextInputComponent solely using the Primary story declared in TextInput.stories.js, but during development, two other distinct visual states have appeared: error and disabled.

If you were to begin styling the component with CSS, you would have to configure the story in various ways to trigger the error or disabled state. Disabled, for instance, requires the disabled attribute set on in-textinput in the template, while error involves mocking user interaction (focus and blur). It’s much easier to maintain different stories for each interaction state than configure one story to handle many interaction patterns.

In TextInput.stories.js make a new story where the disabled state will be visible whenever someone navigates to the story in Storybook. Start by declaring a const named DisabledTemplate, a function that returns a LitHTML template that sets the disabled attribute. Then export a story called Disabled, making it equal to DisabledTemplate.bind({}).

Observe the new Disabled story appears in the Storybook sidebar, displaying the input with the default browser styling associated with the disabled state.

Using the same format, declare another const named ErrorTemplate. The template is very similar to PrimaryTemplate. This time, however, precede the return with a call to setTimeout. In the setTimeout callback, query for the input, set the $validator property to the available username validator, then call focus and blur on the element. This should simulate the action of a user interacting with the component and, as a result, display the validation message below the input. Make sure to call setTimeout with 0 in the second argument, to defer the setTimeout callback until after the LitHTML template compiles.

To be able to focus and blur the input element via TextInputComponent, you’ll need to circle back to TextInput.ts and add two methods that pass the function calls to the child input element.

Observe a new Error story appears in the Storybook sidebar and now the component displays Error: Required and has the error CSS class set on the input element. Verify each story is displaying the correct interaction states before styling.

Styling with CSS variables

Now you have three distinct stories to style from: Primary, Error, and Disabled. Reference the mockup in Figma and style each of the interaction states using CSS variables from the global stylesheet.

Style the Primary story

Navigate to the Primary story in Storybook. In the constructor of TextInputComponent, make a new <style> tag at the start of the template string that sets the template.

Custom elements by default have a position of inline, and HTMLInputElement is defaulted to inline-block. However, most designs in the application do not show inputs displayed inline. Instead, the mockups seem to indicate that form controls should have display set to block, which makes them behave more like a div. Set the font-family and font-size to establish a baseline for elements in the TextInputComponent ShadowDOM.

Style the input element, establishing the height and width. Style the border using the --border-default CSS variable, and set the border-radius. Override browser defaults for font-size and outline. Disable outline because the border effectively does the same thing. Set padding-left to satisfy the mockup and box-sizing to border-box to make styling more predictable.

Since you’ve disabled the outline that would normally appear when the input is focused, return the user feedback by setting the border to a different color using the CSS pseudo selector :focus, making sure to also override :focus:hover and :active. This styling will make the border darker whenever the input is focused or active.

Style the Error story

Navigate to the Error story in Storybook to begin styling the error state. Select the .error class with CSS while also targeting all the pseudo classes so that whenever the form control has an error state, the border and font color changes to bright red.

The element that contains the error messages also requires some styling. Select the .message class with CSS and apply the styles from the mockup.

Style the Disabled story

After you’ve observed the new error styling taking effect in Storybook, navigate to the Disabled story to style the disabled state. To select the disabled state with CSS, target the attribute using square brackets. Change the opacity, background, and border styles using the appropriate CSS variables, making sure to also override the :focus, :hover, and :active states.

Styling TextInputComponent in the context of the template means the styling is encapsulated by Shadow DOM. This is one of the clear benefits of using Shadow DOM, although as we’ve seen, this encapsulation makes it impossible for the HTMLInputElement to fully participate in HTMLFormElement without also using the APIs provided by a form-associated custom element. In the next sections, you’ll wrap up development of TextInputComponent by granting the component all the same features of the HTMLInputElement and making sure the HTMLFormElement state is updated whenever the user changes the value of the form control.

Emulating HTMLInputElement

In previous sections, you declared getters and setters for required, disabled, and value and used observedAttributes to watch for changes to these attributes on TextInputComponent, but what about the rest of the attributes usually provided by HTMLInputElement that are still missing on TextInputComponent? Since the input element is encapsulated by Shadow DOM, it’s not easily accessible from the outside world. Developers could access the input element using the $input property, but things could get out of sync between TextInputComponent and HTMLInputElement fairly quickly.

It’s a fairly safe bet to assume that state is managed by HTMLInputElement because it does a lot of heavy lifting, providing attributes and properties that handle fairly complex problems. Setting pattern on HTMLInputElement, for instance, allows the developer to ensure the value of the input matches RegExp, while list allows developers to specify the id of a <datalist> element that contains autocomplete options. Without HTMLInputElement, you’d have to figure out how to implement some of these complex features. When coding form-associated custom elements, it makes a lot of sense to reuse behaviors of existing inputs, even if it means the input is completely hidden from the view, like you will see in later chapters when you develop CheckBoxComponent.

Ensure that TextInputComponent has many of the same features of HTMLInputElement by implementing the same attributes, getters, and setters that are also provided by an input element where type is equal to text.

Update observedAttributes to listen for changes on several attributes usually found on HTMLInputElement.

Add cases for each of the attributes in attributeChangedCallback, setting the appropriate attribute of the HTMLInputElement whenever the attribute on TextInputComponent is updated.

type

Code getters and setters for type. The getter should return text by default or type when it’s present on this.$input. Set the type using this.$input.setAttribute.

list

list is only a getter on HTMLInputElement. The only way to set list is via setAttribute, which is handled in attributeChangedCallback.

Set up getters and setters for minLength, which establishes the minimum length of characters for the value of the input.

maxLength

Code getters and setters for maxLength, which establishes the maximum number of characters for the value of the input.

readOnly

readOnly is only a getter on HTMLInputElement, so replicate the same readonly property on TextInputComponent.

pattern

pattern can be set via setAttribute or a setter on HTMLInputElement, so replicate the same getters and setters on TextInputComponent.

placeholder

placeholder is typically set on HTMLInputElement with setAttribute, but the element also provides a getter.

spellcheck

spellcheck is typically set on HTMLInputElement with setAttribute, but the element also provides a getter.

All those getters and setters may seem like a lot of busywork, but they go a long way to providing a stable API for developers. When developers implement user interfaces with TextInputComponent, they can expect the same API as HTMLInputElement directly on the form-associated custom element. For the sake of brevity, we’ve omitted some APIs involved with making selections in HTMLInputElement, but even those could be added to the TextInputComponent using the same techniques. For a complete reference, read The Input (Form Input) element on MDN.

Making a form

In the final push to implement the rest of TextInputComponent, you’ll need another story to test how the form control participates in form submission. This story will support two inputs for a login view: one input for username and another that handles the password. This will allow you to also test some of the new features added in the last section, namely type, minlength, and pattern.

The login form must be validated in such a way that both inputs are required and have a minimum length, while the password input should include at least one lowercase letter, uppercase letter, number, and special character.

Update the validators Object in TextInput.stories.js. Add another property called password. Give both username and password the following validations:

Add another validation to the password validator that validates against the pattern.

Declare a new template called FormTemplate. This template injects a few more arguments than previously: headline, onSubmit, onFormData, in addition to onValidate.

Just like the other templates, this function returns a call to html followed by a template string that includes the HTML template. Place a new h4 element before the form element and bind the headline argument to its content. Bind the two new callbacks onFormData and onSubmit the same way as onValidate, using the @ template syntax provided by LitHTML that calls addEventListener on the form element.

Add a fieldset to the form. Place a label with the name of the input prior to each in-textinput, ensuring the label has a for attribute that matches the name attribute of the in-textinput it describes. We’ll go into much better detail about this relationship in the next chapter when discussing accessibility.

Make sure each in-textinput has the appropriate type attribute, is marked required, and has the minlength set to 8. The password input should have an additional pattern attribute with the provided RegExp that validates the password meets the minimum requirements.

Don’t forget to add the $validator property to each input so that both form controls take advantage of the validate function you coded earlier.

Add another input to the template at the end of the fieldset, this time with the type attribute set to submit.

Inputs of the type submit are how browsers handle form submission by default. When the input is rendered as a button, clicking on this element will make the browser user agent attempt form submission. Single-page applications may not use that approach, but in the story, the input will provide a handy means to test TextInputComponent is participating in form submission.

When you are finished, FormTemplate should look like this:

Export a new const called Form and call bind on the FormTemplate function.

Declare several new properties on the story args for the template. These properties get passed to the FormTemplate function you just declared. First, set the headline property to Login so that the proper headline appears in the h4.

When you click on the submit button, the template is expecting a callback named onSubmit. In this callback, you’ll want to call preventDefault on the event. Otherwise, Storybook will try to navigate away when you click on the button. In this callback, create a new FormData Object, passing in the HTMLFormElement into the first argument. Wrapping that in console.log will allow you to inspect the FormData.

Oddly enough, just by instantiating the FormData in this callback, you’ve triggered another event on the form element called formdata, which you’ve already bound to the element in the FormTemplate with the callback onFormData. Declare onFormData on the args Object, being sure to log the event.

One way to inspect the values of each input is to loop over the values property on the formData Object, as seen in the above example. The value logged there is the value of each input on form submission.

Add one more property to the args for validation. Similar to the callback in the Primary story, onValidate checks the truthiness of the validity.valid on each input, but this time in a loop because you’re dealing with more than one input.

When you are finished, the Form story should appear like below.

That’s it for story creation! Now let’s wire up the final parts of TextInputComponent so the form control can participate in form submission.

Handling FormData

If you click the submit button with both inputs passing validation and then inspect the FormData Object in Dev Tools, you’ll notice the entries and values Iterators are empty. That means TextInputComponent still isn’t fully working with form submission. This is actually fairly easy to fix, but it means exploring two more lifecycle hooks provided by form-associated custom elements, formStateRestoreCallback and formResetCallback, which handle form state at different times. You’ll also use another method on ElementInternals to update the form with the value of the input: setFormValue.

To update the form with the value of the input, we should consider when the user updates the value of the input. As of yet, you’ve only handled changes to the input value on blur in the connectedCallback, but you’ll need to also attach a callback, listening to the change event on the HTMLInputElement.

In TextInput.ts, add the following to the connectedCallback:

Declare a method on TextInputComponent called onChange. In this method, call this.internals.setFormValue, passing in the value of the input into both arguments. The first argument of setFormValue sets the value of the input on the FormData Object, which fulfills the requirement during form submission.

While you’re in this method, clean up some of the logic from validation. Clear out the messages in the div by setting innerHTML to an empty string, and remove the error class from the HTMLInputElement. This will have the effect of clearing the error state when the user types.

The second argument of setFormValue is for when the user navigates away from the form and back again. The second argument allows the browser to retain the value of the input element so the user doesn’t have to enter the value again, but only when the formStateRestoreCallback is defined.

formStateRestoreCallback is called when the browser wants to restore the state of form control. Use-cases may include when the user navigates away from the form and back again, the browser reloads, or when the browser wants to autofill the value. The second argument of setFormValue is optional, but we’ll use it and the formStateRestoreCallback for the time being. However, with further development, setting this argument could be configurable via the TextInputComponent interface.

Similarly, formResetCallback is called whenever the form resets, and each form control could return to its original value. This callback is a convenient means to reset the value of the form control to whatever is specified by the value attribute.

In Storybook, enter values into both inputs that pass validation and click the Submit button. Observe the FormData now has values for each input thanks to setFormValue.

Testing TextInputComponent

Integration tests are important for TextInputComponent because you can validate the component’s outward facing API: the attributes, getters, and setters you defined in previous sections operate as expected. Snapshot tests will validate the interaction states you styled.

For the integration tests, you’ll be using the Form Story from the previous section as a test bed. Before you begin writing integration tests, ensure there is a submit classname added to the submit button in the FormTemplate so it can be easily queried during testing.

Make a new file in the cypress/integration directory named TextInput.spec.js.

Ensure Storybook is running in a Terminal window.

In a separate Terminal tab or window, start up Cypress in open mode.

In TestInput.spec.js, set up the test by declaring a describe block.

Make an assertion that tests if the error message displays on blur. First tell Cypress to navigate to the Form story in Storybook, referencing the URL of the story in the browser address bar to set a query param for iframe.html.

Query for each element in Light DOM with get, checking each element is visible using should, and then use Cypress to click on each input and the submit button by chaining click().

Find the message container elements in Shadow DOM, and check they contain the appropriate error messages using similar chained methods, but this time querying in ShadowDOM using the shadow and find methods.

Test that both inputs in the FormTemplate don’t display error messages when the inputs are valid. Write a new test titled should not display error message when valid and visit the same story in Storybook.

Select each input, and call type to enter a value that should pass validation.

Use Cypress to click the submit button.

Verify that both message containers are empty.

You just tested the validations you developed in this chapter work when the value of TextInputComponent is invalid and that no user feedback is visible when TextInputComponent is valid. There are many more aspects to the TextInputComponent that could be validated with integration tests, although we’ll stop here for the sake of brevity.

Make sure you stop the process running Cypress before proceeding with the snapshot tests.

Snapshots

With Storybook still running generate snapshots for the component.

After snapshots have been generated for each TextInput story, add them to your commit. Commit your changes in git to complete this section. Now you’ve completed integration and snapshot tests for TextInputComponent. Let’s review the content of Chapter Two.

Summary

In this chapter, you accomplished a lot! You developed a form-associated custom element, TextInputComponent, that handles several states for a text input: default, error, and disabled. By setting formAssociated on the component class, you enabled TextInputComponent to participate in form validation and submission. ElementInternals provided several methods to aid in validation, but didn’t provide a handy method for validating an entire form using the value from TextInputComponent, so you dispatched a validate Event to the HTMLFormElement, which allowed you to hook into a custom validation model. setFormValue on ElementInternals allowed you to update form FormData and loop over the form’s entries on submission.

Later in this book in Chapter Nine, you’ll reuse some of the functionality mocked in Storybook to develop the login view in the application.

Examples in this chapter are practical, so the potential of form-associated custom elements may not be obvious. Adding ElementInternals to a custom element gives you the best of both worlds:

  • Template and styling encapsulation with Shadow DOM
  • The ability to participate in form validation and submission

Form-associated custom elements don’t have to include a typical form control like input or textarea. You can craft new user interfaces and with ElementInternals have these custom experiences participate in forms like any other form control. That is the real potential of form-associated custom elements: completely new user interfaces that work seamlessly with HTML forms as if they were native form control in the browser.

In the next chapter, you’ll expand on the topic of forms by making the TextInputComponent follow Accessibility best practices, and you’ll enhance the submit button with another Web Components specification: customized built-in elements.

Customized built-in elements

Chapter Three

Introduction

The internet should be a place that is accessible and inclusive for everyone. When coding for the web browser, developers should consider users that require assistive devices to interact with the content. It could even be required by law. To conduct business with the U.S. federal government or follow best practices in accordance with the European Trade Commission (EU), web developers need to follow Web Content Accessibility Guidelines defined by the W3C Web Content Accessibility Group (WCAG).

In the previous chapter, I mentioned that ElementInternals provides the entire Accessibility Object Model (AOM) to a form-associated custom element. AOM is a browser specification that attempts to reduce the friction developers face when implementing accessible user interfaces. AOM provides properties on the DOM node that allow developers to programmatically read and write accessibility-based properties.

Prior to the addition of AOM, developers were limited to WAI-ARIA, a set of HTML attributes that provide context to assistive technologies. By providing an attribute such as aria-labelled-by, WAI-ARIA allowed engineers to provide context to screen readers.

Web developers tend to choose the path of least resistance, whether pressured by product owners or lack of knowledge. As an example, let’s look at the button type="submit" from the last chapter. Developers may not choose button element because the default styling is cumbersome to override. For whatever reason, a developer may opt to use a div and apply the WAI-ARIA role attribute to notify assistive devices this div is actually a button.

If you used the techniques in the previous two chapters to develop a new button component using autonomous custom elements, you’d declare a new class that extends from HTMLElement, although this comes at a similar cost as the example of the div. Since you’re not implementing a HTMLButtonElement, you lose all the accessibility characteristics of a native button, namely the ability for users to press the button using only the keyboard. HTMLButtonElement allows users to press Enter or Spacebar on their keyboard instead of a mouse click. To gain these same accessible behaviors, you’d have to implement them on the class that extends HTMLElement.

Customized built-in elements allow you to inherit the characteristics of native browser elements by giving you the ability to extend from their base class. By extending from HTMLButtonElement instead of HTMLElement, the component inherits all the behaviors of the native button element.

Registering customized built-in elements is done the same way. However, calling define requires a third argument that specifies an Object that sets the extends property to the tag name of the element that you’re extending from.

To use the customized built-in element in a template, the element must use the required is attribute set to the name of the element in the CustomElementRegistry. This is mainly so that browsers can parse the custom element from HTML source.

Customized built-in elements can be created dynamically with document.createElement by adding a second argument when calling the function.

At first, it may seem a little awkward that customized built-ins require different syntactical sugar or may behave differently from autonomous or form-associated custom elements, but the use value of customized built-in elements is undeniable. Being able to inherit user-agent supplied behaviors when developing custom elements ensures users are already familiar with the characteristics of the component. The complexity of the component source is reduced when developers don’t have to re-implement user-agent based behaviors. Customized built-in elements are essential in terms of accessibility because the component retains accessible behaviors supplied by the browser.

What you will build

One obvious use case for a customized built-in element is a button. In this chapter, you’ll code ButtonComponent, a customized built-in element that is used throughout the application. The component must work in and out of the context of HTMLFormElement. Looking at Figma, ButtonComponent has three different variants: primary, secondary, and icon. The component has different states for hover, active, focus, and disabled.

This exercise mostly involves styling the different states of ButtonComponent. Since you’ll retain all the accessibility characteristics of a button, there’s no need to include any logic on the class other than dealing with the various interaction states. If engineers wish to customize the button further, they can do so by extending the ButtonComponent class.

Only some native elements can encapsulate styling and template with Shadow DOM: HTMLBodyElement, HTMLDivElement, HTMLHeadingElement, HTMLParagraphElement, and HTMLSpanElement, which means the CSS for most customized built-in elements has to be in a <style> tag external to the element. You could, as a rule of thumb, add CSS classnames to customized built-in elements so they could be targeted via external stylesheet. Traditionally, the CSS would be declared in the <head>, but if the customized built-in element is used within the context of another element’s ShadowRoot, that styling won’t be able to cross the shadow boundary, leaving the element unstyled. To work around this limitation, later in this book, you’re going to code a function that traverses DOM for the nearest ShadowRoot and injects the styles there. Since the button is slotted into the CardComponent template, it’s exposed to Light DOM and can be styled with a stylesheet in the document.head. As you code more complex custom elements, this will not always be the case.

After completing the styling for ButtonComponent, you’ll circle back and fix accessibility issues that remain in the form. Using a screen reader, you’ll make the form accessible by utilizing the Accessibility Object Model on the ElementInternals interface or through the use of WAI-ARIA attributes.

What you will learn

  • What is a customized built-in element?
  • What are the benefits of a customized built-in element?
  • What is the Accessibility Object Model? (AOM)
  • How do I provide a label for screen readers?
  • How do I use a screen reader to test for accessibility?
  • How do I provide an accessible validation message for screen readers?
  • Why doesn’t a customized built-in element work in Safari?

Acceptance criteria

  • ButtonComponent displays primary, secondary, and icon buttons
  • ButtonComponent is styled properly in the context of another element’s ShadowRoot, or via stylesheet declared in <head>
  • User can navigate the form using a screen reader

Getting started

Navigate to the project directory.

Checkout a new branch named chapter-3 from where you left off at the end of chapter 2.

Run Storybook using yarn. Storybook should appear, and the development environment is ready.

Scaffolding ButtonComponent

If the following steps look familiar by now, that’s because they resemble the same process for scaffolding TextInputComponent and CardComponent from the previous two chapters. First, you’ll declare a new custom element, this time registering the component as a customized built-in element. Then, you’ll import that component into a new story file where all the ButtonComponent stories will be declared. Throughout the chapter, you will code several stories to visualize the different variants of the ButtonComponent: primary, secondary, and icon, as well as at least one story that demonstrates the disabled state.

To get started, make a new TypeScript file called Button.ts in a new directory: packages/component/src/button.

In the input directory, make a new file and name it TextInput.ts.

In Button.ts, export a new class named ButtonComponent that extends HTMLButtonElement. Give the class a constructor, making sure to call super so that when the component initializes, it also instantiates the constructor of the HTMLButtonElement class.

One difference you should notice by now between ButtonComponent and the last two components you coded is the class no longer extends from HTMLElement but instead extends from HTMLButtonElement, an interface that provides methods and properties common to the native button element. Find a complete reference of HTMLButtonElement on MDN.

There are at least two advantages gained by extending from HTMLButtomElement as opposed to HTMLElement. HTMLButtonElement natively participates in forms by implementing the form, formAction, formEnctype, formMethod, formNoValidate, and formTarget properties. If you had opted for a form-associated custom element, you would have to provide the ElementInternals interface to make the button participate in the form. In the above example, you don’t have to do anything. You get form participation for free. By extending from a native element, the component inherits all the behaviors of that element. Another example may not be evident looking at the documentation for HTMLButtonElement. The button element includes features that promote accessibility out of the box, including the ability to press the button using the Enter key or Spacebar. Had you chosen to extend from HTMLElement, you would have to duplicate this functionality with a custom implementation.

Like the previous two components, you register the ButtonComponent on the CustomElementRegistry, this time passing in the optional third argument, an Object with extends property set to button. The extends property is necessary to tell the browser you’re registering the element that progressively enhances a native element.

Create a new file named Button.stories.js in the same directory as Button.ts.

Import ButtonComponent into Button.stories.js.

Declare the story by exporting a default Object that sets the title property as Components/Inputs/Button and the component property as in-button.

Before you declare the first story template, import html from the lit-html package since Storybook uses LitHTML to render Web Components.

Declare a new const named Template, and make it equal to a function that returns html. Pass a new template string to html, and include a button element in the template, making sure to use start and end button tags. A quirky requirement of customized built-in elements is the requirement of declaring the is attribute on the button element, setting the name of the registered element, in this case, in-button.

To support the three button variants: primary, secondary, and icon, you could set an attribute and use observedAttributes and attributeChangedCallback, but that seems like overkill when you could achieve the same with a CSS classname. The variants, after all, are just various styles of the same button element. We need a way to set the variant in the story, so pass in the variant using destructuring to the class attribute. Finally, pass in a label in the same way, setting the content of the button element with the value of label.

Next, export a const named Primary and make it equal to Template.bind({}). Set the Primary.args, passing in the variant and label. This establishes the first story for the primary variant in Storybook.

Styling ButtonComponent

While extending HTMLButtomElement has benefits, it means that Shadow DOM is not available in the context of ButtonComponent. That’s because the native button element cannot have a ShadowRoot, so we lose the ability to encapsulate styling for the customized built-in element. That means you’ll have to rely on CSS styles in a <style> tag external to the button element. Since you won’t be able to target the button with :host, specify a unique CSS class name that can be used to select the custom element. The only place to do this safely in a customized built-in element is the connectedCallback lifecycle.

In Button.ts, add the connectedCallback method and use the add method on classList to give the button a class name when added to DOM.

Inspect the element with Dev Tools and notice the primary and in-button class names are set, the first by Storybook and the second through the connectedCallback. The element should have the is attribute set to in-button, the name of the registered customized built-in element.

Primary

You don’t have to give up modern conveniences like CSS-in-JS even though the CSS has to be declared in an external <style> tag that can be accessed by instances of ButtonComponent. In Button.ts, declare a const named buttonStyles and make it equal to a template string. Select the primary button variant with the selector .in-button.primary and set the styling per the mockup in Figma.

To get the button styles in DOM, add a new method on the ButtonComponent class called addStylsheet.

In this method, create a new style element using document.createElement and set the id attribute to in-button-style. Using textContent, set the buttonStyles you declared earlier as the content of the style element, then append the style element to the document.head. When there are multiple instances of ButtonComponent in the same view, we don’t want to keep adding the same stylesheet to document.head, so implement a conditional that prevents this from happening.

When you are finished coding addStylesheet, make sure to call the method in the connectedCallback.

In Storybook, you should see a button that is styled as the primary variant.

Inspect the<head> tag in Dev Tools and observe a new <style> tag with the CSS declared as buttonStyles injected into the style element. If you have trouble seeing the tag, ensure the JavaScript context is set to storybook-preview-iframe in Dev Tools.

That’s it for the default primary styles. Style the secondary and icon variants before you work on the styles for each button state: disabled, active, and focused. That’ll save time because looking at the Figma, it appears all the buttons share the styling for the various states, while they differ in their default styles.

Secondary

Declare another story in Button.stories.js for the secondary button variant, naming the story Secondary and making sure to call Template.bind({}). Pass in variant and label through Secondary.args, setting the variant to secondary.

In Figma, the secondary buttons appear to have a white background with a blue border. The label is the same color as the border. Update buttonStyles with the CSS for the secondary button. To select secondary buttons, use the .in-button.secondary selector.

In Button.ts, style the element based on the mockup in Figma by adding the secondary styles to buttonStyles.

When you are finished, the default secondary button should be styled like the example below.

Icon

Scaffolding the icon button variant requires a little more work than primary and secondary. You’ll need a way to source an SVG to place in the button in lieu of the text label. FontAwesome is installed in the repository to help you achieve this goal. In Figma, the example icon button is used throughout the application as the “close” button. This icon could be used to close dialogs and menus. The closest icon FontAwesome provides is a “plus” icon, so you’ll need to use CSS to rotate the “plus” 45 degrees to display a “cross.” You can achieve this style through a CSS classname modifier specific to the close button. While all icon variants should use the CSS classname icon, this specific icon will require the CSS classname icon-close.

FontAwesome provides a package called @fortawesome/fontawesome-free, which is already installed in the repository and integrated with Storybook. In Button.stories.js, use the window.FontAwesome.icon method to select the “plus” SVG. Set a let named icon to the SVG returned by window.FontAwesome.icon.

If you inspect icon, you’ll observe the Object provides an interface for consuming an SVG. The SVG can be accessed via icon.node[0]. In case you need to process the SVG later, set a new const named svg to the SVG node.

Scaffold the Icon story, making sure to export a const named Icon. This time, specify the variant as icon icon-close. Since variant merely sets the class attribute on the button element in Template, the element can now be styled with both classnames. Set the label property to the svg. The SVG node will be inserted into the content of the button element using LitHTML.

Now that everything is scaffolded for the icon variant, proceed to style the button. In buttonStyles, select the icon variant with .in-button.icon CSS selector, and while referencing Figma, style the element in the CSS declaration block.

To ensure the SVG fits within the dimensions of the 44px button, select the svg with a CSS selector and style its width and height to 100%. Since the icon variant has some padding, the SVG will actually display smaller. In order to transform the “plus” into a “cross”, select the svg contained by the element with class name .icon-close and use CSS transform to rotate the SVG 45deg.

When you are finished, the icon variant should appear by default as it does in Figma.

Interaction States

Referencing Figma again, you notice each button variant shares the same interaction states. Let’s start by styling the focus state. To style the focus state, select each of the variants with the :focus CSS pseudo selector. In the CSS declaration block, style the focus state as it appears in Figma.

The active state is styled in the same way, this time selecting each variant with the :active pseudo selector. Style the active state according to the mockup.

All the variants should now have the focus and active states styled. Test out these new behaviors in Storybook by navigating to the Primary, Secondary, and Icon stories. Click on the whitespace in the Storybook canvas and then focus on the button element by pressing the Tab key. With the button focused, press the Spacebar or Return key on the keyboard to see the active state appear.

Buttons have a disabled state as well, usually set with the disabled attribute on the button element. To achieve the disabled state in Storybook, declare a new template in Button.stories.js named DisabledTemplate. This template should look remarkably similar to Template. However, the disabled attribute is set.

In Button.ts, style the different variants using the CSS attribute selector [disabled] and style the disabled state per the mockup in Figma.

When the button is disabled, the element should not appear focused or active. This means you need a way to override the focus and active styles declared earlier. Using CSS specificity, select each of the variants with :focus and :active pseudo selectors, this time increasing the specificity of the selection by adding the [disabled] attribute selector. Style the disabled button like the mockup.

When you are finished styling the disabled state, the button should appear like below.

So far, coding the ButtonComponent has been an exercise in styling the different states of the button with CSS. Since the button element cannot use Shadow DOM to encapsulate CSS styles, you injected a stylesheet into the <head> and selected CSS classnames applied to the instance of ButtonComponent to style the variants of the button. It’s worth noting the CSS for ButtonComponent could be part of a global stylesheet, but as you’ll observe in later chapters, when ButtonComponent is a child of another component’s ShadowRoot, the shadow boundary will block any global styling. You’ll account for this behavior in later chapters.

Since ButtonComponent extends from HTMLButtonElement, you didn’t have to implement behaviors of the button element. If ButtonComponent had extended from HTMLElement you would have had to implement event listeners to provide the same accessibility behaviors of HTMLButtonElement, namely the ability for users to activate the button when pressing the Select or Return keys on the keyboard.

Making the form accessible

The decisions we’ve made have so far developing the login form resulted in a half-baked accessible experience for users who rely on the keyboard to navigate. TextInputComponent has some accessibility limitations. We’ve provided a CSS classname to provide visual feedback, but this poses a problem for the visually impaired, who cannot observe the feedback when the input becomes invalid. Furthermore, validations appended to Shadow DOM cannot be accessed by screen readers unless we provide some additional context using WAI-ARIA.

While ButtonComponent is useable via keyboard input by virtue of extending from HTMLButtonElement, the addition of an SVG in the icon variant prohibits visually impaired users from understanding the context of the button element. Screen readers rely on the content of the button to provide a label, which the primary and secondary button variants handle already. The icon variant lacks a text label that screen readers can analyze and read aloud to the user.

In this section, you’ll use WAI-ARIA attributes to solve two distinct problems with the form:

  • Screen readers cannot analyze the button label in the icon variant
  • Screen readers cannot read the validation messages so that users who rely on screen readers can understand what is needed to validate each form field

First, you’ll add ButtonComponent to the Form story in TextInput.stories.js so that you can use FormTemplate as your development environment. After a brief introduction to using a screen reader during development, you’ll use WAI-ARIA attributes to provide all the necessary context the screen reader requires to aid in navigating the form.

Button Form

In this chapter, you’ve developed ButtonComponent in isolation, so let’s see what happens when you integrate the component into the existing Form story in TextInput.stories.js.

Import ButtonComponent into TextInput.stories.js.

Swap out the input type="submit" in FormTemplate for the button. Set the is attribute to in-button on the button element in FormTemplate so that the browser can interpret the buttons as a customized built-in element. Add the appropriate classnames to the submit button. According to Figma, the submit button is a primary variant of the ButtonComponent.

That’s it! Since ButtonComponent is a customized built-in element, integration was a snap. The elements in the layout appear very close vertically and don’t have the same margin between them as the mockup in Figma. To fix this issue with the layout, add a global style to packages/style/style.css. Select each instance of TextInputComponent with a CSS classname: .form-control and set margin-bottom.

For the remainder of this chapter, use the Form and Icon stories as a test bed for providing accessibility features to ButtonComponent and TextInputComponent.

Using a screen reader

Screen readers are applications that blind, visually impaired, and dyslexic people use to interact with operating systems. Through the use of a synthesized voice and other visual cues, screen readers provide contextual information about what the user currently has focused in a user interface. NVDA is the most popular screen reader application for Windows, while VoiceOver is built into MacOS and other Apple operating systems.

If you’ve never used a screen reader application before, follow the steps below to install and open NVDA or VoiceOver for Windows and MacOS, respectively.

Windows

NVDA, short for NonVisual Desktop Access, is a Windows application available for free on the Microsoft Store. To install NVDA, sign in to the Microsoft Store in the Microsoft Store application.

After you have signed in to the Microsoft Store, search for NVDA, select the application in the search results, and click the Install button. Follow on-screen prompts to install NVDA.

Once NVDA is installed, access NVDA application preferences in the Windows Taskbar.

NVDA uses a synthesized voice to announce contextual information about the currently focused user interface for visually impaired and blind users in Microsoft Windows.

To stop NVDA at any time, click the NVDA icon in the Windows Taskbar and choose Exit from the dialog.

MacOS

VoiceOver is a screen reader provided by Apple Inc. in all of its operating systems. In MacOS, access VoiceOver in the System Preferences Accessibility Pane. When you click Enable VoiceOver, a contextual overlay appears in the lower left of the screen. VoiceOver announces what is currently in focus through a synthesized voice.

During development, you may have to change context rapidly between IDE and browser. If the synthesized voice becomes a burden, you can turn it off by clicking Open VoiceOver Utility… in the System Preferences Accessibility Pane. When the VoiceOver Utility Pane appears, select Speech in the Sidebar, and click Mute Speech.

Another option you may find useful during development is the ability to hide the VoiceOver cursor. In your IDE, the VoiceOver cursor displays an overlayed cursor for the visually impaired. However, this can interfere with typing for some users.

Once you have a screen reader installed, proceed to the following sections. If you’ve never used a screen reader before, hopefully you’ll find a process for developing with a screen reader that works best for you.

Providing context to the icon variant

Earlier in this chapter, you developed the icon variant of ButtonComponent. However, since the label is effectively replaced by an SVG, screen readers can no longer analyze the content of the button element.

Depending on your operating system, activate NVDA or VoiceOver and leave them running when testing your changes during development for the remainder of this chapter.

If you haven’t already, activate the screen reader application and navigate to the Primary button story in Storybook. Click on the whitespace in the Storybook canvas to give it focus, then press the Tab key to focus the primary button. Observe how the screen reader announces the label, followed by the element name.

Navigate to the Icon story and focus the close button. Notice how the screen reader only provides the element because there is no contextual information that labels the button element.

To provide context for the screen reader, you’ll need to use WAI-ARIA attributes, namely aria-labelledby and hidden.

Icon.args need to be updated to support the SVG and the label. This change will conflict with other stories in the same file. So you don’t interfere with other stories in Button.stories.js, make a new template for the icon variant named IconTemplate based off the existing Template.

Don’t forget to update the Icon story, which should now reference IconTemplate.
