Update Icon.args to support both a label and SVG, making sure the destructured properties in IconTemplate match the names of each property on Icon.args. Set the value of the label property to Close, and move the SVG to a new property named svg.

Update IconTemplate to passing the svg where label was once in the template.

Next, create a <span> tag before the svg and set the span element’s content with the label. To hide the span visually, add the hidden attribute, which tells the browser this element should be hidden from view. Add the id attribute to the span element, setting the id to close-button-label. This id is required for the WAI-ARIA attribute aria-labelledby, which needs a unique id.

On the button element, set aria-labelledby to the id of the span, linking the two elements together for screen readers.

Finally, to ensure that screen readers do not analyze the SVG, set the aria-hidden attribute to true on the svg element in Button.stories.js.

Navigate again to the Icon story in Storybook and focus the icon button with the screen reader activated. Notice how the screen reader now behaves the same way as if the button was directly labeled, like in the case of primary and secondary buttons.

aria-labelledby provides a pointer to an element with an id that contains the label for the button element. You visually hid the span element using hidden and used the aria-hidden attribute to hide the SVG from screen readers. A combination of all of these WAI-ARIA attributes allows the icon variant of ButtonComponent to work with a screen reader.

Providing validation messages to screen readers

The validation messages that appear when TextInputComponent is invalid are a custom implementation. Browsers don’t have a native container for validation messages that screen readers automatically analyze. While the validation messages appear visually, we need to provide the same contextual information for the screen reader. This can be achieved through the use of WAI-ARIA attributes aria-describedby, aria-role, aria-live, and aria-invalid.

In TextInputComponent template, set an id attribute to message on the messages container. Link the input element to the messages container by setting the aria-describedby attribute to the same id: message. Since the messages container is just a div, give the screen reader more information about this element. aria-role set to alert notifies the screen reader this element contains an alert notification, while the aria-live attribute set to assertive gives the messages contained in the div element precendence over other announcements made by the screen reader.

Navigate to the Form story and test the validations with a screen reader. Notice how the application reads back the messages. This is a huge win for accessibility because each validation message provides context for how the user can correct the form field.

We can do a little bit more work to enhance the functionality for screen readers during validation while also making the user experience for everyone else much better. Right now, when the form field is invalid, the validation messages are not hidden until the input element is blurred. If the validations were cleared as the user was typing, it would allow the visually impaired to focus on what they are typing rather than listen to the feedback of the validation messages. When the user blurs, validation will kick in and announce validation messages again, but not until then.

There’s also one other problem we need to solve. Currently, the input element receives a classname error to show the field is invalid, but there isn’t similar feedback for the screen reader. Correct this behavior by finding where the error classname is set in validator.ts and use the aria-invalid attribute set to true to notify screen readers the input is invalid.

To clear out the validation messages as the user types, add a new onkeyup event listener in the TextInputComponent connectedCallback lifecycle. In the event listener callback, call a new method on TextInputComponent called onChange.

In the onChange method, clear out the content of the messages element, remove the error classname and aria-invalid attribute from the input, and optionally, update the form with the value of the input.

Test the new functionality in the Form story. When an instance of TextInputComponent is invalid and the user starts typing, the element should appear focused and no longer display validation messages until the user blurs and the form control is invalid. When development is complete you may turn off the screen reader.

Testing ButtonComponent

We could set up an integration test for ButtonComponent. However, that kind of end-to-end testing will be reserved for part three of this book when you develop a login form in the context of an application. Snapshot tests provide the most value at this point in time. After developing several interaction states for ButtonComponent, you can validate the styling of the button most effectively with snapshots.

Ensure Storybook is running in a Terminal window.

With Storybook running, generate snapshots for the component in another Terminal window.

When running the snapshots you’ll notice a failure in the Form snapshot. Open the image file that displays the differences between the previous snapshot and current in the directory packages/component/src/input/snapshots/diff_output. Upon inspection, you realize the diff is because you added a bottom margin with CSS to the form controls in the layout. No harm, no foul. This change was intentional. To fix the snapshots, delete the diff_output directory and delete the existing snapshot.

Run the snapshot tests again. Since you deleted the offending snapshot, a new file will be generated in place.

After snapshots have been generated for each story, add them to your commit.

Before concluding this chapter, check if any tests are broken due to the most recent changes. You did refactor the code in packages/component/src/input/TextInput.stories.js quite a bit to include the HTMLButtonElement element in the template.

A test failure happens in the TextInputComponent test suite due to a timeout. The test cannot find an element with the class name .submit. That happened because we failed to give the button element this class name in packages/component/src/input/TextInput.stories.js.

Update FormTemplate in packages/component/src/input/TextInput.stories.js with the class name the test expects.

Run the tests again to observe All specs passed!.

Commit your changes to complete this section. Now you’ve created snapshots for ButtonComponent let’s review the content of Chapter Three.

Summary

In this chapter, you learned how to implement ButtonComponent with customized built-in elements. By extending HTMLButtonElement instead of HTMLElement, you retained the accessibility characteristics of the native button. The primary benefit of customized built-in elements is the ability to extend existing HTML elements, thus retaining their default behaviors. In the example of the button component, this meant you didn’t have to attach event listeners that handle events from keyboard input because the button element natively activates using the select or enter keys. Retaining the default behavior of native elements comes at a cost. For those elements that cannot implement Shadow DOM, styling has to be handled via a <style> tag either in the <head>, or when applicable, the ShadowRoot of another custom element. In later chapters, you’ll correct this behavior when you encounter it.

You also learned how form-associated custom elements participate in accessibility. Since TextInputComponent implemented formAssociated, instances of the element can be associated with label elements like any native form control. When you used a screen reader to navigate the form, you found the user was missing context from the validation messages found in the ShadowRoot. To provide appropriate validation messages to the screen reader, you implemented WAI-ARIA attributes.

So far, you’ve covered the three kinds of custom elements: autonomous, form-associated, and customized built-in elements. In the FormCard story, you’ve experienced how all three custom element specifications work together to provide a custom, accessible, and reusable interface. You also learned about the other technologies that comprise the set of specifications known as Web Components: Shadow DOM and HTML templates.

This marks the completion of Part One of this book. You may be thinking, “if I just learned about the full specification, why would I need to learn more?”

In Part Two, you’ll handle some of the quirks and features of custom elements in a more elegant way by developing a micro-library that enables custom element development. In subsequent chapters, you’ll implement more complex interface patterns with custom elements and learn how to distribute a UI component library that contains Web Components.

In Part Three, you’ll reuse much of the code mocked in each Storybook story to develop a web application with custom elements, learning how to handle client-side routing and server-side rendering along the way.

Part Two

Part Two

UI Library

Now that you’ve learned about the set of specifications known as Web Components, it’s time to streamline custom element development by coding a micro-library that will help you wrangle the component template, styling, and registering custom elements with the registry. After coding reusable functions to use throughout your components, you’ll learn how to develop more complex component layouts with Web Components: TableComponent, and DialogComponent. Through the exercises in Chapters Five and Six, you’ll expand your knowledge of HTML templates and learn different methods custom elements can use to communicate. In Chapter Seven, you’ll package the custom elements you coded in previous chapters into a reusable UI component library for distribution.

What you will learn

While developing editable table, checkbox and dialog components with Web Components, you’ll explore the following concepts:

  • How to code reusable functions that handle common tasks in custom element development
  • How to implement TypeScript decorators to streamline UI component development
  • The differences between autonomous, form-associated and customized built-in elements
  • How to dispatch and listen for CustomEvent in custom elements
  • How to effectively pass data through custom element attributes
  • How to code a dynamic table with custom elements
  • How to architect a solution for stacking dialogs in a web application
  • How to handle communication between top level and deeply nested custom elements using BroadcastChannel
  • How to implement a separation of concerns in complex custom element layouts
  • Best practices for distributing a UI library with Web Components
  • How to work effectively in a monorepo that contains separate packages for a micro-library and UI library

Developing in Part Two

You’ll use Storybook as the primary development environment throughout Part Two. For each chapter, run yarn storybook in the Terminal. Every change made to the codebase will be reflected in the Storybook UI while Storybook is running in Terminal. When you are finished developing, cancel the server by holding down Ctrl on the keyboard and pressing C.

Micro-library

Chapter Four

Introduction

In Part One, we relied heavily on the set of specifications that make up Web Components: Custom Elements, HTML Templates, Shadow DOM, and CustomElementRegistry. The main benefits Web Components bring to the table: reuse, interoperable, accessible, having a long lifespan, are due to their reliance on browser specifications. Had we adopted a library or framework, we may have lost some or all of these characteristics in the user interfaces built with it. UI components coded with some libraries aren’t interoperable with other JavaScript libraries or frameworks, which puts a hard limit on reuse.

Even though we gain these benefits from Web Components, we have lost any benefit JavaScript libraries have to offer. Frameworks and libraries like React, Vue, Angular and Svelte often provide an abstraction around browser specifications. Under the hood, frameworks are built with TypeScript or JavaScript, but behind the wheel engineers have an interface for component-level development. React, for example, famously opted for a purely functional approach, giving engineers “hooks” to manage side effects in user interfaces. JavaScript libraries and frameworks exist mostly to provide architectural patterns that make life easier on the part of the web developer, offering features not available with browser specifications alone, like data binding and state management. As browser standards evolve over time, the HTML living standard may gain some of the most popular features from JavaScript libraries. Web Components may gain more specifications that make styling components easier or enable data to be passed more efficiently and securely between components, for example.

What if we could retain the benefits of Web Components while also gaining the architectural design of a JavaScript framework? Indeed, many have tried. webcomponents.dev tracks over fifty implementations of custom elements coded with a JavaScript library. This service provides performance and scalability metrics on a semi-annual basis to help inform the decision making process when selecting a library. With so many options for Web Component development, it may seem daunting to pick a library or futile to develop one on your own. It must be really difficult, right?

In this chapter we’ll demystify the inner workings of Web Component libraries. Using TypeScript decorators, we’ll develop a new interface that simplifies development, but doesn’t compromise performance. The micro-library we’ll code optimizes to less than 1Kb of minified JavaScript (optimized with brotli). Components we’ve already developed will transform from something like this:

to instead use a TypeScript decorator named Component like this:

Decorators are denoted by the @ symbol, followed by the name of the decorator function, in this case Component. In the above example, the Component function is called with a single argument: an Object where the developer can declare the tag name, CSS style, and HTML template.

The side effect of using a class decorator to handle template and styling is readily apparent. Not only have we abstracted the creation of Shadow DOM, we’ve removed the line of code responsible for registering the class definition with the CustomElementRegistry. The constructor is much cleaner now. Component logic that should instantiate in the constructor is no longer aside template specific code. That’s because all of that code has been abstracted to reusable function named attachShadow.

Decorators are found in other programming languages but currently not in the ECMAScript standard, although a proposal exists. You can’t use a decorator and expect it to run in the browser, at least not yet. TypeScript has supported a decorator pattern for quite some time, anticipating the time when decorators land in ECMAScript. We can use decorators in TypeScript now by configuring the tsconfig.json with the experimentalDecorators property. You don’t need to change the tsconfig.json because the repository is already setup to work with decorators.

Don’t let that property spook you just because “experimental” is in the name. Several applications in production right now use TypeScript decorators. The entire Angular ecosystem has relied on TypeScript decorators since Angular 2. When TypeScript compiles down to JavaScript, a minimal amount of code is injected that polyfills the decorator pattern for ES2015 class.

In addition to making a class decorator that allows you declare tag name, styling and template with a cleaner interface than before, you’ll also code a method decorator that simplifies binding event listeners to custom elements. Instead of typing this.addEventListener('click', this.onClick), what if you could decorate the onClick method and still provide the same functionality? It could look something like this:

If all of this seems foreign, don’t fret! Coding decorators is just like coding any JavaScript function. Providing these framework-like features to custom elements may be easier than you think. This chapter provides step-by-step instructions for coding the decorators and applying them to the components you’ve already developed.

What is a micro-library?

The definition of micro-library is kind of murky because over time engineers may have used the term in different contexts. For the purposes of this chapter, let’s define micro-library as a collection of prewritten code used for common development tasks that has a small footprint. Micro-libraries may have similar functionality as much larger libraries, but with way less code that optimizes down to a few Kb or maybe even less than 1 Kb. That’s why they are “micro”. This trend isn’t by any means new. Micro-libraries have existed for awhile. Famously, Preact is a ~3 Kb alternative to the ~45 Kb React. Micro-libraries exist, in part, to provide a more performant alternative to popular JavaScript libraries. In the context of custom elements, micro-libraries are an interesting solution because we can gain the functionality of a JavaScript library with little expense to performance.

Coding in a monorepo

In Part One you mainly relied on the yarn storybook command for your development environment. The components you developed so far are part of the @in/ui package in the packages/component directory. The package name is defined in the package.json. If you inspect that file you would find several scripts declared on the package.json. These scripts are pointers to different build tasks for the package. That’s right! You’ve been developing in a npm package this entire time. In Chapter Seven we’ll return to this package.json in a lesson about UI library best practices, but for now it’s important you’re aware this file exists.

Starting with this chapter, you’re going to branch out and work in other parts of the monorepo. When developing against the micro-library, you’ll code in files found in the packages/common directory. Essentially, you are going to export parts of the library for use in the @in/ui package. For any code you write in the @in/common package to be used in the @in/ui package, you’ll need to build the @in/common package first, then start refactoring code in the @in/ui package.

This process may seem confusing at first, mainly because IDE like VS Code and Storybook may react strangely to updates in @in/common that are being referenced by files in the @in/ui package. That’s due to VS Code and Storybook not interpreting dependencies in the monorepo as intuitively as we may like.

Any time you update the micro-library in the @in/common package and run the build, you may need to restart Storybook or potentially VS Code to force update the TypeScript AST.

Even with the quirky nature of the monorepo in regards to TypeScript compilation, we’ll achieve interesting results. We’ll be able to import function from one package into another as if the package were already published on npm.

What you will build

In this chapter you’ll identify reusable parts of component and abstract logic away from each component implementation in a functional manner. You’ll code a class decorator that handles declaration of a component selector, styling and template. In the next section, you’ll learn how to use method decorators to attach event listeners to DOM elements. By the end of this chapter TextInputComponent, ButtonComponent, and CardComponent will be refactored to use the new decorator pattern. In following chapters, you’ll use and build upon the micro-library where needed.

What you will learn

You’ll explore the following concepts:

  • How to code reusable functions that handle common tasks in custom elements
  • Code function that appends templates to Shadow DOM
  • Code function that handles component CSS styles
  • Code function that handles templates to custom elements that cannot evoke Shadow DOM
  • How to use a class decorator to declare the selector, template and style
  • How to use a method decorator to handle event listeners
  • When to apply reusable functions in everyday development

Acceptance criteria

  • TextInputComponent, ButtonComponent and CardComponent have been refactored to use the new decorators
  • Component and Listen decorators are exported from common package
  • html, css, attachShadow, attachStyle and attachTemplate functions are exported from @in/common package
  • All tests are passing

Class Decorator

Implementing a class decorator is going to improve the ergonomics of Web Component development quite significantly. We’ll enhance the class-based implementation which custom elements rely on by cleaning up each constructor, choosing to move the declaration of a HTML template and CSS to a new function that decorates the class. This, combined with abstracting template and style generation to reusable function will have the positive effect of reducing the boilerplate for each component. For example, when you are finished with this section, ButtonComponent will look something like this.

We’re working in the packages/common directory of the monorepo for the first time, which currently only has one source file: index.ts. To keep this package organized, we should figure out a way to divide the code into logical chunks. Making a directory for all decorators seems prudent, then organizing the decorators by function.

To start developing the component decorator, create a new directory in packages/common/src/decorator, then make a new file at packages/common/src/decorator/index.ts, and another file at packages/common/src/decorator/component.ts.

Any file named index.ts manages exports for several files in the same directory. Other files in a directory contain library code.

Open packages/common/src/decorator/component.ts in your IDE to begin.

Define the Interface

First let’s define the interface used by the component decorator. We’ll need this interface to keep the first argument of the decorator function type safe. Declare a new interface named ElementMeta and ensure it is exported with the export keyword.

There are three properties on this interface we should define: selector, style, and template. All three properties are optional, denoted by the ? prior to :. Each of these properties are optional to allow flexibility for the end-user. selector will be used to automatically call customElements.define in the context of the decorator, but what if the end-user for some reason has to register components in some other way? The user could omit the selector and register the component however they like. There are times an engineer may want to style the component, or not. Alternatively, there may be no need for a template, perhaps only styling. Making each property optional allows for flexibility, but as we’ll observe programmatically, we’ll have to check each property on ElementMeta exists and react accordingly.

Component Decorator

TypeScript class decorators are factory functions, that is, they return a function that constructs an Object. The Object we’re concerned with is the class definition of the component using this decorator. Based on the values of properties on the ElementMeta, we want to modify the prototype of the class so we can use those properties to register the component with the CustomElementRegistry and instantiate a HTML template with Shadow DOM.

The basic structure of the function is as follows: Declare a new function named Component and make sure it’s exportable with the export keyword. Name the first argument of the function meta and type define the argument with the interface you just created: ElementMeta. return a function. The first argument of this function is defined by TypeScript when you use Component in the context of a class decorator. target is the class definition of the class that is being decorated. Inside this factory function, return the class definition. target should be type defined as any here because so many different class will use the decorator. It would be difficult to implement type safety here, nor should we.

What happens before the target is returned is the most interesting part of the class decorator. Before we start modifying the class definition, let’s put a fail-safe mechanism in for users who haven’t specified an ElementMeta in the first argument of Component.

The above conditional checks if meta is undefined and when truthy, displays a console error for developers in Dev Tools, then aborts the rest of the algorithm that depends on ElementMeta.

We have two objectives for the class decorator: register the component using the selector property, then add metadata on the class definition to later append a HTML template to Shadow DOM using the style and template properties on the ElementMeta.

Let’s start with registering the component via the decorator function. In the factory function, reference the selector and pass it and the class definition, here named target, to customElements.define.

This one line allows the end-user to omit a call from customElements.define in their implementation, as you’ll later observe when refactoring TextInputComponent, ButtonComponent, and CardComponent, but the user has the option to ignore selector entirely in the ElementMeta, so be sure to wrap the call to define in a conditional.

That was easy enough, although we’re not yet using the class decorator for its main function: modifying the prototype of the class it decorates. This just happens to be a convenient place to also make the call to customElements.define. We can’t use this space to call attachShadow and create a HTML template, then append it to the shadowRoot like we’ve done in previous chapters, because the class decorator doesn’t have access to the instance of the class, only the definition.

Class decorators are a place where you can modify the prototype of a class, so that’s exactly what we’re going to do. We’re going to store the ElementMeta passed through the Component function arguments on the prototype of the class, so we can later access the template and style in the constructor of the component class.

Set a new property called elementMeta on the prototype to the meta that was passed into the Component function.

If we want to avoid the style and template properties from ever being undefined, here is a good place for some conditionals that set both of these properties to empty string in the case they are undefined.

Abstracting attachShadow

Now that we have ElementMeta stored on the prototype of any class using the Component decorator, we can write a reusable function that could be used in the constructor of the same class to instantiate Shadow DOM much like we already did in the components developed in Part One. By abstracting this logic to a reusable function we can reduce several lines of code in each component implementation down to one line.

Basically we want to take something like this…

and reduce it to one line.

The first argument of attachShadow is the instance of the class which in the constructor you can reference as this. The second argument is the Object that configures the call to element.attachShadow. According to MDN, this Object can accept three fields: mode and delegatesFocus. The type definition exported from TypeScript’s lib.dom.d.ts called ShadowRootInit reveals a third field: slotAssignment. You’ve set the fields on this Object in prior chapters for TextInputComponent, ButtonComponent, and CardComponent.

To start development of this new function, make a new directory named template in packages/common/src and create a new file in that directory named index.ts. Create another file in the directory named shadow.ts.

In packages/common/src/template/shadow.ts, create a new function named attachShadow and export it from the file. Declare two arguments for attachShadow: context and options, making options optional with ? and type defining context as any for now and options as ShadowRootInit, a type definition exported from lib.dom.d.ts.

Follow up in packages/common/src/template/index.ts and ensure attachShadow is exported for the main index.ts.

Finally in packages/common/index.ts export the attachShadow function.

Jumping back to packages/common/src/template/shadow.ts, fill in the algorithm for attachShadow, referencing the constructor in ButtonComponent at packages/component/src/button/Button.ts as a guide. Make a const named shadowRoot, type defined as ShadowRoot, equal to context.attachShadow. Since we’ve opted to make options optional, we need to at the very least give context.attachShadow the minimum ShadowRootInit, which requires mode.

On the next line, make a const named template equal to document.createElement('template'). This line creates a new HTML template.

Set the content of the HTML template using the ElementMeta stored on the prototype of whatever class will use this attachShadow function. Pass in context.elementMeta.style to a <style> tag and context.elementMeta.template afterward.

Finally, append a clone of the HTML template to the ShadowRoot.

Customized built-in elements

Supporting customized built-in elements in the Component decorator is actually fairly trivial, partly because we separated template logic (attachShadow) from the logic that registers the component with the CustomElementRegistry in Component. If you recall from Chapter 3, the only real difference between registering a customized built-in element is the third argument in the call to customElements.define. This Object is called ElementDefinitionOptions in lib.dom.d.ts.

The template logic is more of a challenge. In ButtonComponent we included logic to add a stylesheet for the component styles to the document.head when the element was instantiated on the page.

It would be a shame if we had to add this logic for every customized built-in element we wanted to develop. Similar to attachShadow, we’ll create a reusable function called attachStyle that appends the stylesheet where it needs to be located in DOM to effectively style the instance of the element. For elements that want to handle a template without Shadow DOM, we’ll make a function named attachTemplate that appends a template to the element instance.

ElementDefinitionOptions

Go ahead and add a new property to ElementMeta in packages/common/src/decorator/component.ts named custom and type define it as ElementDefinitionOptions. Make sure this new property is optional by declaring it with ?.

In the Component decorator, update the logic surrounding the call to customElements.define. Since the user can inject ElementDefinitionOptions through the ElementMeta and it’s optional, we’ll need to check if meta.custom exists and react accordingly. This is mostly architected this way due to the fact ElementDefinitionOptions has a required property: extends.

attachStyle and attachTemplate

With the absence of Shadow DOM in most elements, we’ll add new functions for handling the template and styling. So far, we have no need for a function that appends a template to an element, but we’ll create one anyways, anticipating the need for one in the future.

The style sheet is another problem.

Appending a style sheet to the custom element’s template without Shadow DOM poses a host of problems, so we opted to add the style tag to the document.head before. That implementation has another problem we haven’t encountered yet. Suppose there is a customized built-in element appended to the Shadow DOM of an autonomous custom element. Shadow DOM would prohibit the styles located in the <style> tag in document.head to penetrate the shadow boundary and style the customized built-in element. We’ve observed only CSS variables can penetrate the shadow boundary thus far. How could we work around this problem? Luckily we always know where the instance of the customized built-in element exists in DOM. We can write an algorithm that walks up the DOM tree, checking for shadow boundaries, and if the algorithm encounters one, append the <style> tag there, otherwise inject the style sheet into the document.head like we did before.

getRootNode is a method that exists on HTML elements to solve problems like this one. Calling getRootNode() returns the element’s known root, which could be a ShadowRoot or document. We need a function that returns the nearest root node so we can append the <style> tag to it.

In packages/common/src/template make a new file named style.ts.

In this new file, make a new function called closestRoot. This function takes one argument we’ll call base, and type define that argument as Element. closestRoot will return a Node, but unfortunately there isn’t a type definition in lib.dom.d.ts that can satisfy how we need to interact with the Node, so we’ll opt for any here.

Write an algorithm that checks if the base.getRootNode() equals document and if truthy return document.head, the Node we want to append the <style> tag. Next, check if base.getRootNode() is truthy, that means the algorithm has found a ShadowRoot, and return the Node returned by base.getRootNode(). Finally, return document.head if neither condition is satisfied. When you are done, the closestRoot function should be as follows:

Next, make a function named attachStyle, which takes one argument named context, type defined as any. This function doesn’t return anything so you can type define the return as void.

attachStyle needs to create a <style> tag, set the content of the element with the style property from elementMeta and then append the <style> tag to the closest root node. In attachStyle, make a new const called closest equal to closestRoot(context). Make another const named template and create a new HTMLStyleElement with it. Set the innerText of template to context.elementMeta.style. Finally, append the template to closest.

That would work if there was one instance of the element. That element would call attachStyle, appending the styling it requires to display correctly. If there are many instances of the element though, a <style> tag would get appended for each instance, so we need to find a way to mitigate that. One solution is to get the HTMLStyleElement a unique id and check if the element exists before appending another. We have a unique identifier of sorts: the selector property on ElementMeta. Use that to set an id attribute on the template, appending another string to the selector. -in-style should work. This reduces the chances of any two elements having the same unique id attribute.

Next, implement two checks to determine if the HTMLStyleElement already exists. If closest is equal to document.head, the element will have a tagName of HEAD. There we can query the document for the HTMLStyleElement. If closest has the method getElementById, it’s an Element near a shadow boundary, where we can implement a similar check. If either condition returns truthy, return so that any new HTMLStyleElement isn’t created. When you are finished, attachStyle should appear like below.

When you are finished coding attachStyle, ensure it is exported from style.ts.

Update packages/common/src/template/index.ts with the new export.

Finally export attachStyle from packages/common/index.ts.

Coding a generic attachTemplate

We have coverage for every template so far with attachShadow and attachStyle. These functions handle CSS styles scoped to any component implementation whether or not the component relies on Shadow DOM. ButtonComponent uses attachStyle, but doesn’t employ it’s own custom template. Shadow DOM is only supported by a handful of DOM elements. For the rest we may need a way to append a template directly to the element using the Component decorator. In this section, you’ll code a simple function named attachTemplate that appends a HTML template to the element.

Make a new file named template.ts in the packages/common/src/template directory.

In this file, export a new function named attachTemplate. This function takes one argument, the context, i.e. the element the template will be appended. context could be any element in DOM, so type define the argument as any. attachTemplate doesn’t return anything, so the return type is void.

attachTemplate should create a HTML template, set the template innerHTML to the content of the ElementMeta template property, then append a clone of the template to the context. When completed, the function should be as follows:

For some, this implementation may seem trivial, it simply takes a string and sets the content of the template, then appends that content to the element. This implementation could get more complicated over time. Perhaps the content needs to be injected into a child element or prepended before all other content in the element. Maybe the end-user wants to reference a HTML template already available in DOM, so we don’t need to create a new HTML template. These are valid use cases we may explore later, but for now we just need a function in the micro-library that can handle a very simple use case because the Component decorator supports a template string for any element, not just those that can use Shadow DOM.

Enhancing developer experience with html and css

You’ve completed the necessary tasks to provide a micro-library that handles the component selector, styling, and template. Each component looks much cleaner since refactoring them to use the new Component decorator. There’s still one problem to solve though. Our IDE has no way to detect the strings setting style and template in the decorator function are CSS and HTML. This means no syntax highlighting, which developers have come to expect.

It is possible to gain syntax highlighting in the template strings with a little help from simple function and the proper extension for your IDE. es6-string-html is an extension for VS Code that adds syntax highlighting support for multi-line JavaScript template strings. After installing this extension, nothing happens at first to CardComponent, TextInputComponent, or ButtonComponent. If you poke around a little, you may notice the template returned by FormTemplate in packages/component/src/input/TextInput.stories.js has HTML that is syntax highlighted. That’s due to the template string being set as an argument on the html function imported from lit-html. This function has some superpowers, like being able to interpet @event attribute syntax, but we haven’t yet chosen to adopt lit-html in the component library. As alluring as that may be, the micro-library we just developed will produce a smaller bundle than lit-html. We’d lose that benefit. For some people this may also be confusing, because isn’t a function supposed to be called with parenthesis like html()? It turns out there’s an odd quirk with JavaScript that allows the html function to be called with a single argument, the template string sitting directly beside html This is known as a tagged template literal and has been around since ES2015.

In addition to the VS Code extension, we’ll need two functions exported from @in/common that let the extension interpret the template strings as HTML and CSS. All that is really needed for the extension to work is the keyword html or css prior to the multi-line string.

In packages/common/src/template/template.ts, export two new functions named css and html. These two functions will handle tagged template literals for CSS and HTML templates. As tagged template literals, both functions should take a TemplateStringsArray named template in their first argument and return a string. template must be properly typed TemplateStringsArray because tagged template literals pass as an immutable array-like Object TypeScript defines as TemplateStringsArray. The second argument is a bit more ambiguous. Template literals in JavaScript can accept variable members used for string interpolation, with the notation ${}. TemplateStringsArray is an Array of string separated by any instances of string interpolation. These instances are found in another Array that can be spread from the second argument. The items in this Array are ambiguous because they could be anything; a string, number, or function. If the engineer using these functions were to use string interpolation, you would need some special handling for this in html and css, so loop over the TemplateStringsArray and concatenate the same index of an item in the rest Array in every loop, handling the case where there is no such item. Finally, return the string. Make sure to export both html and css.

Follow through, exporting html and css in packages/common/src/template/index.ts

Export html and css from packages/common/index.ts.

When you are finished updating the exports, build the @in/common package.

In packages/component/src/card/Card.ts import both html and css from #in/common and apply each function to the template and style properties, respectively.

Repeat the process for TextInputComponent in packages/component/src/input/TextInput.ts. In ButtonComponent you’ll only need to import css and use it to provide syntax highlighting for the inline CSS. When all three components now display syntax highlighting for the template and style properties, your work is completed.

We’ve made some extraordinary progress with fairly little code exported from @in/common to support component development. There is so much functionality we could provide from the micro-library, but at the expense of bundle size and performance. Keeping the component implementation close to the metal, as they say, is beneficial for performance. Sticking to browser specification while providing some syntactical sugar for developers as they work with spec is the best of both worlds. In the next section, we’ll expand the micro-library with one more feature before swtiching back to component development: a method decorator that handles callbacks passed to addEventListener.

Method Decorator

In the last section, you refactored each component to use the Component class decorator. That cleaned up the constructor of each component class fairly nicely. Another method on the class that has started to get polluted with logic is the connectedCallback. In TextInputComponent, the connectedCallback features several event listeners that bind each function callback to a class method using arrow brackets to ensure the context (this) is the class and not this.$input.

Binding event listeners to function callbacks is fairly common practice in connectedCallback because the component template can be reliably queried in this lifecycle method. Listening for events is fairly common practice in web development, so perhaps the micro-library could provide a better interface for binding class methods to event listeners. Enter method decorators. In the example below, a method decorator named Listen augments the behavior of onValidate. Listen is a function that takes two arguments: the Event name and optionally, a selector that could be passed to querySelector to bind the event to an element using addEventListener. This all happens behind the scenes now. Listen has direct access to the method it decorates, so we can pass the method to the second argument of addEventListener making the class method the callback that is called when the Event happens.

Method decorators are composible. If the same callback applies to two different event listeners, you can stack the decorators on the method and expect both to work just fine.

If we were to implement the method decorator pattern, this would virtually eliminate the need to bind event listeners in connectedCallback, freeing up the method for other logic.

Method decorators are arguably more statically analyzable as well, given that engineers have the option of calling methods on the element (onchange) or using addEventListener('change') for event listening. A method decorator standardizes the practice of coding for events. Developers can forget to remove event listeners when an element is removed from DOM. To be safe, you have to call removeEventListener on the disconnectedCallback, passing in the function callback to remove the event listener. That is another potential flaw method decorators can remedy. When coding the Listen decorator you’ll observe that we still bind event listeners in much the same way, along with the connectedCallback, but we can also automate removal of event listeners in the disconnectedCallback, all without interfering with an engineer’s code.

Method decorators, unlike class decorators, have access to the class instance. When modifying the class with a decorator you only had access to the prototype, but with method decorators you can expect the context (this) to point to the instance of the class. Method decorators can deconstruct the class and do things with the prototype, but for reliability the safest place to modify a prototype is the class decorator.

For the rest of this section, you’ll code a method decorator named Listen, then apply that decorator to TextInputComponent. The decorator needs to bind the method it modifies to the second argument of addEventListener. Method decorators are just functions, so you’ll pass the event name as the first argument and the element that addEventListener should be called on as the second argument. This second argument will be optional, as the method decorator can by default call this.addEventListener if the end-user doesn’t specify a second argument.

To get started, make a new directory in packages/common/src named event.

Create a new file named listen.ts in packages/common/src/event.

Define the Listen decorator

In this file, you’ll develop the Listen decorator, then export the function from the @in/common package for use in other packages of the monorepo. First mock the function, being sure to make it exportable. The first argument is named eventName, type defined as a string. This argument will be passed to addEventListener. The second argument named selector is optional, denoted with ? in TypeScript and also typed as string. This string will be passed to querySelector.

Listen returns a factory function that can be type defined. Make a new type definition using the type keyword and name it MethodDecoratorFactoryFunction. This type definition will describe the function returned by any method decorator. This function has three arguments: target is the instance of the class the method is found, key is the name of the method as a string, and descriptor is a PropertyDescriptor, which gets its type definition from lib.dom.d.ts. PropertyDescriptor is an Object that describes the configuration of the property on class Object. What’s important to remember about the PropertyDescriptor is that it stores a property named value that equals the actual method being decorated.

Apply the MethodDecoratorFactoryFunction type to the returns type of the Listen function, then return a function named decorator and declare all three arguments. The boilerplate for the Listen decorator is below.

In the decorator function, we’ll need a few things to achieve the end goal.

  • function that calls addEventListener
  • function that calls removeEventListener
  • Store the method set as the function callback on addEventListener so we can call removeEventListener with the same method
  • Hook into connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback to call both function that add and remove the listeners
  • Call addEventListener and removeEventListener on this unless a selector is specified, then query for an element using the selector and attach addEventListener and removeEventListener

That’s a lot to unpack. It’s not by virtue of being a method decorator that Listen is more complex than Component. The problem we have to solve is that much more sophisticated. Let’s take it step by step.

In decorator, access the connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback methods from the target instance using Object destructuring. Assign both to noop functions because we don’t want to override the user’s declared connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback methods.

We need a reliable way to access the method over time. In one function, we’ll need to pass the method that is decorated to addEventListener and in another method, the same function has to be passed to removeEventListener. One way to ensure the method never changes is to assign the method to a Symbol, which is guaranteed to be unique. Make a new const named symbolMethod and set this to a new Symbol, passing in the key (the name of the method decorated by Listen). This is mainly so we can access the method like this[symbolMethod] throughout the decorator.

Next let’s write a function named getContext that takes the context in the first argument and detects if a selector is provided in the second argument of Listen and if truthy, queries the root node of the element, depending on if there’s Shadow DOM or not. If selector is undefined, just return context. Ternary operators work out nicely here.

This function allows us to determine if the context is this or an element returned by querySelector when the user passes in a second argument to Listen.

Declare a new function named addListener. In this function make a new const named handler and set it equal to this[symbolMethod] and an anonymous function that passes in any arguments to a call to descriptor.value.apply(this, args). Lets unpack that. descriptor.value references the method decorated by Listen, but as we find out in the next line, handler is passed to addEventListener as the function callback. Callbacks like this expect an Event to be passed through the event handler. This is what is happening here. This algorithm passes the Event to the appropriate method by calling apply with this as the context, and the arguments typically passed to the event handler callback.

After the handler is declared, use the getContext function to determine where the event listener should be attached, then call addEventListener, passing in eventName in the first argument and handler in the second.

Removing the event listener is simpler, but only because we’ve stored the method on this[symbolMethod]. Make a new function named removeListener. Inside this function use getContext again to call removeEventListener, passing eventName in the first argument and this[symbolMethod] in the second argument.

Finally, override both the target instance connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback by setting both to new function that calls the connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback we originally deconstructed from the class, the user’s code declared in the same class decorated by Listen. connectedCallbackWrapper and disconnectedCallbackWrapper should also should call the addListener, and removeListener, respectively.

When you are finished, the Listen method decorator should look like the example below.

To use the Listen decorator in the context of TextInputComponent, you still need to properly export the function from the @in/common package.

Make a new file named index.ts at packages/common/src/event.

Export Listen from packages/common/src/event/index.ts.

Export Listen from packages/common/index.ts.

Build the @in/common package.

Refactor TextInputComponent

To start refactoring TextInputComponent, start up Storybook again with yarn storybook. If you already have Storybook running you may need to restart it now the @in/common package has been updated.

Open packages/component/src/input/TextInput.ts to start refactoring TextInputComponent.

In this class we want to integrate the new Listen method decorator. In connectedCallback, we set up three event listeners in prior chapters to handle blur, change, and keyup events on the HTMLInputElement in this component’s template. Before, we accessed this HTMLInputElement with a getter on the class named $input, although now, we have Listen which takes a string that is passed to querySelector to select the HTMLInputElement.

There is another problem to overcome. If we apply the Listen decorator to onValidate, the first argument passed to this method will now be the Event because that’s how we set up the logic in the decorator, although onValidate takes a boolean right now. This boolean is ultimately passed to the reusable validate function, so it’s possible we could deprecate the first argument of onValidate and rely only on validate instead. This boolean is used to toggle whether validate messages and error styling is displayed for the end-user.

Import Listen from the @in/common package.

Deprecate the event listeners one by one. Let’s start with the call to onValidate that happens when onblur is triggered on the HTMLInputElement.

Remove the following lines from the connectedCallback.

Change the call to this.onValidate(false) at the end of connectedCallback to instead call validate directly.

Find the onValidate method and remove the first argument. We don’t need to access anything on the Event so it’s ok to leave the argument blank. This method will only be called onblur so change the call to validate to always set true for the second argument.

Add the Listen decorator to the onValidate method. The first argument of Listen should be set to blur, while the second argument needs to be a string that can query for the HTMLInputElement. Since there is only one HTMLInputElement, the string can be set to input.

Navigate to the Form story in Storybook’s UI and blur each instance of TextInputComponent. Notice the functionality remains the same. The method decorator works!

Find the remaining two event listeners in connectedCallback.

Both of these event listeners call the onChange method, but listen for different events: change and keyup. Remove these two event listeners and apply the Listen decorator to the onChange method instead, stacking two calls to Listen atop onChange, one for each Event.

That’s it for the refactor! Run the tests to ensure nothing is broken.

Summary

In this chapter we streamlined Web Component development by coding two TypeScript decorators and several reusable functions.

  • Component handles custom element registration, template and styling.
  • Listen creates and destroys event listeners, binding class methods to the callback of addEventListener
  • attachShadow handles appending a ShadowRoot to any custom element that can accept ShadowDOM
  • attachStyle handles CSS for any custom element that can’t encapsulate styles with ShadowDOM
  • attachTemplate appends a HTML template to a custom element that can’t use ShadowDOM
  • html and css enable syntax highlighting in a user’s IDE

We exported these function from a new package called @in/common, then refactored the three components from Part One to leverage this new micro-library. By learning how to use TypeScript decorators to provide a similar interface as a major JavaScript framework like Angular, we wrangled the primary use cases for custom element development. One feature we didn’t tackle was data binding, but even that could be added to the micro-library with a minimal hit to performance. Right now the micro-library is sitting pretty. Without Listen, @in/common can optimize down to 597 bytes gzipped (Closure Compiler Simple Optimizations). By importing Listen into a project, the bundle size for the micro-library becomes 903 bytes gzipped (Closure Compiler Simple Optimizations). Not too shabby for the interface we gain out of @in/common.

If you wanted more features out of a library you could adopt one of the many open source projects out there. There are many people out there who don’t want to “reinvent the wheel” and that is a perfectly valid choice. We focused on this functionality so we can have the best of both worlds: an intuitive and scaffoldable interface for development that compiles down with a minimal performance hit for the end-user. Hopefully by the end of this chapter you understand how some Web Component libraries are coded and even be able to help fix bugs in an open source project or write your own library. Whatever you decide for your next Web Components project: to adopt a library or code your own, it’s considered a best practice to use data to guide your decision making process. One thing you’ve proven in this chapter is that micro-libraries are a viable alternative to JavaScript libraries, often providing a similar solution with much less code.

Compound Custom Elements

Chapter Five

Component Communication

Thus far, we’ve developed custom elements in isolation. Aside from the CardComponent being able to dynamically accept any child element using HTML template slots, we haven’t looked at any way custom elements can work seamlessly together. In this chapter, you’ll focus exactly on that by building an interactive table component. You’ll use browser specifications that enable each component of the table to interact with each other.

Take a moment to review Figma. Users can edit the content of each cell in the table, create and delete table rows, and cancel editing; resetting the value of the table to a state before it was edited. Not only does the table component have to handle CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete), the component will also have to have at least three visible states: read-only, editable, and add row. This means we not only have to provide some sort of state mechanism for HTMLTableElement, but we also have to manipulate DOM elements based on changes to table state and react accordingly to different event-based patterns we’ll discover while developing the table.

TableCardComponent has three modes: read-only, editable, and add row. In read-only, table cells are displayed as text. When the user presses “edit”, the table cells transform into editable text fields and focus is placed on the first cell. If the user clicks the “add” button in any mode, the table enters edit mode if needed, and a row of blank text inputs appear for the user to enter a row of information. When the user presses “save”, the current state of the table is saved. If the user presses “cancel”, the table returns to read-only mode with the state from before the user started editing.

TableComponent

In this exercise, you’ll stick with best practices when architecting the components that comprise the interactive experience. You’ll use a strict separation of concerns between the card that displays the entire layout: a table and footer with interactive buttons for adding a row, initiating edit mode, cancelling or saving the current edit; the table itself, table rows, and table cells. You’ll create several different components that are only concerned with their discrete functionality.

To maintain a separation of concerns, you’ll need mechanisms that allow instances of each component to communicate with one another. A robust event-based pattern helps in this regard. The buttons in TableCardComponent should dispatch an event that triggers some logic in TableComponent to add a row (TrComponent). TrComponent will control some aspect of how TdComponent are displayed.

The three methods for component communication you’ll explore in this chapter are passing data through HTML attributes, dispatching CustomEvent to HTML elements directly, and utilizing BroadcastChannel for dispatching events where elements that should receive them are not directly accessible.

HTML Attributes

Setting HTML attributes of a custom element are one way two elements can communicate. When a custom element is easily queried, it’s relatively simple to set the value of an attribute using setAttribute. This method is alright for simple data types, although anything passed through HTML attributes is typically treated as a string. If you wanted to pass a number through a HTML attribute, it gets converted to a string, so you have to coerce it back to a number. This behavior is validated in MDN documentation. Complex data types are not out of the question. As long as you can coerce the data into a string, it can pass through an attribute, although it should be warned, passing PII (Personal Identifiable Information) through HTML attributes is not recommended. Anything passed to a HTML attribute is easily statically analyzable in the DOM by scrapers.

Even though passing data through HTML attributes is rather limiting, it can be extremely useful and convenient. Custom elements provide an API for listening for attribute changes (observedAttributes) and doing something when attributes change (attributeChangedCallback). When a custom element is reliably a direct descendant or sibling to another custom element, it can be easily queried and natively react to attribute changes.

CustomEvent

When you have to pass complex data types from one element to another and the element receiving the data is easily selectable via a query, CustomEvent is an attractive solution. CustomEvent can include a property named details that can equal an Object, Array, FormData, or whatever other complex data type you can throw at it. CustomEvent can behave like other DOM events (MouseEvent), bubbling up the DOM tree, making CustomEvent ideal for dispatching events to parent custom elements.

BroadcastChannel

Sometimes elements are not easily accessible either by position in the DOM tree or selectable via a query. BroadcastChannel provides a method to dispatch events on a discrete channel that elements can listen to and do something whenever a message is broadcast to the channel. BroadcastChannel can dispatch events across DOM and instances of DOM like an embedded iframe or another browser tab, while also overcoming limitations of CustomEvent that merely bubbles events up DOM. For some, BroadcastChannel may be overkill for simple event dispatching between two elements, but using BroadcastChannel prevents attribute drilling, which may be necessary to communicate the selector used to query for another custom element and dispatch a CustomEvent or use setAttribute. BroadcastChannel promotes a loose coupling of user interfaces by not having to pass identifiers around to select another element.

In this chapter, you’ll use HTML Attributes, CustomEvent, and BroadcastChannel while developing the interactive table. The table consists of several different elements that should work cohesively to provide a rich user experience. Throughout this exercise, we’ll call the table a “compound component”. This isn’t an overly technical term, but it fits the scenario: a group of components contained by one another.

What you will build

  • TableCardComponent, autonomous custom element that displays a specialized CardComponent with an editable table and footer with interactive buttons
  • TableComponent, customized built-in element that extends HTMLTableElement, an editable table that displays read-only cells or editable cells
  • TrComponent, customized built-in element that extends HTMLTableRowElement and holds state for a table row
  • TdComponent, customized built-in element that extends HTMLTableCellElement and handles display of a read-only or editable table cell

What you will learn

You’ll explore the following concepts:

  • How to dispatch and listen for CustomEvent
  • The limitations of event bubbling and Shadow DOM
  • How to use BroadcastChannel to dispatch events across DOM
  • How to pass data through custom element HTML attributes
  • How to handle communication with deeply nested custom elements
  • How to work with a separation of concerns in complex custom elements

Acceptance criteria

  • TableCardComponent displays a specialized CardComponent with an editable table and footer with interactive buttons
  • TableCardComponent uses BroadcastChannel to dispatch events to other custom elements
  • TableComponent displays a HTMLTableHeaderElement with read only column names
  • TableComponent handles rendering of HTMLTableRowElement
  • TableComponent handles validation of HTMLTableRowElement
  • TableComponent handles state of table data, provides method for creation and deletion of HTMLTableRowElement
  • TableComponent handles state of table modes, i.e. read only or editable
  • TrComponent handles state of a single table row
  • TdComponent handles the display of a single table cell
  • All components appear to follow the design guidelines in Figma

Coding Compound Components

In this section, you’ll explore two ways for custom elements to communicate with one another: setting HTML attributes and sending messages over BroadcastChannel. First, you’ll use HTML attributes to provide the channel name to both TableCardComponent and TableComponent. Currently the channel name is set on an attribute of an instance of TableCardComponent. You’ll need to update the template of TableCardComponent to include an instance of TableComponent and pass the name of the channel using attribute drilling to TableComponent.

TableComponent is ultimately the component that requires the mock data to render columns and rows. You’ll use the channel name passed through an attribute on TableComponent to set up BroadcastChannel internally and subscribe to messages broadcast on the channel. In the story file, you’ll broadcast a message that contains the mock data to TableComponent.

Attribute Drilling

Custom elements have robust ways to listen for changes on HTML attributes (observedAttributes) and react to those changes (attributeChangedCallback). Setting HTML attributes on a custom element is a perfectly viable way to communicate with the element, provided the element is queriable. Since TableComponent is a direct child of TableCardComponent, you can select the element with querySelector and use setAttribute to change the attribute.

To get started, update the template of TableCardComponent to include a CardComponent. CardComponent has several HTML template slots you can set content.

TableComponent is a customized built-in element, so you can use it like any other HTMLTableElement. Add a HTMLTableElement to the inner content of the CardComponent and set the slot attribute to content so the table displays in the main content area of the card. Next, add a HTMLDivElement, give it a CSS class name set to table-footer, and set the slot attribute to footer. You’ll use the class name later to style the footer.

Import CardComponent into Table.stories.js so you can use the component in the context of the story.

Additionally, export CardComponent to satisfy Storybook’s Webpack compilation.

Back in TableCard.ts, add the observedAttributes method as a static getter on TableCardComponent and return an Array with the String channel set as the only item in the Array. This enables the custom element to listen for changes on a HTML attribute with the name channel.

To pass the value of the TableCardComponent channel HTML attribute to TableComponent you’ll first need to select the instance of TableComponent using querySelector. An easy way to do this is via a getter on TableCardComponent named $table. With this method you can keep TableComponent strictly typed by setting the return type of the getter method to HTMLTableElement. Finally, return this.shadowRoot.querySelector('table') in the getter method. You need to query for the HTMLTableElement on the shadowRoot because TableCardComponent is an autonomous custom element employing Shadow DOM.

In the attributeChangedCallback you’ll reference this.$table to pass the value of the channel attribute from TableCardComponent to TableComponent. You’ll also set up a new instance of BroadcastChannel in the attributeChangedCallback and store the instance on a new property of TableCardComponent we’ll name channel. In TableComponent, we still need a way to listen for changes to the channel attribute that you just set via the attributeChangedCallback in TableCardComponent. Set up a similar observedAttributes static getter in Table.ts to listen for changes on the channel attribute.

Just like in TableCardComponent, you’ll need to create an instance of BroadcastChannel in TableComponent to listen for messages on the channel. Setup a property on the TableComponent class type defined as BroadcastChannel.

The attributeChangedCallback on TableComponent should be similar to TableCardComponent. Listen for changes on the channel attribute and set up an instance of BroadcastChannel. This time, call onmessage, a method available on the instance of BroadcastChannel that lets you bind a function and listen for messages. Set the value of this.channel.onmessage to a class method we haven’t made yet: this.onMessage, making sure to call the method with bind otherwise the context inside onMessage will be the BroadcastChannel instead of TableComponent.

Add the onMessage method on TableComponent. onMessage behaves like other event listeners. Whenever a message is broadcast on the channel, an event passes through the first argument of onMessage since it’s bound to this.channel.onmessage. Set up a console.log temporarily to easily inspect messages on BroadcastChannel.

BroadcastChannel

So far you’ve set up TableComponent to listen for messages on BroadcastChannel but nothing is actually dispatching messages on the channel. Earlier in Table.stories.js you established the channelName that was set on the channel HTML attribute of TableCardComponent.

In Template, use the channelName to instantiate yet another instance of BroadcastChannel, only this time dispatch a message on the channel using the postMessage method, passing this method an Object containing two properties: type and detail. This Object can contain any custom properties you desire. Since many different messages are going to be broadcast on the same channel, it’s a good idea to assign type to distinguish one kind of message from another. Set type to data because this message contains the data model for the table. detail should contain the message you want to transmit on the channel.

Earlier, you set the column and row data on an Object named TableContext and passed that to the template with the context argument. Set detail to the context.

Now that you’re dispatching a message on the BroadcastChannel and TableComponent is listening via the this.channel.onmessage callback, you should inspect the console log. Open up Dev Tools and notice nothing is logged. This is because Storybook, more accurately LitElement html, requires at least one tick of the JavaScript engine to compile the template. Wrap the call to postMessage in a setTimeout to address this behavior.

You should now see the console log in Dev Tools.

Rendering Columns and Rows

Messages are flowing from the story to TableComponent but we don’t have a method to react to the message except for a console.log at this point. The message broadcast to TableComponent contains a data model for displaying columns and rows in the table. To react to this data model, replace the console.log in onMessage with a call to a yet unrealized method: onTableData, making sure to pass ev.data.detail to the new method.

Declare the onTableData method and give it an argument. We’ll call this argument next for lack of a better name. Rendering the header and body of the table are completely different algorithms, so split up the rendering of these table sections into two methods: renderHeader and renderRows. Pass each their respective property on the data model: next.columnData and next.rowData.

Rendering Column Data

We need to set up a couple of items before diving into the renderHeader method. We’ll store the columnar data on a new property declared on TableComponent: columnData.

We’ll need a way to reference the TableHeadElement and one way to do that without multiple calls to querySelector is to provide a getter on the TableComponent class.

Declare the renderHeader method and pass in the ColumnData through the first argument.

If you inspect the ColumnData (through console.log or breakpoint), you’ll observe the columns are out of order in the Array, but each Column contains a property for index. TableComponent should display the columns indexed properly from left to right. Use Array.prototype.sort to order the columns and set the ordered Array on this.columnData.

Next is a matter of generating the appropriate DOM elements in the TableHeaderElement. A TableRowElement should be created that will display a row of TableHeaderElement, each responsible for displaying the column label in the table header.

Loop through the cols data model using Array.prototype.forEach. On each iteration of the loop, make a new TableHeaderElement, set the innerText of the TableHeaderElement with the label property on Column, then append the TableHeaderElement to TableRowElement.

Finally, reset the content of the TableHeadElement every time renderHeader is called. This will allow re-rendering the TableHeadElement with different columns. On the last line of renderHeader, append the TableRowElement to TableHeadElement.

When you are finished with the renderHeader method, it should appear as below.

Rendering Row Data

The algorithm for rendering rows is similar to renderHeader that renders columns, although this time we should need to store the rows on the class. The reason we have to store columnData on the class should become apparent in the implementation of renderRows, which relies on columnData to render each TableDataCellElement.

columnData is an ordered Array which is necessary to display the TableDataCellElement in the correct order.

To get started, you’ll need a way to reference the TableBodyElement in the renderRows method. Rows will be appended to this element. Make another getter named $body on TableComponent and make it return the tbody.

Declare a new method named renderRows and pass in the rows in the first argument. You can type define rows as any[] for the time being, because literally any data model could be displayed in the row.

Reset the content of the TableBodyElement so this method can be used to render the rows more than once, allowing users of this component to replace the data displayed in the table.

Using Array.prototype.forEach, loop over each row and generate an empty TableRowElement.

Inside the loop, on every iteration, place a nested loop using Array.prototype.forEach yet again to loop over the Array of Column in this.columnData. On each iteration of the nested loop, generate a new TableDataCellElement, set the innerText to the intended content of the cell. Earlier, we had mapped a known property on the data model to the Column. Use the colData.property now to reference the data for the TableDataCellElement. Finally, append the TableDataCellElement to the TableRowElement.

After the nested forEach, make sure you append the TableRowElement to the TableBodyElement to complete the iteration of the loop that iterates over each row.

When you are finished coding renderRows it should appear like the example below:

After completing renderRows and renderHeader, you could observe the row and column data being displayed in Storybook. However, the content is not styled and appears to be cut off in the CardComponent, so let’s fix that.

Styling TableComponent

One of the problems with coding compound components is finding architectural patterns that satisfy many different combinations of components, as is the case with CardComponent, which is currently styled in a way where the component’s width is restricted to 320px. In earlier chapters, this styling was to facilitiate the display of a marketing card and login form; however, this styling is now prohibiting us from using CardComponent to display much larger user experiences like TableComponent.

To fix this problem, remove the max-width: 320px style in CardComponent.

In Card.stories.js, add this style back as an inline style for now to satisfy the requirements of those stories. Verify in Storybook that the existing card stories retain the expected width.

Moving back to the Table story in Storybook to observe styling updates to TableComponent, focus now on Table.ts. Earlier, we had set up this customized built-in element with a call to attachStyle which should place a <style> tag in the document.head ( or parent component shadowRoot ) based off the work you did in Chapter Four.

In Table.ts, fill out the style property on the Component decorator with the appropriate styles. Reference Figma to obtain the font, alignment, and sizing of the TableComponent and its children, TableRowElement and TableDataCellElement. You may inspect your work in Storybook as you progress through styling TableComponent.

First, select the TableComponent using an attribute selector [is="in-table"] since this component is a customized built-in element. Style the font properties of the table, specifiying font-family, font-size, font-weight, and color. Make TableComponent always fill the width of its container by specifying width: 100%.

Turning our attention to the TableHeaderElement, specify the necessary styles to reflect the mockup in Figma. Set the display to table-cell to normalize the styling for different browsers. Center the label vertically using vertical-align: middle, which overrides the default. Set the box-sizing: border-box to more predictably size the element using only width, height, padding and border. Give the TableHeaderElement the appropriate margin-top and height and set the font-weight to override the browser default.

Figma specifies the height of each TableRowElement should be 58px. To center content vertically, override the browser default with vertical-align: middle.

Each TableDataCellElement requires some padding to match the Figma mockup.

When you are finished styling TableComponent, the style property on the Component decorator should appear as below.

After taking a brief detour to style TableComponent, let’s circle back to other functions of the user experience that require more work.

Handling CRUD Events with BroadcastChannel

If we are going to support CRUD (Create, Read, Update and Delete) in TableComponent, we need a way to tell TableComponent when to create, update, delete, or read rows. Looking back at Figma, several buttons are visible in the layout that appear to initiate such actions. Edit button puts TableComponent in a mode that makes each cell editable. In “edit mode”, two buttons appear: Save and Cancel. When the user presses Save, TableComponent should revert to “read only mode” with any changes saved to each cell. When the user presses Cancel, TableComponent should revert to “read only mode” with the state prior to the user making any changes. Later, we’ll include an Add button for creating a new row and icons in each row to support Delete, but for now let’s focus on the R (Read) and U (Update) in CRUD.

Add a new HTMLDivElement to TableCardComponent template, giving it an identifiable CSS class name save-actions. In this HTMLDivElement, add three ButtonComponent we developed in prior chapters using customized built-in elements. The three buttons should have the appropriate labels: save, cancel, and edit. save is a primary button, while cancel and edit are secondary buttons. Initially, the first two buttons (save and cancel ) should be hidden. This can be achieved with the hidden HTML attribute.

Add three getters on TableCardComponent, one for each of the buttons you just introduced to the template. If you haven’t already, give each ButtonComponent a unique CSS class name so you can query for each element easily using querySelector.

Focusing on the edit button, make a new event listener using the Listen decorator from Chapter 4. Import Listen from @in/common and declare the decorator atop a new method named editMode. The event listener should listen for click on the element with class name .button-edit.
