In the callback, add the hidden HTML attribute to this.$editButton and remove the same attribute on this.$saveButton and this.$cancelButton to hide the edit button and show the cancel and save buttons. Call postMessage on this.channel, setting the type of the message to edit. There isn’t a payload needed here, so we’ll leave detail out. When the user clicks the edit button, a new message is broadcast via BroadcastChannel that specifies that the mode has changed to “edit mode”.

The cancel button should have a similar event listener. Use another instance of the Listen decorator to establish a click event listener on the element with class name .button-cancel. Attach the decorator to a new method named readOnlyMode. Show the edit button, while hiding the save and cancel buttons by removing and adding the hidden attribute respectively. Dispatch a message on the BroadcastChannel, this time setting the type to edit.

Declare a third event listener attached to the save button. In a new save method, dispatch an event on the BroadcastChannel with the type property set to save. We could hide and show buttons similar to the cancel callback, but will reserve that functionality only for the readOnlyMode method that can be called independent of the event listener callback since it is a class member of TableCardComponent.

Ultimately these messages should be received by TableComponent, so update that class with new case in the switch statement found in the onMessage method. React to each of the types of messages: edit, readOnly, and save. In each case, call a new method for each use case.

Add the new methods to TableComponent.

In this section you worked with several components to develop a rich user experience. TableCardComponent, TableComponent, CardComponent and ButtonComponent all work together through the use of attribute drilling or dispatching messages on the BroadcastChannel event bus. In the next section, you’ll focus mainly on TableComponent to achieve all the features necessary to make an editable table.

Making the Table Editable

In this section, you’ll work on giving TableComponent the various modes required by the acceptance criteria: read-only and editable, while also giving the user the ability to add and delete rows. You’ll further practice a separation of concerns by developing two new components: TrComponent and TdComponent that handle the functionality of a row and cell, respectively.

We used attribute drilling and BroadcastChannel in the previous section to communicate between components in the same layout. We’ll add CustomEvent as a method for custom element communication in this section. You’ll also learn how to dynamically create new instances of customized built-in elements with createElement and give custom elements data with HTML data attributes.

Separation of Concerns

In the last section, you dynamically created HTMLTableRowElement and HTMLTableCellElement in TableComponent in response to receiving a message over BroadcastChannel. To further promote a separation of concerns, let’s break out these two elements into new components. Otherwise, logic that should probably be contained by the HTMLTableCellElement will be leaking all over TableComponent. TrComponent and TdComponent will be customized built-in elements because we want them to retain the characteristics of the native DOM elements, while enhancing the element with more functionality. TrComponent will manage state for the entire row, while TdComponent will manage the view of the HTMLTableCellElement, whether it’s in “edit mode” or “read-only mode”, and set the value of the cell.

To start, make a new file in the same directory named Tr.ts. This file will contain the component logic for TrComponent.

Open Tr.ts in your IDE and begin developing the component by importing the Component decorator from @in/common.

Declare a new class named TrComponent and have it extend HTMLTableRowElement. Make the constructor and insert a call to super(). Ensure the class is exported using the export keyword.

Use the Component decorator to set the custom element tag name as in-tr, making sure to also provide the necessary custom property needed to register customized built-in elements.

In Table.stories.js import TrComponent from Tr.ts.

Export TrComponent for the Storybook Webpack configuration.

Set up TrComponent the same way. Start by making a new file named Td.ts in the same directory.

Import all the necessary API from @in/common. You’ll need to style parts of a custom template in TdComponent so be sure to import attachTemplate and attachStyle in addition to Component.

Export a class named TrComponent that extends HTMLTableCellElement. Call super() in the class constructor as well as attachTemplate and attachStyle.

Set up the Component decorator, passing in the tag name as in-td to the selector property, the appropriate Object for registering the customized built-in element with the CustomElementRegistry. Leave the style and template properties blank for now.

TableComponent should display two modes: read-only and editable. In read-only mode, each TdComponent should display non-editable read-only text, while in edit mode the component should display a text input, more specifically TextInputComponent. Add two HTMLSpanElement to the template, tagging each with a unique CSS class name. In the span classed td-input, add an instance of TextInputComponent.

Before proceeding with styling TdComponent, head back on over to Table.stories.js and import TextInputComponent into the file.

Export TextInputComponent from Table.stories.js to satisfy Storybook’s Webpack compilation.

Moving back to TdComponent, add styling for both the HTMLSpanElement you introduced in the template. We need to ensure the read-only content is styled per the spec in Figma, while also retaining the characteristics of a HTMLTableCellElement. To hide/show the read-only value, let’s use a similar method to the buttons in TableCardComponent. Add a style for when the hidden HTML attribute is truthy. The element should be display: none.

Add getters for each of the elements you introduced to the layout: both HTMLSpanElement and the TextInputComponent. You’ll need to reference each of these elements in the component logic you’ll develop in TdComponent.

Make another method on TdComponent for setting the value of the read-only HTMLSpanElement. Pass an argument named value through the method and set value on the innerText of the HTMLSpanElement.

You’ll need a way for TableComponent to communicate the value of the cell to TdComponent. Since you’re already looping over HTMLTableCellElement in the context of TableComponent it seems appropriate to set the value via a HTML attribute. Listen for changes to a value attribute in TdComponent with the observedAttributes static getter.

Declare the attributeChangedCallback method. While using a switch statement, watch for the case of value and call setValue there.

We’ll require another method for toggling the mode of the TdComponent from read-only to editable. Declare a method named setMode and pass an argument named readOnly, type defined as boolean, to an if statement. Depending on the truthiness of readOnly, hide or show the appropriate HTMLSpanElement.

Add readonly to the Array of observedAttributes and make a new case in the attributeChangedCallback, being sure to call setMode with the value of the readonly attribute. Since HTML attributes are String, we need to coerce the value of the attribute to a boolean because setMode expects a boolean. You can do this with the expression next === 'true', which will return a boolean that is truthy, otherwise falsy.

TdComponent is now set up to render different user interfaces based on the mode passed through the readonly HTML attribute. However; we still need to refactor TableComponent to accommodate the new customized built-in elements.

Rendering Modes

In the last section, we dynamically created HTMLTableRowElement and HTMLTableCellElement with createElement in the renderRows method in TableComponent. Since then, we made these elements customized built-in elements and need to update the logic in renderRows to accommodate the change. createElement takes a second argument, an Object that specifies for the browser that these should be instances of a customized built-in element with a tag name set on the is property.

Update the calls to createElement in renderRows to create customized built-in elements with the tag names you declared earlier in this section.

The initial state of each table cell should be read-only as opposed to edit mode, so ensure each TdComponent has a call to setAttribute that sets the readonly HTML attribute to true on initial render.

Using CustomEvent to Transmit Row Data

Thus far we haven’t done much with TrComponent, even though the purpose of this component is to store row state. TrComponent is a direct descendant of TableComponent and in the renderRows method we already have a reference to each TrComponent. One of the requirements for using CustomEvent is being able to easily select the element. The main reason we’ve stuck with BroadcastChannel is because the deeply nested elements that required events were not immediately queriable from higher up in DOM. Even then, we needed to use attribute drilling so the nested TableComponent could listen to the same channel. Although this only required passing a String through HTML attributes and not a complex Object or Array. CustomEvent can be a viable means for component communication, especially when complex data has to be transmitted.

The Object that corresponds to each row in the loop is rowData. Use the dispatchEvent on HTMLElement to send a new CustomEvent named data, passing in rowData in the detail property.

Let’s react to this CustomEvent in TrComponent before providing a method that displays each mode in TableComponent. In Tr.ts, add a new public property on the class called $rowData. This property should be publicly accessible so TableComponent can access it.

Import Listen from @in/common to set up a new event listener.

In TableComponent, you dispatched a CustomEvent to the instance of TrComponent, so let’s declare a new event listener with Listen. Declare a new method named setValue that serves as the event listener callback method. Pass the event through the first argument ev and set the value of this.$rowData to the detail.

We’ll circle back to TrComponent later, but for now, let’s stick with managing the rendering of nodes in TableComponent. Make a new method on TableComponent named onReadOnly. the purpose of this method is to display the TdComponent in read-only mode. When the method is called, select all the cells with querySelectorAll and loop over the NodeList with forEach. On every iteration of the loop, set the readonly HTML attribute of each TdComponent to true.

Table Modes and State

Read-only mode was fairly trivial. To set the display of each TdComponent, all you had to do was set the readonly HTML attribute. Edit mode is a bit more complex. After the user initiates edit mode by pressing the edit button, they have the option of editing each cell or canceling the edits they made. We need a way to store the state of the rows in the table when the user enters edit mode, in the event the user wants to revert the changes. This is why we went to the trouble of storing the data for each row on TrComponent, but we still need a way to store the state of all rows in the context of TableComponent. To get started, import TrComponent into Table.ts because you’ll need to reference the $rowData property that exists on each instance of TrComponent in upcoming logic.

Declare a getter method on TableComponent that queries for all TrComponent in the TableBodyElement using querySelectorAll. We don’t need an Array of TrComponent, but instead an Array of row data, so we need to use a method on Array.prototype not available to us on the NodeList. To access map on a NodeList you have to coerse the NodeList into an Array using Array.prototype.from.

Add a new private method on TableComponent named savedState. We’ll use this property to store the state of the rows when the user enters edit mode.

Declare another method on TableComponent named onEdit. This method will handle the display of elements in edit mode and changes to row state. In onEdit check if this.savedState exists and if truthy, set this.savedState to the Array returned from the this.state getter. Wrap the Array in a call to JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) to copy the Array and make it ready to dispatch the saved state in a CustomEvent or message on BroadcastChannel if necessary.

Update the onReadOnly method to check for this.savedState and if truthy, call renderRows with the data model stores in savedState, then reset savedState, making it equal to undefined for the event. If the user enters edit mode once again, the check for savedState in onEdit can execute as expected.

Orchestrating Edit Mode

The acceptance criteria for the editable table suggests that users should be able to edit each cell in the table and either save or cancel the edit. We’ve chosen to create a separation of concerns where needed, placing row state on instances of TrComponent, the display state for each cell on TdComponent, and the overall rendering of rows and cells on TableComponent. This separation of concerns begins to break down when considering the complexity of edit mode. Some concerns regarding edit mode are below.

  • When a user edits a field and moves on to another input, row state should be updated
  • Upon using the keyboard to navigate, users should expect to use the Tab key to focus the next logical cell, i.e. when focused on the last cell of a row and the user presses Tab, focus should flow to the first cell of the next row or the buttons in the footer.

These user experience enhancements require some binding of event listeners on the TextInputComponent embedded in TdComponent. Some may argue that this is the concern of TdComponent so any event listener logic should be declared in the context of TdComponent. Another argument for handling this logic in TableComponent is that TableComponent is responsible for rendering of nodes and should track which nodes are currently being edited as well as rendered. For the sake of development, we’ll take this stance, relegating TdComponent to merely being concerned with view logic, while TableComponent is responsible for tracking not only which rows and cells are rendered, but are also being edited. For this purpose, let’s add a new property on TableComponent named editIndex and type define that property as number, then set the initial value to 0; the index of the first cell in the table.

TableComponent can only interpret a cell is being edited when the user focuses on the TextInputComponent visible in edit mode. To listen for the focus event, we’ll need to set up event listeners and react to events on each TextInputComponent. Import TdComponent into Table.ts to get started.

Declare a new method on TableComponent named handleCellListeners. The first argument of this method should be the TdComponent so we’ll name it td, followed by the index, which has a type of number. Setup the method some more by making a new const named tr, selecting the TrComponent that is the parent of the TdComponent using the parentNode method on HTMLElement. Declare another const named input and use querySelector to select the HTMLInputElement. We could type define this input as TextInputComponent as well, but that isn’t necessary since we are only going to reference methods found on HTMLInputElement.

In onEdit, select all the HTMLTableCellElement using querySelectorAll and using forEach, call this.handleCellListeners on the Array of HTMLTableCellElement, ensuring to bind the context to this (TableComponent).

Back in handleCellListeners, check if the input exists with an if statement. This is the safest approach because later we may want to add elements other than HTMLInputElement in each HTMLTableCellElement. Declare three event listeners on the input, one for onclick, another for onkeyup, and the third for onkeydown.

In the onclick event listener, set this.editIndex to the index of the HTMLTableCellElement in the Array of all HTMLTableCellElement using indexOf on Array.prototype. You’ll have to coerce the NodeList into an Array with Array.prototype.from because NodeList lacks many methods found on the Array prototype.

Whenever the user edits the value of the HTMLInputElement, we want to update the value of the cell in state, which is currently stored in two places: on TrComponent and the value HTML attribute on TdComponent. We can listen for changes to the HTMLInputElement using the onkeyup event listener and set the value in both of these places, although we’ll need to create a larger interface in both places. TrComponent has no way of listening for changes in row state and reacting to those changes.

The state of each row is an Object that contains multiple properties. Each property is mapped to a cell. In the context we are working in handleCellListeners, we have access to the TrComponent and TdComponent, although the TdComponent only stores the value of the cell, not the property on the row state ($rowData) the cell is mapped to. To add the name of the property on TdComponent, we need to turn to the renderRows method, where the elements are rendered. Set a new HTML data attribute with the value of the property in the loop.

Returning to the handleCellListeners, declare a new event listener for onkeyup. Set the value HTML attribute on TdComponent using the current input.value. Dispatch a CustomEvent to the TrComponent with a new event name: patch, meaning we’re going to update a property on the Object held in row state on TrComponent. In the CustomEvent detail, pass the value of the TdComponent as it was just set via the HTML attribute (or use the input.value) and the property set on the HTML data attribute data-property.

React to the new CustomEvent in TrComponent by adding a new method named patchData that includes the Listen decorator. Set the value of the property on this.$rowData to the appropriate value using the properties on the CustomEvent detail.

Back in the handleCellListeners method on TableComponent declare the last event listener, this time, listening for onkeydown events on the HTMLInputElement. We want to evoke ev.stopPropagation() here to prevent the browser default and insert a check if the user pressed Tab. When the user presses the Tab key we want to set the current editIndex to the index of the cell, which is available via index.

There’s more to do here. When the user presses the Tab key, the focus should advance to the next editable input in the table. We need another method that handles this functionality because it will need to be evoked in multiple places to focus not just the next input, but also the first input when the user enters edit mode. For lack of a better name we’ll call this method onNext.

In the onNext method, query for all the TdComponent. Check if a cell exists at the current index using the expression !cells[this.editIndex] and if this expression returns truthy, return so any further code is not executed on an element that does not exist. Next, select the TdComponent at the current index and query for the TextInputComponent. Checking again if the input exists, call focus() on the HTMLInputElement. This has the effect of focusing the next input in the table.

To focus the first cell when the user initiates edit mode, add a call to onNext in the onEdit method.

Call onNext in the context of the handleCellListeners method after checking if the user pressed the Tab key.

To reset the editIndex back to the initial value of 0 before the user enters edit mode, you can hijack onReadOnly which occurs before onEdit. Set editIndex to 0 at the end of this method.

That’s it for the functionality surrounding editing table cells in edit mode. So far you’ve tackled the the R (Read) and U (Update) in CRUD, but soon you’ll work on the C (Create) and D (Delete). Before you get there, you’ll add the functionality for the user to save edited fields and fix styling issues that have appeared in the TableComponent.

Save

We need to take care of some issues with saving data. After the user presses the save button, the table should revert to read-only mode with all the changes the user made. We’ll need to clean up the current view by setting the cell the user last edited to read-only mode and reinitialize savedState and editIndex. For convenience we can also post a message whenever the user saves on the BroadcastChannel which can be listened for outside of the context of TableComponent, like in the context of the Story or application source code. Lastly, we need to re-render the table in read-only mode.

Make a new method on TableComponent named onSave. Make a const named data equal to this.state and give it the proper type definition. Call setAttribute on the current TdComponent if it exists. Reset the values of savedState and editIndex to their defaults, in case the user enters edit mode again. Post a message on the BroadcastChannel, this time setting the type property to change and pass the data to the detail property, data in this case being all the table rows serialized to JSON in the state getter. Finally, call renderRows, passing the method the data to render the table in read-only mode with the current state.

Fix Styling Issues

When developing the initial boilerplate for TdComponent we made a call to attachStyle in the constructor. Due to the way TdComponent are dynamically being added to DOM, a much safer implementation would be to call this function in the connectedCallback. attachStyle then appends a <style> tag to the nearest ShadowRoot or document.head to style the customized built-in element.

After making TableComponent switch between two modes, some styling issues have cropped up. The TableHeadElement is misaligned with the rest of the layout. We just need to update the padding a tad to fix these issues.

In the style property on the Component decorator, add the following padding to the TableHeadElement:

When you are finished, the style declaration for the TableHeadElement should be as follows.

Similarly, to match the Figma mockups, the padding of all cells in the table need to be normalized, with special styling for the first and last cells in each row.

In TableCardComponent, some other styling issues should be addressed. The button widths could be normalized with min-width and have even spacing between them using margin-left. The items in the footer need some adjustment. By giving the footer a display:flex and justify-content: space-between, we can set up the footer to accept a button on the left side as well as right. Additionally, we can give child elements that have the HTML attribute hidden the style of display: none to properly hide them.

Now that styling issues are out of the way, it’s time to focus on the C in CRUD: Create.

Create a Row

With the bulk of the logic finished for TableComponent we can now focus on the functionality for creating and deleting rows. According to the mockup, the user initiates the creation of a row by pressing a button in the TableCardComponent footer that looks like a “+”. For the sake of the flexbox layout we just added to the footer, let’s add a new container in the TableCardComponent template to encapsulate the button. Make a new HTMLDivElement and give it a CSS class name crud-actions.

Inside of this HTMLDivElement place the template of the HTMLButtonElement with an embedded SVG that displays a plus sign. If this seems cumbersome, that’s perfectly fine. In the next chapter we’ll streamline this process of adding complex complex layouts to a template using HTML templates. Until then, adding a static layout is a good solution.

Add another getter on TableCardComponent to reference the button you just added to the template.

Declare another method on TableCardComponent named add. This method will contain all the logic for adding a row in the context of TableCardComponent. Use the Listen decorator to set up an event listener for the click event on the element with the CSS class name .button-add. When the user clicks the add button, blur the button to allow focus to eventually travel to the first HTMLInputElement in the blank row that will be created. Hide and show the appropriate buttons in the TableCardComponent layout. Finally, post a message via BroadcastChannel with the type property set to add.

In TableComponent react to the new message by adding a case in the onMessage method for add and call a new method yet to be declared: onAdd.

Declare the new onAdd method on TableComponent.

Similar to edit mode, we want to check if savesState exists and if not, set savedState.

Currently state for rows is stored in the context of each TrComponent, but we haven’t generated a new instance of TrComponent for the blank row of data yet. We can use a property on TableComponent to store a temporary Object that initializes the data for a blank row.

In onAdd set the blankRowData property to an empty Object. Loop over columnData and set the property associated with each column to a property name on blankRowData, making sure to set each property on blankRowData to an empty string.

Make a new const named rowData and set it to this.blankRowData.

The rest of the algorithm looks a lot like renderRows. Generate a new TrComponent. Loop over the columns in columnData and on each iteration, generate a new TdComponent, being sure to initialize the appropriate HTML attributes on TdComponent. This time, set the readonly HTML attribute to false so the cells display with TextInputComponent. Finally, call appendChild on the TableBodyElement and pass in the TrComponent to display a blank row.

Dispatch a new CustomEvent with type data to the TrComponent, being sure to set the detail with the rowData. This initializes the TrComponent that was just appended to DOM with the correct state. Loop through the cells of the row and attach the event listeners to each cell with the handleCellListeners method. Set the edit index to the index of the first TdComponent in the blank row. Call onNext to focus the input in the row.

You should now be able to observe in Storybook that when a user presses the add button, a blank row is created. Upon editing the row, the blank row behaves similar to existing rows thanks to the various methods on TableComponent.

Delete a Row

Looking at the mockup in Figma, it appears every row should have a delete button in the last cell of the row, on the right hand side. So far every cell has the same functionality: display read-only text or editable input. This cell is different. A button should be displayed. When the user presses the button, the row should be deleted. The delete button is only visible in edit mode.

The delete button will be visible in edit mode and should be visible when the user creates a new row. Let’s abstract the generation of the DOM elements that make up the delete button cell in a method on TableComponent named createDeleteButton. This method will have to be called in renderRows and onAdd. In both contexts, we have access to the TrComponent.

In the new createDeleteButton pass in the TrComponent in the first argument of the method. The delete button needs to be encapsulated by a HTMLTableCellElement. Use createElement to generate a new instance of HTMLTableCellElement. Add a CSS class name with classList.add that differentiates this cell from other editable cells: delete-cell. Use setAttribute to set the readonly property of the cell to true. Set the innerHTML of the HTMLTableCellElement to a ButtonComponent with an inline SVG that displays the “X”. Append the HTMLTableCellElement to the TrComponent.

The delete button should be rendered in whenever rows are generated after all other TdComponent have been appended to the TrComponent The delete button should be the last cell displayed in each row. Just before the TrComponent is appended to the TableBodyElement, call createDeleteButton, passing the instance of TrComponent into the method’s arguments.

Repeat this same step in the onAdd method.

In Storybook you should now observe a delete button at the end of each row in edit mode or when you add a new row, although the buttons are also visible in read-only mode. Let’s fix this with some additional styling. In TableComponent, add a style that targets the element with CSS class name .delete-cell and readonly HTML attribute set to true and style the element with display: none so it’s hidden in read-only mode.

Fix the position of the button with a slight adjustment to the vertical position of the element using a transform.

The buttons are not visible, but we haven’t done anything to react to when the user clicks the button. The handleCellListeners method on TableComponent seems like an appropriate place. Near the start of the method, select the button by querying for an instance of ButtonComponent.

Just like we checked if an input existed, establish an if statement that checks for the ButtonComponent. If the ButtonComponent exists it means this TdComponent has the readonly HTML attribute set to true, so toggle that to true for edit mode.

Set up an event listener for onclick and in the event listener callback, set the editIndex on the current cell in case the user wants to keep editing other fields. Dispatch a CustomEvent on the TrComponent with the event name delete. We’ll set this up in a moment in TrComponent, but the intent is to send an event to the row to destroy itself. Add a second event listener for onkeydown so users triggering the button with a keyboard can have the desired effect. Call ev.stopPropagation() to prevent the browser default. Check if the key pressed was Tab and if so, navigate the focus to the next row by setting the editIndex to the current index and calling onNext. When the user presses Enter or Select, do the same thing, except this time dispatch the same CustomEvent to the TrComponent.

In TrComponent, set up an event listener using the Listen decorator and a new method named delete. Inside this method call removeChild on the parentNode of the instance of TrComponent using the current context (this).

In Storybook you should now observe that when the user clicks on the delete button of each row, the row is deleted. If the user presses save, the current state of the table is retained.

Testing the Table

Integration tests are important for TableComponent mainly because there are several components that should work harmoniously together. With so many touch points, it’s easy for compound components to break down. In this section, you’ll test if the table can enter read-only mode, validate if the user can edit a text field, and also if the user can cancel edit mode. This should provide a comprehensive set of integration tests that could be further developed upon for more discrete test cases.

Integration Tests

For the integration tests, you’ll be using the Table Story from the previous section as a test bed.

Make a new file in the cypress/integration directory named Table.spec.js.

Add a describe block to the test file and use a beforeEach to mitigate any issues with testing the components in Storybook.

First let’s test if edit mode can be initiated in the table. After the beforeEach make your first assertion and tell cypress to visit the appropriate route in Storybook.

Should Enter Edit Mode

Using Cypress, target the root element in Storybook’s iframe, then drill down to find the element with HTML attribute [channel="table:one"], which should be the instance of TableCardComponent. Use the shadow method to target the autonomous custom element’s Shadow DOM and the find method to select the footer slot. Chain the find method again to select the edit button and call click(). This should simulate when the user presses the edit button in the test environment.

To validate the table is in edit mode after clicking the edit button, we’re going to check that TextInputComponent exists in the first cell, which would otherwise be hidden in read-only mode. Target the root element again and drill down into the Shadow Root of the TableCardComponent. This time, select the content slot with [slot="content"] and find the TableBodyElement. Since we’re working with customized built-in elements here, querying is much simpler. Drill down using consecutive find calls until you select the TextInputComponent and check if the element exists.

The next test validates that the user can edit a cell with TextInputComponent, click the save button, and the table retains the value of the field in read-only mode. Set up a new test and visit the same route.

Should Edit a Text Field

The start of the test is similar to the first. The test should click the edit button to initiate edit mode.

This time instead of checking TextInputComponent exists, call click on the input to bring it into focus, query against the TextInputComponent Shadow DOM with shadow() and find the internal HTMLInputElement and clear it. This is to prevent issues with testing in various environments.

For the next part of the test, drill down exactly the same way, only now call type on the HTMLInputElement and specify a string Cypress should insert.

Click the TextInputComponent again to bring it back into focus. This is to prevent issues with Cypress trying to focus on the save button in the next step.

Wait a second before clicking the save button. This should make the test more reliable.

Select the footer slot of TableCardComponent again and select the save button this time. Click the save button with Cypress.

Wait another second to improve reliability of the test.

The table should now be in read-only mode, so you’ll need to query against the TdComponent as if they only display a HTMLSpanElement. Assert the HTMLSpanElement contains the same text that was previously entered in the TextInputComponent.

The next test validates the user can cancel editing and the table reverts to the previous value of a cell. Establish a third test using the it keyword and have Cypress visit the same story.

Should Cancel Edit Mode

Just like the previous tests, click the edit button with Cypress.

Clear the HTMLInputElement to reduce issues with testing.

Set the value of the HTMLInputElement to the string 'jane@doe.com'.

Use Cypress to click the cancel button.

Validate the same cell contains the default value prior to editing: 'joe@gmail.com'

That’s it for basic integration tests for the editable table. We could validate more test cases like adding and deleting rows or edge cases but for now we’ll leave the tests here to concentrate on other material.

Snapshots

With Storybook still running, generate snapshots for the component.

When snapshots have been generated for the Table story, add them to your commit. Commit your changes in git to complete this section. After you’ve completed integration and snapshot tests for TableComponent let’s review the content of this chapter.

Summary

The editable table is a compound component that requires several discrete units of functionality to work seamlessly together in order to provide a rich user experience. In this chapter, you coded four different components: TableCardComponent, TableComponent, TrComponent, and TdComponent while using Storybook as both development environment and test bed. Compound components demand some architectural design, otherwise maintenance can become a nightmare. By abstracting reusable code into class and method, we were able to keep the implementation fairly DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself). A strict separation of concerns was further provided by the library developed in the previous chapter. Since high level component functionality was abstracted to library functions, we focused mainly on developing the features required by the editable table experience.

Compound components have several ways to communicate. HTML attributes, CustomEvent and BroadcastChannel all have their relative strengths and weaknesses. In this chapter, we used all three methods in the development of the table. Knowing whether to use one over the other can make or break the developer experience or cause performance issues for the end-user (forgetting to remove event listeners, for instance). HTML attributes and CustomEvent may have made a lot of sense but BroadcastChannel may have seemed out of place. BroadcastChannel was originally intended to provide a messaging system for communication across browser contexts. Using BroadcastChannel to overcome the limitations of event bubbling is an interesting solution, however, another specification that allows custom elements to pass data between components may be on the horizon. The Context API Proposal would replace the need for BroadcastChannel if the proposal makes it’s way into mainstream browsers.

We coded autonomous custom elements and customized built-in elements where it made sense. An autonomous custom element was reserved for the TableCardComponent. TableComponent, TrComponent and TdComponent are customized built-in elements so they retain the characteristics of the table elements they extend from. We enhanced the typical HTML table by making the cells editable and providing the ability to add and delete rows, while styling the table per the mockup in Figma.

If there was one unrelated nuisance in TableComponent, it would be the inline SVGs that bloat the template strings. Suppose designers wanted to update the icons used in the add and delete buttons. It would mean tracking down template strings where these SVGs exist in the codebase. HTML templates could make the SVG implementation in TableComponent easier to maintain over time if they were abstracted away from the component implementation and stored elsewhere. In the next chapter you’ll unlock the magic of HTML templates while developing the DialogComponent.

Powering Dialogs with HTML Templates

Chapter Six

HTML Templates

Programmatically making a template used to be difficult. Templating HTML was either the purview of ES2015 template strings or the domain of JavaScript frameworks. Either way, HTML templates were bundled into JavaScript, separated from the DOM where they were native. This is even the case in the UI library that you’ve been working on in the course of this book. HTML templates are declared in ES2015 template strings and packaged with the component.

When creating a HTML template dynamically with JavaScript, you used document.createElement like you would when instantiating any DOM node, passing in the string template to hold a reference to a HTMLTemplateElement. You then set the innerHTML of the HTMLTemplateElement to a custom template declared as an ES2015 template string. HTMLTemplateElement differ itself from other DOM nodes in at least two important ways. Instances of HTMLTemplateElement have a property named content, which is unlike other DOM nodes which lack this property. The cloneNode method on content allows you to copy the HTML template that was originally set with innerHTML and use it in the context of other methods like appendChild. You can essentially reuse HTML templates as if they were a rubber stamp. Each time cloneNode is called in the context of appendChild you are stamping the HTML template.

So far, we haven’t harnessed the full potential of HTML templates. Instances of HTMLTemplateElement declared in DOM (not created dynamically like in the above example) are not parsed by the user agent, they are essentially hidden from users. You could place an HTML template in the document and the elements contained within the template won’t be rendered until the template is cloned. Below is the same HTML template as it would appear if in the DOM.

Using DOM to store HTML templates seems natural. When server-side rendered (SSR), HTML templates can be a powerful means to reuse templates. If SSR were implemented with some sort of metadata engine, each SSR rendered page could render initially with the HTML templates required for the user experiences on that page. In the context of single-page applications (SPA), the appeal of HTML templates may not seem obvious. Templates may be bundled with the SPA and parsed as JavaScript, although this bloats the JavaScript bundle. What if HTML templates could be attached to each route via the SPA router and appended to DOM so they could be reused? Perhaps there are templates in a global scope of an application, like in the case of a “discard changes” or “are you sure?” dialog, where the user must confirm they want to proceed. The HTML template could be stored in DOM and reused throughout the application.

Dialogs seem like a good fit for HTML templates. If we coded a dialog custom element, it would be tempting to provide an inline template, but we could code the dialog in such a way that queries for HTML templates that exist in DOM and reuses them. This way, the dialog would only be concerned with positioning, or in the case of multiple instances of the dialog, the layer in which the dialog is drawn. By creating a separation of concerns between template and dialog, we can reduce code duplication in an application. The HTML template could be declared once with an identifier and instances of dialogs could query for the template and clone template content upon instantiation.

In this chapter, you’ll build a DialogComponent that manages the state of a dialog instance (open or closed), the type of dialog that should be instantiated, and the dialog’s relationship with the DOM element that triggers the dialog to open (an instance of ButtonComponent or HTMLAnchorElement most likely). This new component will query for HTML template and pass a clone of the template to the custom element that should be displayed. DialogComponent won’t handle any display characteristics of the displayed user interface of a dialog, the instance of the DialogComponent will essentially be hidden from the user experience. In this way, this is the first time we’re using a custom element class in the role of a “controller”; a class that updates both “model” and “view” in the traditional sense of MVC. DialogComponent doesn’t have to be a custom element, although by making it one we can give engineers the ability to declare instances of DialogComponent in a template, which may seem more intuitive.

There are two types of known dialogs in the application: modals and tooltips. Each type of dialog distinguishes itself by how the dialog is displayed. Since DialogComponent is not concerned with any display characteristics, we’ll create two other autonomous custom elements that handle the display and positioning of a modal or tooltip. Modals are typically displayed centered above all other content, while tooltips are displayed contextually to the element the user clicks to instantiate an instance of the tooltip, just beneath the cursor. You can review the dialogs in Figma.

While developing each dialog, we’ll come across an interesting use case where a dialog is embedded in the template of another dialog. When the user clicks on a link in a modal, a tooltip should appear, layered above the modal, just below the position of the HTMLAnchorElement the user clicked on. If the user closes the modal by clicking the close button or pressing the Escape key on a keyboard, both the tooltip and modal should close. This means we need some sort of controller that tracks the parent/child relationships of dialogs and the order the dialogs appear in the view. DialogComponent won’t cut it for this task because the custom element isn’t necessarily global or available during the lifespan of all dialogs that could be stacked on top of one another. DialogComponent is only concerned with the lifecycle of a single dialog. To handle the orchestration of all dialogs in a view, we’ll code a DialogStack class that will exist on the window, or could be declared elsewhere in a global scope.

What you will build

  • DialogComponent which handles the lifecycle of a single dialog
  • ModalComponent which displays a model centered in the view
  • TooltipComponent which displays a contextual tooltip just beneath an element
  • DialogStack which orchestrates the state of all dialogs in a view

What you will learn

  • How to unlock the potential of HTML templates
  • How to use a custom element as a “controller”
  • How to create and destroy custom elements on the fly
  • How to create a custom dialog that displays anywhere
  • How to control the order and position of dialogs
  • How to reliably query DOM across shadow boundaries
  • How to use data attributes to store information

Acceptance criteria

  • DialogComponent handles state of a single dialog
  • DialogComponent attaches an event listener to the DOM element that triggers opening a dialog on click
  • DialogComponent calls methods on DialogStack to register dialogs and remove templates
  • ModalComponent handles display and positioning of a modal
  • TooltipComponent handles display and position of a tooltip
  • DialogStack handles the order, focus, and storage of template

Getting started

Navigate to the project directory:

Checkout a new branch named chapter-6 from where you left off at the end of chapter 5.

Mocking the Dialog in Storybook

Just like in previous chapters, we’ll start by creating a directory that stores all the files associated with dialogs. In a new file named Dialog.stories.js we’ll explore the outward facing API of DialogComponent: a set of HTML attributes. We’ll scaffold DialogComponent in a separate file. By the end of this section you should have a development environment in Storybook that allows you to develop DialogComponent.

Define the Story

Make a new directory named dialog that’s a sibling to other components.

Create a new file named Dialog.stories.js in the dialog directory you just created.

In Dialog.stories.js export the configuration in Component Story Format. Storybook needs to display a new story in the sidebar. The title of this Story is Components/Dialog. The tag name we’ll use for DialogComponent will be in-dialog, which we can set on the component property. If you haven’t already, start up Storybook with yarn storybook.

Import the html function from the lit-html package. We’ll use this in the Story template.

Declare a new const called DialogTemplate and make it equal to a function that returns html. We can pass a template string into html first argument using shorthand syntax. In the template string, add a new tag named in-dialog and an instance of ButtonComponent that displays a primary button with the call to action “Open”.

Import ButtonComponent into the story file so it will appear in Storybook.

Export ButtonComponent from Dialog.stories.js to satisfy Webpack compilation in Storybook.

Declare a new const named Primary and make it equal to a call to DialogTemplate using bind. Add a line so you can set args on the Primary story.

DialogComponent

We need to at the very least provide a boilerplate custom element of DialogComponent for the story. This will also enable development of DialogComponent in the next section. Make a new file named Dialog.ts in the same directory as the story.

Import the necessary reusable function from @in/common. For the autonomous custom element you’re about to develop, you will need Component and attachShadow.

Export a class named DialogComponent that extends HTMLElement, being sure to call super and attachShadow in the constructor. This will give us a Shadow DOM template we can work with in the Component decorator.

Decorate the class with the Component decorator, setting the selector to in-dialog. Give the component all the styling it requires via the style property. Since DialogComponent will have no visual component, we can safely set display: none on the :host.

Import DialogComponent into Dialog.stories.js so we can use it in the context of the story.

Export DialogComponent from Dialog.stories.js.

That’s all the DialogComponent boilerplate we need for now. In the next section, we’ll focus on this class implementation.

Binding Mock Data with HTML Attributes

In Dialog.stories.js let’s figure out the outward facing APIs we’ll need so a user can click on the ButtonComponent to open a dialog. Most importantly, we need a stable API that can be applied to any element the user can click and the instance of DialogComponent. This could be achieved many ways, but we’re going to choose a method that works via the template. HTML data attributes present an easy way to set custom attributes on an element, so let’s opt to use them to store an identifier for the dialog on the ButtonComponent. If we have a predictable id specified on the ButtonComponent, we have a way to query for that element. Give the args a new property named targetId set to dialog-hello-target. From here forward, we’ll refer to the DOM element that triggers the dialog to open as the “target”.

Pass the targetId through DialogTemplate so you can set a new HTML data-dialog-id data attribute on the ButtonComponent.

We could strictly enforce that any target should be specified with the data-dialog-id HTML data attribute. However; it seems more likely engineers may need more than one way to select the target in order to query for it in DOM. This query will happen in DialogComponent, where we’ll attach and detach event listeners on the target. Add a new property on args named targetSelector and set it to the selector needed to query for the ButtonComponent.

Just like before, pass the targetSelector through DialogTemplate, this time, setting a HTML attribute named target on the DialogComponent.

Each dialog is associated not just with a target, but also a HTML template. HTML templates are available in the Storybook iframe and just need to be selected via a query to be used. Each HTMLTemplateElement has a HTML data attribute declared on the template named data-template-id. The first template we’ll reference is named dialog-hello. Add another property to args named templateSelector and set it to [data-template-id="dialog-hello"].

Pass the templateSelector through the DialogTemplate first argument and set a new HTML attribute on the DialogComponent named template.

Finally, we just need to tell DialogComponent which type of dialog to display: a modal or tooltip. The first example is a modal, so let’s set another property on args named variant to modal.

Pass variant to the DialogComponent by setting a new HTML attribute named variant.

You now have a development environment suitable for developing the DialogComponent. In this section, we set up the story template with an instance of DialogComponent and ButtonComponent and gave each HTML attributes to link a target with a given dialog. If it still isn’t clear what all these HTML attributes will be used for, have no fear! In the next section, you’ll develop DialogComponent and use the value of each of these attributes which should reveal their meaning. By declaring DialogComponent aside the target ButtonComponent in a template, we’ve hopefully given engineers an easy-to-use API to use throughout an application.

DialogComponent

This autonomous custom element is unlike others we’ve developed so far in that there is no view associated with the element. DialogComponent behaves more like a controller in the traditional Model View Controller (MVC) paradigm. This component will pass the model from the values of HTML attributes to the view (a modal), which it will also instantiate. The DialogComponent is already a class which is the ideal interface for a controller. We can store state for the individual dialog here with some class properties. We’ll need to store whether the dialog is opened or closed. Set a new property named $state and type define this as open | close, a strict type definition which means the value of $state can only be one of two strings: open or close. Set the type definitions for properties associated with the three HTML attributes we set in the previous section: $target, $targetSelector, and $templateSelector. Lastly, set a property named $target we’ll eventually use to store a reference of the ButtonComponent (or any other target).

Observing Attributes

Declare the observedAttributes static getter on the class and listen for the three HTML attributes: target, template, and variant.

Set up the attributeChangedCallback with the usual arguments: name, prev and next and a switch statement. If the case the name matches template, set the value of $templateSelector. In the case of variant, set the value of $variant. You’ll reference these properties later in the component logic.

To associate the dialog with a target, declare a new method named setTarget, which requires a single argument named selector typed as a string. This will be the selector needed to query for the ButtonComponent.

Update the switch in the attributeChangedCallback to call setTarget when the case matches target. This may have to be wrapped in a setTimeout to work properly in the context of the LitHTML html function. We need to wait for a tick of the JavaScript engine before querying for the element, which is achievable by passing 0 to the second argument of setTarget.

Setting the Target

In the setTarget method, set the value of the $targetSelector property you declared earlier on the class type definition. Query for the ButtonComponent using document.querySelector and set the reference of the ButtonComponent to $target for use later in this method.

First thing we’ll do in this method is add some error handling for when the target is not found via querySelector. If this is the case, we want the method to fail silently for the end-user, so we’ll return, but only after notifying a developer of the problem via console.error.

The entire reason we’re querying for the ButtonComponent is so we can attach an event listener on click that will change $state from close to open. Declare a new method on DialogComponent for this purpose named targetListener. We may need access to the event, so add the first argument type defined as MouseEvent. If $state doesn’t equal open, call another method that doesn’t exist yet: onOpen.

Declare onOpen on DialogComponent and add a console.log here temporarily for testing out the method works.

In the setTarget method, call addEventListener on $target, being sure to listen for the click event. Bind the event listener callback to targetListener using bind. Optionally, set the capture to false in the third argument of addEventListener, which should be the default anyways.

You should be able to observe in Storybook that a console message is logged when clicking the ButtonComponent. Remove that console.log in onOpen when you’ve verified that the logic is working.

Displaying the HTML Template

The purpose of DialogComponent is to take a model provided by HTML attributes and display a dialog. The content of the dialog is provided by a HTML template already in DOM. Previously you provided a selector for that template via HTML attribute to set the value of the $templateSelector property. We’re going to return to the onOpen method to query for a HTML template with this selector in a moment, but first let’s declare a new property named $container on the class where we can store a reference to the instance of the dialog that will be displayed.

In the onOpen method, set a local const named template to a reference of the HTMLTemplateElement. Use $templateSelector when querying for the template on the document.

Similar to the setTarget method, let’s add some error handling here for the use case that the HTML template does not exist. Provide some feedback for an engineer with console.error and use return if template is undefined so the rest of the method’s logic can’t run and cause a bad experience for the end-user.

Eventually $container will be set to instances of ModalComponent or TooltipComponent, but we have yet to develop those components. For now use createElement to instantiate a new HTMLDivElement and set $container with that. Clone the template using cloneNode and set a new const named clone to the cloned template. So we verify the variant can be correctly passed, set a new CSS classname equal to $variant on the $container. Set the content of the $container, passing the clone to appendChild. Call appendChild on the document.body with $container. This ensures the dialog is the last element in the DOM tree, which will help ensure the dialog gains the correct z-index, which we’ll focus more on later. Finally, set $state to open.

If you open the Elements tab in Dev Tools, you should now observe a clone of the HTML template has been appended to the document.body. You just coded the core functionality of DialogComponent. You passed the value of HTML attributes using observedAttributes and attributeChangedCallback, then declared methods on the class that handles the target and opening a dialog. In the next section you’ll stand up two new autonomous custom elements: ModalComponent and TooltipComponent that will handle some basic view behaviors for each dialog variant.

Modal and Tooltip

We’ve abstracted a single dialog’s state to DialogComponent, which so far handles opening the dialog and based on the model passed through HTML attributes, displays the appropriate variant: modal or tooltip.

Modals in the application are classified as dialogs that take complete focus away from the current view. Modals typically appear in the center of the view, display a custom template, but can universally be cancelled via a button in the top right when the user clicks outside of the modal, or if the user presses the Escape key when the modal is in focus.

Tooltips are contextual dialogs that display in relation to content the user activated. Tooltips typically display beneath the content in a small dialog that can hold contextual information, usually a short phrase or instruction for the user.

The first dialog we activated in the last section was wrapped by a generic HTMlDivElement. We’ll change that soon. Using the variant, DialogComponent should display a ModalComponent or TooltipComponent. In this section, we’ll introduce the boilerplate for these components and begin displaying the HTML templates in the context of each Shadow DOM template. That means ModalComponent and TooltipComponent should both be autonomous custom elements. We’ll use template slots to inject the HTML templates into each component.

In this section we’ll stand up the components, import them into Dialog.stories.js so they can be displayed in the story, integrate them with DialogComponent and observe how they behave before proceeding to the next section.

ModalComponent

To start development on ModalComponent create a new file in the dialog directory named Modal.ts.

Import the relevant function from @in/common for an autonomous custom element.

Export a class named ModalComponent that extends HTMLElement. In the constructor call attachShadow.

Use the Component decorator to decorate the class, passing in the ElementMeta with a selector that specifies the custom element should be registered with the tag name in-modal. Provide empty template strings for the style and template properties so you can begin to fill them in.

The template for ModalComponent is as simple as it gets. Since we’re levering HTML templates for each dialog, we simply have to pass the template to a slot.

After observing the styling for a modal in Figma we need to come up with a way ModalComponent can appear on top of the rest of the layout, while positioned at the center. This can be achieved by selecting the :host and ensuring the custom element is a block element with display: block. This will allow every ModalComponent to be reliably positioned and sized. To center the modal, give the element position: fixed and adjust the top and left to 50% (relative to the document.body which roughly centers the component. Use a CSS transform to affix the modal perfectly in the center of the view with a horizontal and vertical translation set to -50% (relative to the size of the modal). Give the modal a z-index set to 9000. This is a relatively high index in the z-index layering over that ensures all other elements have an opportunity to properly layer, while dialogs can always display above all other content.

We want to also fix some potential issues that could happen with elements passing through the slot. Due to giving the modal a fixed position, direct descendants of the element won’t display with the appropriate size that fills out the dialog. To fix this, select all slotted elements with the pseudo selector ::slotted(*) and give them an absolute position, a width set to 100% and auto height.

In Figma, it appears ModalComponent have a different box shadow compared to CardComponent, which appear inside the context of a modal. According to design, this is because dialogs have a much greater z-index so they get a different visual treatment. box-shadow is typically the domain of CardComponent so override the default styling in that component using the ::slotted pseudo selector once more. Pass box-shadow a CSS variable derived from the design stylesheet named var(--shadow-modal).

Once styling is complete for ModalComponent, head back over to Dialog.stories.js and import the class.

Add ModalComponent to the exports in Dialog.stories.js as well so the Webpack config for Storybook can properly build the story.

You shouldn’t be able to observe any changes yet in the story because you haven’t integrated ModalComponent with DialogComponent yet. In the previous section, you listened for HTML attributes on DialogComponent and set the value of the $variant property, which can be equal to either modal or tooltip.

Update the onOpen method by deprecating the div that was there for test purposes, instead opting for the tag name of the variant.

You should now be able to observe a styled ModalComponent in Storybook when you press the button labeled “Open” in the Primary dialog story. Keen observers will notice in the HTML template currently displayed that there is a button labeled “More Info”. Upon clicking that button, another dialog opens. You’re observing the DialogComponent in action. Each HTML template contains an instance of the DialogComponent custom element declared with the proper HTML attributes that specify the relation to a target.

Each modal displays a button in the top right that is intended to be used to close the modal upon user click. We’ll deal with this feature in a bit, along with any other use cases that close the modal dialog.

In the second modal that appears above the first by virtue of being appended to the document.body with the same z-index, you can observe some boilerplate “Lorum ipsum” body copy, followed by a (?). The intention is that anywhere a (?) appears, the user should be able to click and observe a tooltip with contextual information. Let’s continue by standing up another autonomous custom element named TooltipComponent.

TooltipComponent

Make a new file in the dialog directory named Tooltip.ts.

Import Component and attachShadow from the @in/common package.

Export a class named TooltipComponent that extends HTMLElement, being sure to call attachShadow in the constructor.

Declare the Component decorator in the same way you did the modal, although this time specify the tag name as in-tooltip.

The template for TooltipComponent is the same as ModalComponent, a single template slot that is intended for any HTML template that displays a small amounft of information for the end-user.

Styling the TooltipComponent is very similar to ModalComponent; however, you need to omit position styles here because those will have to be dynamic to support the Acceptance Criteria that states “TooltipComponent should display a contextual tooltip just beneath an element the user triggered display”. According to Figma, TooltipComponent should have a maximum width of 300px. You’ll need to apply the same fix for any slotted content so it properly fills its container. Looking once more at the Figma, it appears tooltips should display a different box shadow than modals or the default used by CardComponent. Use this opportunity to also override the CardComponent styles.

Import TooltipComponent into Dialog.stories.js, making sure to also export the class in the same file.

Returning to Storybook, you should be able to click “Open”, then “More Info” to display the second modal. Upon clicking “(?)” you’ll observe an issue. The tooltip doesn’t appear. Pretty anticlimactic, right? This is due to an issue with the implementation in DialogComponent we’ll explore in depth in the next section.

Querying DOM Across Shadow Boundaries

There’s a problem in the DialogComponent that causes the TooltipComponent not to appear when DialogComponent is declared in the context of the ModalComponent Shadow DOM. Since the instances of DialogComponent is embedded in Shadow DOM, DialogComponent can’t simply query for a HTML template using document.querySelector. The querySelector method doesn’t cross the Shadow DOM boundaries imposed by the multiple instances of ModalComponent.

There is one way we could fix this. ModalComponent could be an autonomous custom element that doesn’t use Shadow DOM. We could use other methods from the @in/common package so modals get the appropriate styling, like we have done with customized built-in elements in previous chapters. If we choose this approach, we lose the main benefit of Shadow DOM: the encapsulated style and template. Without Shadow DOM, querySelector would be able to function per normal.

Another approach that would allow us to retain Shadow DOM in ModalComponent is to code a new utility that can query for elements while piercing the Shadow boundary. For that, we’d need a function that can walk the tree of nodes that make up DOM and if an element has a shadowRoot, recursively call the function and walk that tree of nodes, trying to query for the element we need to select.

Luckily, a method exists on the document already that could help walk a tree of nodes. document.createTreeWalker is a specialized method for setting up a TreeWalker Object. While holding a reference to the TreeWalker, you can use a while loop to iterate through every node in a tree of nodes, starting at the document.body or any other node, i.e. the shadowRoot. createTreeWalker doesn’t by default cross the shadow boundary, so we’ll have to code some custom logic to ensure that happens, but TreeWalker does provide an extremely performant means to walk a tree of nodes.

In this section, you’ll move back to the library code in the @in/common package and code a new function named query which returns a recursive function that gets called every time the TreeWalker encounters a node that has a shadowRoot. The recursive function should get called until the last node in the tree has been parsed or a match is found via querySelector. query will be exported from the library and imported into the DialogComponent just like any other function from the @in/common package.

Make a new file named query.ts in the directory packages/common/src/template.

In query.ts export a new function named query. This function will work much like querySelector, in that the first argument takes the selector. Unlike querySelector which exists on the prototype of every Element, query is a “pure” function, so we’ll need to pass the starting point for the query in the second argument named root. query returns an Element, the element we are selecting with the selector.

This algorithm needs to be recursive because there will be instances where the TreeWalker will reach a shadow boundary and stop, but we want to run the algorithm again, starting at the Shadow Root and walking the tree of nodes from there, querying for the element that should match the selector. Return another function named __query that takes similar arguments. This time the second argument represents a match, which only happens once, but we need to pass it recursively and check if there’s a match at the start of the function. The third argument is another Element which we’ll use similarly to the query function, a starting point to query for the element. The arguments get flipped here because element isn’t required in the initial call to __query. Declare the __query function here in the context of query and make sure it returns the Element to satisfy the type definitions for now.

The code we’ll write goes inside of the recursive __query function. At the start of this function check if you can just use querySelector to find the element and set the value of match with what is returned by querySelector. If element is not undefined here, we’ll want to skip to the next line. On the next line, use a conditional to check if match is not undefined and return match. This will short circuit the recursive function if an element is found.

If match is undefined, we want to instantiate a new instance of TreeWalker by setting a new const named walk and passing all the arguments required by document.createTreeWalker. The first argument is the root node to start walking, which should be the document.body if element is undefined. The next argument optional for createTreeWalker is a way to filter types of nodes. We’ll use the NodeFilter.SHOW_ELEMENT which filters only Element nodes and discards other nodes like Comment or DocumentFragment. The next argument is a filter for the nodes that pass the first filter, it tells when TreeWalker should accept a node. We need FILTER_ACCEPT here. Set the fourth argument to false, a boolean that indicates if an entire sub-tree should be discarded when a reference is also discarded. For more information about TreeWalker, view the documentation on MDN.

With a reference to the TreeWalker stored on walk, we can iterate through each Element as the tree is being walked with a while loop, calling the method nextNode on walk.

Inside the while, use an if statement to check if the currentNode can query for the selector. When truthy, set match to the result of the querySelector.

Write another conditional that checks if the currentNode has a shadowRoot which querySelector can’t pierce. Call __query recursively, passing the selector and match (which may still be undefined), and the shadowRoot.

After you’re done with the while loop, make sure the __query function still returns match at the very end. That’s all there is to coding an algorithm that recursively walks a tree of nodes and queries for a single Element, but what if you wanted to replicate the functionality of querySelectorAll? Let’s do just that.

In the same file declare another recursive implementation. This time wrap the recursive function named __queryAll with a function named queryAll. Both function take the same arguments as query and __query with one exception. __queryAll second argument should be an Array of Element because queryAll can return multiple matches.

The start of __queryAll is very similar. Check that element is falsey and the matches Array is empty. Query using the selector from the document using querySelectorAll and concatenate the Array with the results of the query.

The implementation of TreeWalker is exactly the same, although what happens on each loop of the while changes.

Check here if the currentNode has any matches to the selector using querySelector, followed by another if statement that checks if the matches Array doesn’t contain the currentNode. It could because this algorithm walks down the tree. If both conditions are truthy, set matches to the NodeList returned by querySelectorAll, but use Array.form to convert the NodeList into an Array before concatenating the matches.

Still in the while loop, check if the currentNode has a shadowRoot and if so, recursively call __queryAll to walk that tree of nodes.

After making sure __queryAll still returns matches at the end of the function, export both of the functions from query.ts if you haven’t already. Open the index.ts file in packages/common/src/template and add the proper exports.

Open packages/common/index.ts and export query and queryAll from there as well.

Build the @in/common package using lerna so you can pickup the changes in DialogComponent.

If you have the Storybook server running, stop it momentarily, and restart the process.

In Dialog.ts import the query function.

Deprecate the call to querySelector in the onOpen method of DialogComponent and use query instead.

At this point, you should be able to observe that an instance of TooltipComponent appears in the view when you click the (?) in the second modal found in the Primary dialog story. The tooltip still isn’t positioned where it should be, just below the element you clicked, so let’s fix that. Before, when calling onOpen, you declared the first argument of this method to be a MouseEvent because the method is bound to addEventListener.

We need a way to pass the position and size of the element that was clicked to contextually position the TooltipComponent below the element. CustomEvent works well in this scenario because we have direct access to a reference of the element the event should be dispatched to. In the onOpen method, after the #container has been appended to DOM, check if the $variant is equal to tooltip and if truthy, call dispatchEvent on the $container which is sure to be an instance of TooltipComponent. Pass dispatchEvent a CustomEvent named position and set a property named rect on the detail property to the DOMRect of the element the user clicked on, which is available via ev.target. For more information about DOMReact, visit MDN.

Open Toolip.ts and import Listen from @in/common so we can listen for the position event.

Add a new method on TooltipComponent named onPosition and decorate the method with the Listen decorator, passing the decorator the name of the event: position. In the method, set a const named rect to ev.detail.rect.

We’re going to use the information from the DOMRect to position the ToolipComponent properly below the “(?)” and to size the CardComponent. To style the CardComponent, we need an easy way to reference it. CardComponent is not a direct descendant of the TooltipComponent Shadow Root. The CardComponent is injected through a template slot. Set up another method on TooltipComponent that queries for the CardComponent via the assignedNodes on the template slot. CardComponent should be the only child, so you can safely select the first item in the NodeList. Type define $child as an Element.

In the onPosition method, we’re going to style the TooltipComponent position and size using two DomRect: one from the CardComponent which dictates the size of the TooltipComponent and the other from the rect passed from the element the user clicked on. We can use that DomRect to find the position of the bottom of the element and use that position to style the top of the TooltipComponent.

First, calculate the amount of displacement you’ll need to center the tooltip left/right, which is equal to half the width of the CardComponent. Style the top of the TooltipComponent using the rect.bottom while adding 12 pixels to offset the tooltip vertically. Style the left using the rect.left minus the leftDisplacement, which has the effect of centering the tooltip. Style the width and height to the CardComponent width and height. Finally, ensure the element is visible by setting the visibility.

With these styles in place, you should now be able to observe in Storybook that when clicking “(?)” in the second modal, the tooltip appears positioned underneath the cursor. This is partly due to the “(?)” being encapsulated by a HTMLSpanElement, which gives the ev.target a DOMRect.

Now you have considered all the use cases for opening dialogs while developing the ModalComponent and DialogComponent it’s now time to think about how to close the dialogs in a user friendly way. In the next section you’ll do just that.

DialogStack

In DialogComponent, you stored the state of a single dialog, but haven’t yet found a way to orchestrate the rendering of several dialogs at once. You also haven’t handled the “closed” state of a dialog, which is what happens when the user closes the dialog either by pressing the “Escape” key, the close button where available, or by clicking outside of the dialog.

Several problems could arise from the current implementation if we were to attempt to handle all these use cases. Nothing is currently tracking if a dialog is focused. If we add event listeners to each dialog we could end up with many different event listeners which could hurt performance, however unlikely given the number of dialogs in the current implementation. Perhaps it would be a good idea to delegate the focus event listener to a single place that also tracks the currently focused dialog.

Having all dialogs on the same z-index could also cause issues. We’d have to rely on the order of the elements in DOM which means a lot of DOM manipulation each time the order of dialogs changes. Suppose the user clicks on another dialog in the background. The user would expect that dialog to come to the front. In order to do that currently, we’d need to change the order of DOM nodes appended to the document.body. Nothing can handle a change like that yet, but perhaps a more performant solution would be to set the z-index of each dialog in a well defined range of z-index reserved only for dialogs: 9000-9999.

To orchestrate the rendering of several dialogs, let’s introduce a new class named DialogStack. The responsibility of DialogStack will be the following:

  • Store order of dialogs rendered in the view
  • Store template ids
  • Store the currently focused dialog
  • Store the previously focused dialog
  • Delegate focus events for each dialog

DialogStack will require some integration with DialogComponent. When DialogComponent is instantiated and changes state, the component should update DialogStack. DialogStack would be a singleton and requires global scope to operate. For the purposes of this exercise, we’ll instantiate DialogStack on the window so it’s accessible globally.

To begin development on DialogStack, make a new file named DialogStack.ts in the same directory where you’ve been working on all the dialogs.

DialogStack

In DialogStack.ts export a new class named DialogStack and declare a constructor. Add two properties (stack and templateId) we know are required if DialogStack is supposed to store template ids and the order of dialogs rendered in the view.

Let’s first handle the registration and removal of template ids. Add a method named registerTemplate that will eventually be called from the context of DialogComponent. The only argument for the new method is a string named id. If the id is not found in the templateId Array, add the id to the Array.

Declare another method that finds the index of an id in the templateId Array. You’ll need this index to remove an id from the Array.

Make a method on the DialogStack class named removeTemplate. Using the only argument id, call findTemplateIndex. Splice the templateId at the index of the id if it exists. This has the effect of removing the id from the Array.

With templateId state covered, let’s turn our attention to managing the z-index of each dialog in the stack Array. We haven’t populated the Array yet, but supposing we did, the dialog at the last index in the Array would be the dialog that should be layered on top of every other. Set a const named base to 9000, the first (and lowest) z-index. Iterate through the stack with forEach, setting the zIndex of each dialog, incrementing the z-index by the index of the dialog in the Array.
