Make another method that adds a dialog to the stack Array. The argument for this method is typed Element to keep it generic, but it might as well be ModalComponent | TooltipComponent. Call push on the Array.prototype to add the dialog to the stack Array. DialogComponent currently handles rendering the dialog, but in a member you’ll deprecate that functionality from DialogComponent because it makes a lot more sense to add the call to appendChild here. After the dialog is appended to the document.body, call setZIndexes.

Integrate DialogStack with DialogComponent

Import DialogStack into Dialog.ts.

Declare a new type interface for the DialogStack. This class should be global, so we’ll store it on the window for now.

Import DialogStack into Dialog.stories.js so it can be used in the context of the story. You should also export the class from the file.

Instantiate a new instance of DialogStack on the window. By setting a property named __dialogStack on window to an instance of DialogStack, we can reference this instance from DialogComponent.

DialogComponent requires some modification to integrate with DialogStack. Update the attributeChangedCallback with a call to registerTemplate on window.__dialogStack, but only if a template is not found by calling findTemplateIndex.

In the onOpen method, remove the call to document.body.appendChild and update the method with a call to pushDialog on window.__dialogStack. The new API includes the ability to append a dialog to the document.body.

Handling Closed State

DialogStack has the ability to add dialogs and sort their layering order, but we haven’t included any logic to handle removing dialogs from DOM. When the user closes a dialog, the dialog should be removed. Dialogs are stored on the DialogStack class in an Array. We would need to get the index of the dialog via the Array.prototype.findIndex method so we can later call Array.prototype.splice to remove the Element from the Array. Declare a new method on DialogStack that returns the index of an Element in stack Array.

In addition to removing the Element from state, we also need to query for the DialogComponent, which controls the state of a single dialog. Since instances of DialogComponent are not necessarily direct children of the document.body, we can’t use querySelector. Use cases like this one is what query was made for, so we’ll import that function.

Declare another method on DialogStack called removeDialog and pass the method a single argument, an Element. Every dialog has a HTML attribute that contains an id you can use to query for the DialogComponent. DialogComponent use the data-target-id HTML data attribute for this id, while each dialog uses the data-dialog-id HTML data attribute.

Dispatch a CustomEvent to the DialogComponent with the name close. Maintain the current state of dialogs in DialogStack by splicing the Array, effectively removing the dialog from state. Remove the Element from DOM using removeChild and call SetZIndices in case any other dialogs need to be reshuffled.

Update DialogComponent with a new method that handles changing the $state from open to close, being sure to call removeDialog and removeTemplate on the DialogStack.

In the onOpen method, query for a “close” button that should have the CSS class name .dialog-close-button and if there is an instance of the button, use addEventListener to handle the click event on the element. Call onClose in the event handler callback.

Whenever DialogComponent is removed from DOM, also remove the template from DialogStack state.

Handling Focus

To handle the use case when a user clicks outside of a dialog, which should cause it to close, DialogStack needs a way to handle focus events. Delegating the event in DialogStack seems like a good idea so each DialogCompoment doesn’t attach a duplicate event listener. Add two new properties to DialogStack: last and focused that will store the last focused and currently focused Element.

Add another method named addListeners that will eventually be called in the constructor to attach the event listener to the document.body. Pass the event listener callback a new method that hasn’t been declared yet on DialogStack: onFocus.

The click event is on document.body because we’re using event delegation. In the onFocus callback, using the ev.target (the Element the user clicked), call closest and query for the nearest dialog. closest is a method on every Element that walks up the DOM tree to find the closest Element that matches the selector. More info about closest on MDN.

Whenever a tooltip is currently focused, we can assume that the user wants to dismiss the tooltip if they didn’t click on the tooltip. Had the user clicked on the tooltip, closest would return something, but without a match, closest returns null. If the tooltip is the currently focused Element, call removeDialog, passing in the reference to the Element.

To maintain the state of the previous and current focused Element, make a new method named focusDialog that sets last and focused

Call focusDialog in pushDialog to focus the dialog that was just appended to DOM.

In removeDialog, focus the dialog that is the last item in the stack Array.

Add the call to addListeners in the constructor to handle the event listener.

After manually testing out the changes to DialogStack and DialogComponent in Storybook, you observe that modals correctly close and focus based on user interaction. You are now ready to write some automated tests for the dialogs.

Testing Dialogs

In this section, you’ll write some integration tests for the dialog with Cypress, using Storybook as the testbed. Integration tests are crucial for the dialogs, which at this point have several moving parts: DialogComponent, DialogStack, ModalComponent and TooltipComponent. You’ll test the following:

  • Should display a dialog
  • Should close a dialog
  • Should close and open dialog again
  • Should open another dialog
  • Should open and close tooltip
  • Should open and close all dialogs

After coding the integration tests and observing all the tests pass with Cypress, you’ll follow up with some snapshot tests.

Integration Tests

In each of the integration tests, you’ll use the Primary dialog story from this chapter as a test bed.

Make a new file in the cypress/integration directory called Dialog.spec.js.

Add a describe block to the test file and use a beforeEach to mitigate any issues with testing the components in Storybook.

With Cypress, call cy.visit with the query params necessary to navigate to the Primary dialog story in Storybook. Test if an element with tag name in-modal exists in the view.

This next test is a bit more verbose. Building off the last few tests, open the second modal with Cypress.

Direct Cypress to click on the “(?)” in the second modal, which opens the tooltip. Cypress should then click the #root, which should close the tooltip. Tell Cypress to click the “close” button in the footer of the open ModalComponent. This should close the modal.

Direct Cypress to click on the “close” button of the first modal, followed by assertions that neither ModalComponent or TooltipComponent exist.

Snapshots

With Storybook still running, generate snapshots for the component.

When snapshots have been generated for the Dialog story, add them to your commit. Commit your changes in git to complete this section. After you’ve completed integration and snapshot tests for DialogComponent let’s review the content of Chapter Six.

Summary

Dialogs are a common user interface component in enterprise-grade applications. In this chapter you developed two types of dialogs: modals and tooltips. By abstracting each type to autonomous custom elements, you were able to isolate the view (ModalComponent and TooltipComponent) from another autonomous custom element that acted like a controller in the traditional sense of MVC. DialogComponent handled the state of a single dialog, delivering a model through HTML attributes to a dynamically generated instance of a dialog.

While giving engineers an interface to declare dialogs alongside the elements that trigger their display in DOM, you ran into an issue where Shadow DOM could obscure the elements from being queried with querySelector. The query function you wrote traverses Shadow boundaries, querying for DOM nodes with a selector similar to querySelector.

After observing how several dialogs worked together, you built DialogStack which handled the state of many dialogs. You also delegated focus events to DialogStack, a singleton instantiated on the window.

By creating a separation of concerns between several components, hopefully you gained an appreciation of how to architect user interfaces in a sustainable and intuitive fashion. This is the last chapter in Part Two where you’ll participate in development of complex custom elements. In later chapters, the development of the Header, Content, Footer layout should hopefully feel like a cakewalk compared to the development of the dialogs and table. Before developing custom elements in the context of an application, you’ll learn best practices for distributing a UI library of custom elements in the next chapter.

Distributing Custom Element Libraries

Chapter Seven

UI Libraries

Design and Engineering

Cooperation between design and engineering in large enterprise organizations is crucial to ensure scalability and maintainability for a codebase. That cooperation often happens at the level of a UI library, a collection of user interfaces that handle repeatable views in an application. Figma connects everyone involved in the design process, giving designers a venue to publish UI designs and other stakeholders the ability to comment and interact with the design.

Design teams often follow the principals of atomic design, a philosophy popularized by designer and developer Brad Frost. Atomic design prescribes an architecture that begins at the smallest units: atoms, and scales into molecules and organisms. As this happens, the more complex the user interface becomes. Organisms are comprised of molecules, molecules are comprised of atoms. You’ve experienced this design pattern while developing the many user interfaces in this book. CSS variables that represent design tokens serve as atoms. TextInputComponent, CardComponent could be considered molecules, while TableComponent or DialogComponent are organisms. Understanding the atomic design pattern is paramount when designing and developing a UI library.

When realized in the context of a UI library, atomic design promotes a separation of concerns between UI components when components are built with a strict separation of concerns. If the user interfaces are built once and distributed across an organization in a UI library, it promotes consistency and uniformity across a product. UI libraries can reduce maintenance overhead. Unnecessary churn could happen if teams were to code the same user interfaces in many different ways. UI libraries built with JavaScript frameworks and libraries have the cost of dependency maintenance, an issue that is substantially reduced UI libraries are built entirely with browser specifications.

UI libraries can be developed in such a way that allows engineers to move fast and build features. Exporting discrete units of functionality promotes reuse. Distributing components that handle complex user interaction patterns is much more difficult. Suppose a team wanted to use TableComponent but needed the additional feature of selecting multiple rows. There isn’t a mechanism in the library yet for a user interface that allows toggling something, like a checkbox. If a CheckboxComponent were already developed, adding one to each row of TableComponent would be tricky to avoid breaking changes, the feature would have to be opted in, probably by setting a HTML attribute. Making components like TableComponent composable is difficult in any library, but possible. You’ve already abstracted each row and cell to separate components. The TrComponent and TdComponent class could be extended to enhance them with other functionality. This example is just one of many problems that can arise because of how components are architected; however, by exporting the discrete units of functionality that comprise complex components, you can retain design characteristics and user experience behaviors while giving teams the opportunity to construct custom user experiences.

Continuous Integration

How UI libraries are integrated and distributed in an enterprise organization’s development pipeline are as critical to their success as how they are architected. Continuous integration ensures that code which can’t be properly built or tested isn’t being introduced into the main branch of a repository. Although integration depends largely on the tooling that is available, in this chapter, you’ll learn how to set up a continuous integration pipeline with Github Actions. By implementing a package format that teams can easily install and import, you’ll implement best practices for distributing a UI library of Web Components.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to validate a pull request in Github by running integration and snapshot tests via Github Actions. Cypress and Storyshots both require Storybook to be properly built, so you’ll learn how to run Storybook with Github Actions. When an engineer creates a pull request in Github, it’s also a good idea to check the build is successful, otherwise the project cannot be properly built before it’s deployed. Typically, deployment of any npm packages happens when a PR meets some criteria after being merged to the main branch. You’ll set up everything in Github Actions leading up to that point, while also deploying Storybook to Github Pages to observe the current state of the components after merging to the main branch.

Distribution

It should be as easy as possible for teams to install and start using the components. JavaScript packages are usually distributed via npm, the node package manager. npm packages use the package.json file for configuring the package. By implementing a predictable package format that is easily interpreted by build tools like Webpack, Rollup, snowpack or esbuild, it ensures the components in a UI library are reused. These build tools interpret the package.json in order to bundle the JavaScript, using the configuration therein to locate the entry point(s) of the JavaScript that is exported from the package.

Components in the UI library are strictly typed with TypeScript, although browsers cannot interpret TypeScript, only JavaScript. TypeScript also allows you to develop with specifications only available in future iterations of the ECMAScript specification that haven’t been adopted in browsers yet, like the decorator pattern you’ve used when developing the components. TypeScript can be configured to compile down to a version of the ECMAScript spec that is compatible with the browsers you intend to support. To ensure support across a great range of browsers, you can compile the library to ES2015, a version of the ECMAScript specification that is found in all major evergreen browsers (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari, Microsoft Edge). The module pattern that wraps the code can also be configured with TypeScript. ES2015 modules can be interpreted by build tools and in the browser. Internet Explorer 11 was the last major browser to not implement ES2015. If you require support for IE11, additional steps must be taken to compile the code down to ES5, an earlier version of ECMAScript, and commonjs modules, which can be interpreted by IE11 browser. We’re not going to explore configuration for IE11 in this book since Microsoft has signaled a deprecation timeline for the browser. In this chapter, you’ll learn how to distribute a UI library that works in evergreen browsers.

Documentation

Documentation is an important part of the distribution strategy for a UI library. Giving engineers access to clear, concise documentation for each component allows them to easily understand how to integrate the component into their application. Luckily for us, Storybook provides exceptional tooling for documenting UI components. The Custom Elements Manifest Analyzer provides a means to statically analyze the class definitions of each component. The Custom Elements Manifest is a JSON file located in the root of the repository. Storybook references the Custom Elements Manifest to configure documentation for each component. While parts of the components are self-documenting (their methods are analyzable), Custom Elements Manifest will also analyze any JSDoc comments attached to each class. In this chapter, you’ll write inline documentation with JSDoc for each component that describes each component’s tag name, public methods, and HTML attributes that are exposed. These comments, while providing inline documentation for engineers working on the UI library, will also become visible in Storybook in a well formatted set of documentation.

In this chapter, you’re going to take a drastic turn in development. Instead of developing a component, you will mainly write configuration and code scripts that support build tools such as Lerna, TypeScript, Rollup, and Storybook. By the end of the chapter you should have a stable build for the @in/ui package, a UI library filled with the components you developed in previous chapters. You’ll use the library package like any other npm package in Part Three, when you’ll develop an application using the components found in the @in/ui package.

What you will build

  • Bundle a UI library with Rollup
  • Document each component with JSDoc
  • Generate a Custom Elements Manifest
  • Configuration for Github Actions

What you will learn

Distributing Custom Element UI Libraries

In this section, you’ll prepare the UI library for distribution by optimizing the code using techniques that promote treeshaking and fast build times. You’ll format the package so the directory structure is machine readable by TypeScript, which should statically analyze the package when it is a dependency of another project. Developers should be able to inspect the type definitions of each component they are importing into their project from the package. By the end of this section, you will have a library package that is compatible with build tools like Webpack, Rollup, snowpack, and esbuild.

Named Exports

The first thing we’ll do is refactor how the components are exported from each directory in packages/component/src. So far, you only had to export anything from a file that was needed in the context of a story file, but now we have to consider how components should be exported for distribution in the UI library.

One strategy to implement here is the inclusion of a new file in each component directory: index.ts. The purpose of this file is to expose anything that should become part of the library, any public APIs. A tool at our disposal for exporting everything from a file that uses the export keyword is export *. However, this practice causes a bottleneck for build tools that prevents them from “treeshaking” the library, removing unused parts of the library that were not directly imported into another project. Named ES2015 exports are necessary to ensure a library is treeshakable. Named exports allow build tools to statically analyze dependencies far better, enabling them to treeshake ununsed parts of the library.

In each component directory, make a new file named index.ts. Observe in each component file what is currently exported using the export keyword and export the same exports in the index.ts. After we walk through each component, we’ll create another index.ts in the root directory of the @in/ui package that exports everything for the library using named ES2015 exports.

Make a new file in packages/component/src/button named index.ts.

After observing what is exported in Button.ts, add another named export in index.ts for ButtonComponent.

Create another index.ts file in the card directory.

Export CardComponent from the new index.ts file.

Make an index.ts file in the dialog directory.

Export all the necessary dialog components from the index.ts.

Make an index.ts file in the input directory.

Export the necessary parts for anyone to use TextInputComponent.

Make an index.ts file in the table directory.

Export the necessary parts of the table.

Export everything from index.ts in the packages/component directory.

By exporting the components with named 2015 exports, you’ve made the entire library treeshakable. If an engineer only wanted to import CardComponent into their project, they can do so without bundling the rest of the library. This would not have been possible necessarily with export *. Now that you’re done formatting the source code for distribution, let’s consider how the package will look if we build.

Build Optimizations

Building the library package for distribution means transpiling TypeScript down to a specific version of ECMAScript that is compatible with the browsers you have to support. You’ll use the TypeScript compiler for this purpose. After the code is transpiled, another optimization we can provide to anyone using this package is bundling the entire library in one file that exports everything in ES2015 modules. This pattern is called a FESM (Flat ECMAScript Module). By exporting a FESM for bundlers like Webpack, you can optimize how the library is built. Since the bundler only has one file to statically analyze as opposed to many, it can reduce build times. Rollup is an excellent tool for bundling a UI library into a FESM, so we’ll use it.

The necessary build files have been supplied for you in packages/component. Let’s observe what’s happening in each file. Open packages/component/rollup.config.js. In this file, Rollup is configured to use TypeScript and resolve dependencies from npm. When rollup builds the project, it outputs a file in packages/component/dist/fesm2015/index.js formatted as a FESM. Rollup also provides sourcemaps in the same directory, which can greatly enhance developer experience in some use cases like when inspecting code in Google Chrome Dev Tools.

As part of the rollup build, type definitions are outputted in dist/fesm2015 but we want the type definitions to be outputted in the root directory of the package. To do this, we’ll need to run the TypeScript compiler again and provide the following configuration in a tsconfig.json that tells the compiler to only emit type definitions in dist/types.

Language Support

TypeScript has the ability to compile down to a specific version of the ECMAScript specification, which has been updated yearly with new features since 2015. Which version of the ECMAScript specification you compile depends on the end consumer. Decisions surrounding which browsers to support in an enterprise organization are largely guided by user metrics. Browsers support varying parts of the latest ECMAScript specifications, but we can reliably compile down to ES2015 because all evergreen browsers have implemented this version of the specification. Depending on how may browsers you want to support, you maybe able to compile to a newer version of the ECMAScript protocol.

Other tools like Babel solve this problem differently. Relying on browserslist that specifies which browsers are supported, babel transpiles a codebase to a version of ECMAScript that fits the browser support profile. This sounds like an attractive solution, although possibly not the most optimal because another tool is added to the build pipeline. For that reason, we’ll just output the lowest common denominator that works in all evergreen browsers: ES2015.

Build

After the package is transpiled with TypeScript and bundled with Rollup, the build script also copies the package.json file to the dist directory. This is to ensure paths configured in the package.json resolve correctly when the root directory is the dist directory. Inspect the build scripts in the package.json.

Package Format

To distribute a npm package, the root directory must include a package.json. This file specifies the name of the package (@in/ui), the version (0.0.1), information about licensing ("license": "MIT",) and the package’s dependencies. Any package that is imported into the UI library and referenced in source code should be declared in dependencies, while any dependency required for development should be declared in devDependencies. @in/ui only has one dependency: @in/common, the micro-library that exports decorators for component development. We could opt to include the micro-library with the UI library or allow downstream bundlers to resolve the dependency and bundle @in/common accordingly.

Bundlers will need some more configuration in the package.json to interpret the library package. Let’s add the necessary configuration.

The package.json should include an entry that specifies the package exports ES2015 modules. Add the type property to the package.json and set the value to module.

To provide the entry points of the UI library for the latest bundlers, declare the exports. The paths declared in this Object will be referenced by Webpack during development in the monorepo.

For legacy bundlers, use the prior implementation which specified the entry point on the main field and the type definitions entry point on the types field.

If we omit dist from these fields it may cause problems in the monorepo. Lerna and Storybook depend on the main and types fields in the package.json to map each package in the monorepo for development. In Part Three, when you import components from @in/ui into the application, lerna will not be able to function properly if the main and types fields do not point to the correct files in the dist directory. To correct this behavior, while also providing a clean package.json for distribution, we’ll process the the package.json file prior to publishing to npm.

Make sure the main and types fields include dist in the path.

The prepublishOnly script in the package.json found at packages/component/package.json runs prior to publishing to npm. The script currently copies the package.json to dist. We have an opportunity here to insert more custom logic that processes the file.

To make sure the package.json is formatted correctly for distribution, we’ll need some way to process the file and output the edited file in the dist directory. Node includes tools in fs that allow scripts to interact with the local filesystem. The primary reason we need to edit the package.json prior to distribution is due to how it’s formatted for use in the monorepo. Paths in the packages/component/package.json point to the dist/ directory so other packages in the monorepo can source the built package during development. When the library is built in dist, we need a script that edits those paths relative to the files in the dist directory instead.

The function readFile and writeFile can help us with this task. When referencing file paths in node scripts it’s helpful to wrap the string in a function exported from path named resolve. This ensures the path will resolve correctly on any OS filesystem. Make a new file named prepublish.js in packages/component. Open prepublish.js in your IDE and import the necessary function from fs and path.

Call readFile, passing in the package.json that was copied to dist into the first argument. The second argument of readFile specifies the format the read should be reach, which is utf-8. The third argument is a function callback where the contents of the file are passed.

Parse the JSON with JSON.parse and begin editing the fields for the package.json that is distributed with the library package. Change the paths in the main and types fields in relation to the the package.json in dist.

The scripts Object is unnecessary for distribution. it only includes scripts that builds the library, so it can be omitted.

Call writeFile, passing in the path to the package.json in the first argument, JSON in the second argument, and finally the required callback in the third argument where you can log some feedback that will be displayed in the Terminal.

When you are finished, prepublish.js should appear as follows.

This node script should run when lerna calls the prepublishOnly script in the package.json found at packages/component/package.json. Append node prepublish.js to the prepublishOnly script.

The prepublishOnly step copies the package.json to the dist directory and runs the script in prepublish.js. This script reads the package.json in dist, sets the correct paths on the main and types fields, and deletes the scripts property because consumers of the package need not interpret these scripts used during the build process.

That’s all there is to configuring the library build. In this section, you declared named exports to make the UI library treeshakable. You configured TypeScript and Rollup to build a FESM which should optimize build times for downstream consumers of the package. TypeScript also output type definitions for developers to reference whenever importing anything from the @in/ui package. You reviewed how the package is built, inspecting the rollup.config.js, tsconfig.json, and package.json and declared several properties on the package.json that enable bundlers to interpret the package. To resolve an issue with how lerna builds the @in/ui package and how consumers of the package should interpret the package, you implemented a script that edits the package.json for distribution only, while retaining the configuration lerna requires.

Providing Documentation with Custom Elements Manifest and Storybook

We’ve got a stable library package that could be published to npm so others can reuse the components. It should be simple, right? An engineer installs the @in/ui package and imports the component where applicable, but then is faced with a dilemma. How does any of this work? Savvy engineers may inspect the type definitions to get a sense of how a component works, but those lack any context for the HTML attributes which are a heavily used interface for custom elements. The engineer would then have to inspect the source, which is compiled to ES2015 and wrapped in a strange decorator pattern. To solve this dilemma, we can provide documentation for the end-users of the component library.

So far, you’ve used Storybook as a development environment. For each use case, you coded a Story and provided a template and arguments that generated Controls for the Storybook Canvas. Storybook also has built-in tooling to display documentation for each component in the Docs tab. The first Story for each component is prioritized in the Docs tab. The user has the option to display the template in code beneath an example of the Story. When available, any HTML attributes or methods the component exposes are displayed in a table beneath the example.

By default, only the example is displayed for each Story in the Docs tab in Storybook. We need to provide additional documentation for each HTML attribute and method for Storybook to display contextual information about HTML attributes, methods, the tag name, or possibly description of the component. Storybook autogenerates the documentation with a tool called the Custom Elements Manifest. The custom-elements-manifest package analyzes each component class definition, parses HTML attributes, events, methods, the tag name, and description of the component and generates a JSON file which Storybook can use to configure the documentation for each Story. Custom Elements Manifest uses a CLI to run the script that generates the custom-elements.json file.

You’ll eventually run the above command in the packages/component directory that produces a custom-elements.json file Storybook will interpret for parts of the documentation. To provide additional context around each HTML attribute or method, Storybook also interprets JSDoc comments.

JSDoc

JSDoc is a standardized comment pattern for documenting JavaScript inline. Any comment written in JSDoc syntax above a particular code block documents the immediately proceeding code. For instance, a JSDoc comment above a class definition provides contextual information about the class, while a JSDoc comment above a method documents the method.

A document for getting started with JSDoc is available. In short, the multi-line JSDoc comment begins with a description of the code block, followed by contextual tags. function arguments can be tagged with @param. HTML attributes can be denoted with @attr. After documenting each component with JSDoc, we’ll have a format Storybook can interpret while generating the documentation for each component in the UI library. As an added bonus, TypeScript should compile type definitions with the inline JSDoc comments, so engineers can read the documentation right in their IDE.

Before generating the custom-elements.json file, document one component in the @in/ui package with JSDoc.

Starting with the ButtonComponent class in packages/component/src/button/Button.ts, document the class definition with JSDoc. After providing a description, use the @tag tag to define the tag name of the component. Use @attr tags to document the necessary HTML attributes that effect the display of ButtonComponent.

For Storybook to uptake these changes, you’ll have to generate the custom-elements.json file which contains a JSON schema which Storybook uses to interpret each component for the documentation. We have a problem though, mostly caused by running Storybook in the context of a lerna monorepo. Storybook expects the custom-elements.json file to be in the root directory. If we ran the Custom Elements Manifest Analyzer in the packages/component directory, it would generate paths to each component implementation relative to that directory and not the root directory. The analyzer expects JavaScript, not TypeScript, so we have to build the @in/ui package first so the tool can parse the output in the dist/fesm2015 directory. When that happens the custom-elements.json file will be written to packages/component with paths like in the following example:

Set up Continuous Integration with Github Actions

Right now, packages in the monorepo can only be built locally on a developer’s computer. There’s no way to build or test the UI library remotely, which could cause problems not only for other members of the development team, but those engineers who rely on the UI library for development. If an engineer checked in code to the main branch of the repo that couldn’t be built, it may cause unwanted churn for others on the team. Anyone who wants to reference the documentation would have to clone the repository and build it locally. Continuous integration (CI) is a software development practice that automates the process of running builds, validating code against tests, and deploying resources like packages or servers. CI is beneficial for UI libraries because it provides transparency and insight into the development cycle of the library, while maintaining quality and consistency.

There are many tools available for Continuous Integration, but we’re going to focus on getting CI up and running for the UI library using Github Actions. You already check in code to a repository hosted on Github for the purposes of completing this book, so it makes sense to use the tool that is native to the Github platform. Github Actions automates software development workflows whenever an engineer pushes code to a branch in Github. The process can be visualized in pull requests. When an engineer pushes up new commits to a branch associated with a pull request, Github Actions start whatever workflow is run on: [push].

Github Actions are configured using YAML, “a human-friendly data serialization language for all programming languages” according to the yaml.org. A single Github Actions workflow has a name, is performed on an event, and can run several jobs. Jobs have steps that run in parallel or sequentially. A complete guide for Github Actions is available here.

In this section you’ll write YAML to configure four Github Actions workflows:

  • Build validates that all packages in the monorepo can be built without error (on push)
  • Test runs integration tests (on push)
  • Snapshot runs snapshot tests (on push)
  • Storybook builds and deploys Storybook to Github Pages (on push in main branch only)

If you’re not familiar with YAML, don’t worry. A walkthrough for setting up each Github Action is provided along with step-by-step instructions. To validate the Github Actions workflows are working correctly, you’ll need to make changes to each .yaml file, commit the changes and push up the branch to your fork of the fullstack-web-components repository. Open a pull request to merge your branch into the main branch of the forked repo. You should be able to observe Github Actions workflows run on the last commit message in the PR.

Click on the icon in the last commit to view the current status of the workflow. When a pull request is merged to the main branch, an icon appears there as well to display the status of Github Actions workflows associated with pushing to the main branch.

When clicking on details of any Github Actions workflow, you should be able to observe the output of the jobs in that workflow.

Build

The first Github Actions workflow you’ll configure is the build. To start on this workflow, make a new directory named .github in the root directory of the monorepo, making sure to preface the directory name with . which infers the directory is hidden.

Inside of the .github directory, make another directory named workflows. All the Github Actions workflows will be saved in this directory.

Make a new YAML file named build.yml in .github/workflows.

Open build.yml in your favorite IDE to begin configuring the build Github Actions workflow. Start by specifying the name of the workflow: build. YAML is written in succinct key/value pairs separated by a colon. On the second line of the build.yml file, declare the events this workflow should run: on: [push], meaning whenever new commits are pushed to any remote branch.

Next, specify the jobs that should run on this workflow. There is only one job: build which is declared as a key on jobs. The build needs to run on a remote server. The latest Ubuntu linux distribution should work. Declare the steps of the job. Each step should use the actions/checkout@v2, which automates the process of checking out a commit and running the job. Ubuntu doesn’t come with NodeJS installed, so you need to also specify to install node and yarn. After the installation is completed, it’s safe to run two scripts in the monorepo: yarn install which installs all project dependencies and yarn build which calls on lerna to build every package in the monorepo.

When you are done, the workflow should appear as follows:

Commit your changes on the chapter-7 branch and push them to the remote fork of the git repository. Make a new pull request for the main branch of the forked repository and observe that the Github Action is running on the last commit of the PR.

Integration Tests

Setting up Cypress integration tests in Github Actions is a little more involved, but involves many of the same techniques found in the build workflow. Cypress provides a tool for running tests in Github Actions named cypress-io/github-action@v2 and like actions/checkout@v2 and actions/setup-node@v2 in the previous workflow, the job will have to use cypress-io/github-action@v2. cypress-io/github-action@v2 relies on a Github Actions Token that should be installed in Github prior to running the workflow. Navigate to the Settings view for your fork of the fullstack-web-components repository. Find the Secrets menu under Security in the sidebar and click Actions. Click on New repository secret. Give the secret a name. I used the name “GITHUB_TOKEN”, followed by a value, which can literally be anything. Click Add Secret when you are finished.

On your local branch, make a new file to configure the test Github Actions workflow.

In test.yml, give the workflow a name and specify when it should run, on: [push]. In jobs, give the job a name cypress-run, that runs on ubuntu-latest, like the previous workflow. Give the job a name that will be displayed in the Github Actions UI: e2e on Chrome. In the steps, provide actions/checkout@v2 and cypress-io/github-action@v2. cypress-io/github-action@v2 requires a significant amount of configuration including how to install dependencies install-command: yarn install, which browser to run the e2e tests browser: chrome, the name of the repository: repository: [github username]/fullstack-web-components (replace [github username] with your Github username), a branch to reference for failing tests ref: refs/heads/master, the token you specified in Github token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}, a setting that disables the persistence of credentials persist-credentials: false, the command that builds the project build: yarn build, the command that starts the Storybook server start: yarn start and finally, the address where Storybook runs Cypress, should listen and wait for before running the tests wait-on: http://localhost:6006.

After you’ve configured test.yml like the above example, being sure to replace [github username] with your Github username, commit your changes and push them to the branch currently associated with a pull request. Observe the workflow runs in Github Actions.

Snapshot Tests

Make another workflow file named snapshot.yml in the .github/workflows directory.

Name the workflow snapshot and specify that it happens on push of any branch.

Storyshots requires a similar workflow to the Cypress integration tests, although it’s much harder to configure because there isn’t a package like cypress-io/github-action@v2 for Storyshots that makes configuration easier in Github Actions. This means you have to manage the installation of node and yarn, the command that runs in the job much more granualarly. actions/upload-artifact@v2 does exist though, which automates the upload of any artifacts from the snapshot tests. You can use actions/upload-artifact@v2 to temporarily upload any snapshot that failed to observe what may have gone wrong. Any snapshot with a “diff” is stored at packages/component/src/**/__snapshots__/__diff_output__/*. Another important setting in this job is continue-on-error: true which forces the workflow to complete despite any snapshot failing, so you could observe all the failing snapshots instead of just the first that failed.

When you have completed in snapshot.yml, commit and push your changes to the remote branch. Observe the snapshot tests running in Github Actions.

Deploy Storybook

To make a new workflow for deploying Storybook to Github Pages, make a new file at .github/workflows/storybook.yml.

The workflow for deploying Storybook is very similar to the build workflow, with some exceptions. We want to only deploy Storybook to Github Pages when a commit is pushed to the main branch, not just any branch like previous workflows. You can specify the specific branches you wish to run the workflow: main. Run the jobs on ubuntu-latest, being sure to install node and yarn. Install all project dependencies with yarn install. After that, two things need to happen: Storybook should be built and then deployed. A script in the main package.json of the repository handles predeploy tasks, essentially building Storybook. A second script named deploy-storybook uses a CLI from the @storybook/storybook-deployer package to deploy Storybook to Github Pages. That script needs to be run with the --ci argument and uses the token you specified before for the repository, only formatted slightly differently.

Commit your changes and push them to the remote branch. Observe the rest of the workflows run except this one in the pull request. Once Github Actions validates the build, integration and snapshot tests, in your browser, merge the branch to the main branch of your remote fork. The Storybook workflow should run on the main branch. You can observe its progress on the last commit that was merged on the main page of the repository. Once the workflow has completed, the deploy-storybook script should have made a new branch named gh-pages where the current deployment of the Storybook is stored. Github Pages references the gh-pages branch for changes and updates the Storybook portal whenever the gh-pages branch is updated.

To enable Github Pages you still need to navigate to the Settings for the Github repository in your browser. Open Settings and click on Pages in the sidebar.

Specify the gh-pages branch as the source and click Save.

It may take another roundtrip merging to the main branch to finalize the process now that Github Pages is enabled via the Github UI in your browser. When Storybook is properly deployed it will be visible at [github username].github.io/fullstack-web-components.

After writing these four workflows for Github Actions, you are now able to validate your changes in a continuous integration pipeline. One workflow we omitted was deployment of the @in/ui and @in/common packages to the global npm registry. Given what you know now about Github Actions, that shouldn’t be too hard to figure out.

Summary

In this chapter, you took a break from coding components and learned about maintenance of a UI library built with custom elements. You exported components with named 2015 exports so the UI library can be treeshaken by build tools like Webpack and Rollup. You optimized the distributed code by bundling it into one file. By distributing a FESM, build tools only have to interpret the exports from one file as opposed to many. This should speed up build times because build tools do not have to statically analyze the AST sourced from many different files. Next, you discovered how to write documentation for each component using JSDoc and provided rich documentation with Storybook and Custom Elements Manifest. Finally, you set up a continuous integration workflow using Github Actions that builds and validates the codebase, while deploying Storybook to Github Pages using automation.

All this work will come in handy for the final chapters of this book, where you will develop a single page application using the custom elements exported from the @in/ui package. You’ve come a long way since Chapter One. After learning about the various types of custom elements, you built several complex user interfaces using the complete set of specifications known as Web Components: custom elements, HTML templates, and ES Modules. In Part Two, you learned how components can communicate with HTML attributes, CustomEvent and BroadcastChannel while building the table and dialogs. You coded a micro library that reduced the repetitive tasks associated with custom element development and gave engineers easy-to-use interfaces for declaring tag name, template, styling, and events.

All this hard work wasn’t for nought. Through a combination of using a custom micro-library and sticking only with browser specifications, the complete UI library you’ve built so far optimizes to ~6.4kB gzipped when optimized with Closure Compiler in SIMPLE_OPTIMIZATIONS mode and could be optimized further with additional tooling that minifies any template strings. You can test the size of the bundle yourself by pasting the contents of it into the portal at https://closure-compiler.appspot.com along with specifying the language_out should be ES6.

You’ve demonstrated the potential of Web Components by optimizing the way they are distributed and documented. Onward to Part Three where you will develop an entire application using only custom elements and other browser specifications.

Part Three

Part Three

Application

In Part Three of this book, you’ll explore how Web Components can make building applications easier and performant. By reusing the components distributed in the @in/ui package, you’ll code feature-rich views for the “In” application. The web app allows the user to login and interact with a contact list. You’ll start by coding the login view. After developing a splash page and login user interface, you’ll switch gears and code a router that can safely destroy the view and instantiate another: the “In” contact list. Throughout Chapters 8-10, you’ll not just learn how to reuse components from the UI library but also how to make an application performant by server-side rendering custom elements where applicable using Declarative Shadow DOM, the final specification in Web Components you have yet to leverage.

What you will learn

While developing the In application with Web Components, you’ll explore the following concepts:

  • How to build features in a single page application using Web Components
  • How to provide a router that can dynamically add and remove views built with custom elements
  • What is Declarative Shadow DOM?
  • How to server-side render custom elements with Node
  • How to ensure a high percentage lighthouse performance score

Developing in Part Three

In previous chapters, you used Storybook as the primary development environment. In Part Three, you’ll code the front end of the application in the packages/client directory and the backend of the application in the packages/server directory. A script can be executed by running yarn start:app in the root directory of the repository. This script bootstraps both client and backend servers and listens for changes while you are developing, and reloads the browser window on every change. After a successful development build, the server runs at http://localhost:4443. A webpack server drives client-side development, while ts-node and nodemon handle the Node.js server. Client code is written in TypeScript, while server code is written in JavaScript. JavaScript was chosen for the server to maintain stability for the lessons in this book.

If you wish to test the production build during development, you may run yarn build in both client and server packages using lerna, i.e. lerna exec --scope @in/client -- yarn build && lerna exec --scope @in/server -- yarn build. Once built, the production server is invoked with lerna exec --scope @in/server -- yarn start:prod. The production server runs at http://localhost:4443.

In previous chapters, you ran yarn storybook, which may still be useful for the remaining chapters of this book if you want to reference the documentation of each component via Storybook. To run Storybook simultaneously, open a second tab (or window) in your Terminal and run yarn storybook while yarn start:app is running in the first tab. In Part Three, you’ll mainly run the script yarn start:app for development.

Application Development with Custom Elements

Chapter Eight

Application Development with Custom Elements

Application development with custom elements is not unlike application development with any other library or framework. JavaScript libraries prescribe various ways of working. React, for example, prefers a functional implementation, while Vue applications export an Object-based configuration in each file. The absence of such framework-level abstractions can be intimidating for anyone attempting to develop an application purely with Web Components. How you architect an application with vanilla JavaScript and browser specifications is up to you, but the rewards are great. By minimizing library dependencies, you can ensure the application bundle(s) are small in file size. Less JavaScript for the browser to interpret as the page loads can translate to a more performant solution. Users would have less time to wait to interact with content.

There is nothing stopping you from using existing frameworks as inspiration when developing with custom elements. Anyone who has coded with Angular may have noticed the similarity between Angular’s class decorators and the design of the @Component decorator exported from @in/ui. You could come up with low-level functions that enable application development similar to any UI framework you’re comfortable with. In this chapter, you’ll implement patterns for application development using custom elements that are only one opinion of how an application could be developed. The possibilities are seemingly endless! Specifically, you’ll develop the landing page of the application using custom elements and class-based services that communicate with backend APIs over http requests.

During the development of complex user interfaces like TableCardComponent, you implemented a separation of concerns between the various user interface elements: table card, table, row, and cell. We still want to maintain a separation of concerns during application development to ensure the product can scale. For this reason, we’ll abstract any HTTP requests made to server-side REST APIs into their own service-level pattern.

Each service is a class that exposes methods for fetching data or submitting data to the API endpoints the service is concerned with. In the above example, CookieService exposes a method named getPermission that returns a Promise (the result of the http request). CookieService sets and returns user-specified permission for using cookies, while SessionService should report if the user has a current session, for example.

In addition to this service-level abstraction, you’ll abstract reusable application-level UI components to discrete implementations. AppHeader should be displayed in every view of the application, so it makes sense to abstract its implementation so it can be reused. CookieFooter is another UI component that should display a footer with messaging for the end-user to accept or deny cookies for the site. Background is a UI component that lazyloads a background image for each section of the landing page.

AppHeader, CookieFooter and Background will be used in the template for the landing page view. We’ll maintain application views as separate UI components. In this chapter, the MainView is another autonomous custom element mainly concerned with implementing a template for the entire landing page. In the next chapter, MainView will be attached to a Route when you build out a client-side router compatible with custom elements. By providing a separation of concerns sooner than later, we can anticipate the challenges ahead in a multi-view application. For now, we’re only concerned with implementing the landing page.

What you will build

  • Landing page for “In” application using custom elements
  • AppHeader which is the global header for the application
  • CookieFooter which displays a banner the user can accept or deny cookies
  • Background which lazyloads a background image in a container element
  • MainView which displays the entire view for the landing page
  • SessionService which reports if the user has a current session
  • CookieService which sets and returns user-specified permission for using cookies

What you will learn

  • How to make a header, content, and footer template with custom elements
  • How to code a reusable global header with custom elements
  • How to lazyload images with customized built-ins
  • How to code a cookie banner with custom elements
  • How to reuse custom elements from a UI library during application development
  • How to create a separation of concerns between components and view
  • How to make http requests from the context of a custom element using fetch

Acceptance criteria

  • MainView displays all content according to the mockups in Figma
  • AppHeader displays a logo that navigates the user to MainView (/)
  • AppHeader displays a link that navigates the user to LoginView when the user doesn’t have an active session
  • CookieFooter displays a message and two buttons, a primary button that displays “Accept” and secondary button that displays “Deny”
  • When the user clicks “Accept”, CookieBanner is not visible until the backend responds with permission: false
  • When the user clicks “Deny”, CookieBanner remains visible
  • Background lazyloads background images in both sections
  • SessionService has a method UI components can use to check if the user has an active session
  • CookieService has methods to check the status of the user preference and set the user preference for cookies

Landing Page

To begin development of the landing page, we should implement the view. The view is just another custom element, so we’ll import methods from @in/common and establish a template and styling for the entire view. Since any UI components displayed on the landing page will be in the template of MainView, we can use this component as a development environment of sorts for the remainder of this chapter. One difference between the custom elements in the application and user library developed in previous chapters is we’re going to declare the template and styling for each component outside of the class and then set the style and template properties on the @Component decorator. This will help us refactor the components for server-side rendering in Chapter Twelve.

All development in this chapter happens in packages/client/src. A directory named view has already been scaffolded in here, so create a file named MainView.ts in this directory, then open the file with your favorite IDE. Let’s make another directory named main and put MainView.ts in there.

In MainView.ts, import the necessary function and decorators from @in/common needed for an autonomous custom element.

Declare two const for the CSS styling and template for the component named styles and shadowTemplate respectively. You can set these to template strings, calling the appropriate css or html function exported from @in/common.

Using the @Component decorator, declare a new custom element with the selector main-view and set the style and template properties to the two const you declared prior. Export a new class named MainView that extends HTMLElement, like any other autonomous custom element. Opt to use Shadow DOM for this component in the constructor by calling attachShadow.

If you haven’t started the server yet, do so now by running yarn start:app and open http://localhost:4443 in your preferred development browser. Nothing should appear yet. That’s because we haven’t injected an instance of MainView into DOM. Open packages/client/src/index.ts. Using document.createElement, create a new instance of MainView. If you inspect the DOM, you’ll notice an empty HTMLDivElement with the id attribute set to root. Select that element and append the instance of MainView to it. Export MainView from this file. index.ts is the entry point of the entire client-side application, so anything exported here gets bundled with the application.

There’s not much happening yet, but at the very least, the component is now in DOM.

Add a header, content, and footer template to shadowTemplate, being sure to set an attribute to select the content. Here we use semantic HTML elements and a HTMLDivElement with id attribute set to content-root.

If you want, add some temporary content to each element to visualize the style updates.

Add some basic styling that establishes style behaviors for the containing element. We want the header to display at the top, while the footer displays at the bottom, and the content scrolls in between. This layout can be achieved with flex box. After selecting :host, set the display to flex, flex-direction to column so the layout flows vertically, justify-content to space-between so the elements flow where we want them, and set the height to always be 100% of the view: 100vh. To allow the content area to scroll, select #content-root and set overflow-y to scroll.

You’ll circle back to update the MainView class throughout the rest of this chapter, but for now, you have a foundation to develop the AppHeader, CookieFooter and Background components needed to display the content of the landing page. In the next section, you’ll develop the AppHeader while learning how to abstract HTTP requests to a service.

SessionService

We need a way to determine if the login link should be shown or hidden based on if the user currently has a session. That would mean the user has logged in and is authenticated.

We haven’t made any services yet, so let’s make a space for all services to be stored in the application source code. Make a new directory named service in packages/client/src.

Populate the service directory with a new file named session.ts.

Since we haven’t submitted a request to /api/login, the only response /api/session will give is a status code of 401, meaning unauthenticated. When the user has a session, /api/session returns a status code of 200, meaning success. These status codes are meaningless to the developer building out AppHeader. The developer can’t derive any meaning from 200 and 401, so establish a new contract between SessionService and AppHeader before proceeding.

In session.ts declare a new enum named SESSION that stores the state for user sessions: OPEN (when the endpoint responds with 200) or CLOSED (when the endpoint responds with 401). Export a new type named SessionResponse that contains a property named session that can either be SESSION.OPEN or SESSION.CLOSED. This SessionResponse will be returned somewhere in the session service for AppHeader, it is the contract between service and UI element.

Declare and export a new class named SessionService. Set the path for the REST API endpoint on a private property named path and establish the constructor.

Establish a new method on SessionService named getSession, which should return Promise with a SessionResponse that could be used in AppHeader. Use fetch to make a GET request on the API endpoint stored on this.path. The response from the endpoint is accessible via a call to then. Pass the status of the response (res.status) to another new method named processSession.

In processSession, serialize the status to either SESSION.OPEN or SESSION.CLOSED based on if the endpoint responds with a status of 200.

When you are done, import SESSION and SessionService into packages/client/src/component/header/AppHeader.ts.

Establish a new instance of SessionService locally in AppHeader.ts.

Declare a new connectedCallback on the AppHeader class. First, check the user isn’t on the LoginView, which will be at /login. Use window.location.pathname to check if the pathname includes login. If it doesn’t, call getSession and depending on the response, remove the attribute from the element reference by the this.$login getter.

To complete the basic functionality of AppHeader, we need to direct the user to MainView when they click the logo. Import Listen from @in/common to handle this use case.

Decorate a new method named onLogoClick with the Listen decorator and navigate the browser to the root, which should display the MainView component.

In this section, you learned how to reuse components from a UI library and application components directory in the context of a view component named MainView. You abstracted http requests to a service layer named SessionService. Calling methods on SessionService, you were able to hide the link based on the condition of the user session. In the next chapter, you’ll develop the LoginView which allows the user to authenticate with the backend and establish an active session. When that happens, you should observe the link is hidden. Until then, you’ll develop parts of the MainView using a strict separation of concerns, continuing with CookieFooter next.

Cookie Footer

The landing page has a requirement for a banner at the bottom of the page to display legal messaging for the end-user who has to accept or deny cookies per GDPR standards. In Figma, the mockup displays a footer with a message and two buttons. Once the user accepts or denies cookies, a request must be sent to the backend to save their preference in the database. To support this feature, you’ll develop a UI component that displays the footer and service that makes HTTP POST requests to the /api/cookies REST endpoint.

This component’s functionality resembles AppHeader in some ways, although the service you’ll build requires two requests: a GET request to determine whether or not to display the CookieFooter and a POST request to update the backend with the option the user chose by clicking on one of the buttons in CookieFooter. Otherwise, CookieFooter still requires some styling and a template, methods that handle click events and some initial logic that determines if the component should be displayed or hidden.

CookieService

To start developing the CookieService, make a new file in packages/client/src/service named cookies.ts.

Establish the contract between CookieService and CookieFooter with a new type definition named CookiePermission, an Object with one property named permission that can be equal to one of two values on the COOKIES enum. Eventhough the client has this type safe contract, the /api/cookies endpoint responds with a similar JSON Object, although the permission is set to a Boolean. Make another type definition named InternalCookiePermission that describes this behavior of the /api/cookies endpoint. As the name indicates, this type definition will be used to strictly type the response from the endpoint, while CookiePermission will be what CookieFooter references on the COOKIES enum to set the permission.

Export the CookieService class from the file, while giving the class a constructor and path property set to the path of the /api/cookies endpoint.

Declare a new method on CookieService named getPermission that uses fetch to make a GET request, then processes the JSON in the response, with another method named processPermission, which is yet to be declared. If the endpoint doesn’t return a 200 status code, coerce the response into an Object that matches InternalCookiePermission. getPermission should return the fetch, which is described via the type definition Promise<CookiePermission>. getPermission will be used to determine whether to show or hide CookieBanner based on the response from the endpoint.

Make another method named processPermission which takes an InternalCookiePermission in the first argument and returns CookiePermission. The purpose of this method is to provide a type-safe response for UI components consuming it, so transform the Boolean into one of two possibilities declared in the COOKIES enum: COOKIES.ACCEPT or COOKIES.DECLINE.

The user should be able to specify whether they want to accept or deny cookies on the site and their preference should be stored in a database. If UI components like CookieBanner have a contract with CookieService in the form of the CookiePermission, this method should use that type definition in the first argument. The /api/cookies endpoint accepts a POST request in the format of InternalCookiePermission, so establish the Boolean based on the value of the permission property on cookies, passed through the first argument. Just like in getPermission, return fetch, this time specifying the method as POST because the app is sending JSON, set the appropriate headers, and set the body a JSONified version of InternalCookiePermission using JSON.stringify. Process the response in the same way as getPermission.

That’s all there is to the implementation of CookieService. You established two methods that can be reused in any UI component. Next, you’ll import CookieService into CookieFooter so the user can specify whether or not to accept cookies using the givePermission method. You’ll also import CookieService into MainView, which determines whether to show or hide the CookieFooter with the getPermission method.

Summary

In this chapter, you developed a landing page for the application with custom elements. You created a separation of concerns between UI components, views, and services, which should help the application scale. In the next chapter, you’ll continue this trend, coding more services for authentication and navigation that can be used in the context of any view or component.

If you chose not to abstract the styling and templates into separate const in each of these components, that may come back to haunt you in Chapter Ten where you make each application component compatible with server-side rendering (SSR). SSR will be extremely valuable for the landing page, which includes content that could drive visitors to the application. As of now, we can’t guarantee search engines can crawl the page. The relevant page content is hidden in Shadow DOM. In Chapter Ten, you’ll overcome this limitation by implementing Declarative Shadow DOM templates for each component you worked on in this chapter.

You may have noticed that so far, you’ve only used one component from the UI library (ButtonComponent). All that hard work from previous chapters will pay off in the next chapter when you’ll develop the LoginView and DashboardView with the rest of the components exported from the @in/ui package. This should hopefully accelerate development, while keeping you focused on implementing the features at hand. Before working on the login and dashboard components in the next chapter, you’ll develop a client-side router that can navigate between all three views, including the MainView you developed in this chapter.

Routing Custom Elements in a SPA

Chapter Nine

Routing Custom Elements in a SPA

Single-page applications (SPA) are web applications that load only one HTML document. This approach to development can be advantageous for several reasons. Only one HTML file needs to be deployed to production instead of many. Resources don’t have to be loaded over and over again for the end-user. SPA continuously updates the existing document.body as the user navigates, reusing existing CSS and JavaScript resources. SPA have some trade-offs, namely the inability to be optimized for search engines (SEO), the requirement to implement some sort of client-side routing mechanism, and the potential for an increased JavaScript bundle size. The advantages of SPA can result in the degradation of performance for the end-user.

Luckily, we’re implementing custom elements with a micro-library (@in/common) that should have a minimal negative impact on performance. SEO remains a problem in the SPA we’re developing because HTML elements aren’t appended to the document.body until the application bundle loads. To be more performant and SEO compliant, the HTML elements on the landing page could be server-side rendered. We’ll cover server-side rendering in Chapter Ten.

With SEO and performance concerns out of that way, that just leaves the problem of routing. Since the build tooling for this application doesn’t deploy separate HTML files for each view, we need to come up with a way for the application to navigate from MainView to the yet to be developed LoginView. Once authenticated in the LoginView, the application should route to the DashboardView. This kind of navigation requires a client-side router.

Major JavaScript frameworks often include or endorse a client-side router. It could make a lot of sense to adopt a JavaScript framework and exclusively relegate custom elements to UI library that is framework-agnostic, although we’ve already chosen to use custom elements in the view layer of the application. That means we need a router that can interpret custom elements and replace the view content with the template or instance of a custom element like MainView. This task may seem daunting if you’ve never coded a router before, so it’s hard to know where to begin. Let’s start with some characteristics observable in many framework routers.

  • Configurable in some way, usually through a manifest of routes
  • Creates and destroys HTML content at a specified root DOM node, i.e. <body> or <div id="root">
  • Parses the path in the browser address bar and loads a specific route based on the path
  • Manipulates browser history state so user can still use the “Back” button

In this chapter, you’ll develop a minimal client-side router that does all of these things. Router will be a class that can be instantiated with the selector for the root node (main-view) and configuration for each route. When the browser navigates to a path that matches a particular route, the router will instantiate the view component associated with that route and append the element to the container HTMLDivElement available on the document: <div id="root">. When you finish coding the router, you’ll have a simple implementation that can be expanded upon to allow for hashed routes, parsing query params, reacting to “pop” events, and more.

While developing MainView in the last chapter, you coded new custom elements. In this chapter, you’ll reuse AppHeader and several components exported from @in/ui while developing the LoginView and DashboardView. Some of the logic for these views can even be lifted from the stories.js files in Storybook, which provide examples of how to use TextInputComponent in the context of a form or TableComponent. The main difference between the Storybook examples and the application is that the components in the application need to interact with a backend that exposes a REST API. During development of the LoginView and DashboardView, you’ll make several other services that support making HTTP requests to REST API endpoints.

What you will build

  • LoginView which displays the global header and login interface
  • DashboardView which displays the global header and table
  • Router which handles client-side routing between main, login and dashboard views
  • RouteConfig which configures a single route
  • LocationService which gets the current path and navigates the user to another path
  • ContactService which fetches and modifies a user’s contact list

In this section, you’ll develop the Router class, which is responsible for instantiating and appending a view to the root element on the document. After coding the Router implementation, you’ll test the router works by scaffolding the two view components that should be displayed with the user lands on /login and /dashboard. When the user clicks the “login” link on the landing page, the Router should navigate to /login and display the template of the LoginView autonomous custom element. Similarly, when the browser navigates to /dashboard, the DashboardView template should appear.

Router should be configured in the application logic somewhere and that configuration should be injected into the Router class when it is instantiated. By separating the configuration into a separate file, we’re setting ourselves up for success in Chapter Ten, where the server-side renderer will reference the same router configuration to configure each route on the server.

This way, Router will be able to check if a route.path that matches the path in the address bar exists. Router

resolve has a valid Route to display, so let’s use the remaining properties on the Route (tag and title) to display the view component at that route. A POST request to /api/login requires a JSON Object in the body of the request. That Object contains two properties: username and password. Both are typed string.
