Server-side Rendering with Declarative Shadow DOM

Chapter Ten

Server-Side Rendering Custom Elements

There are many reasons why you would want to server-side render user interfaces. Server-side rendering UI may increase performance for the end-user because all the content for a HTML document is pre-rendered, reducing the time to paint each element in the browser window. UI components rendered server-side may already be “hydrated” with content. By offloading processing of UI components to a server, the overall time it takes to render HTML can be more predictable. Client-side rendering can be less predictable because different browsers have varied performance.

Server-side rendering promotes SEO compliance, making server-side renderable pages more compatible with search engine crawlers and social media. UI components rendered with a single-page application framework are less compatible with SEO because nothing is rendered in a timely fashion for a web crawler to statically analyze a HTML document. By offloading network requests to the server and hydrating UI components server-side with content, you can improve the security of an application by removing the possibility of exposing sensitive customer data.

For awhile, it was seemingly impossible to server-side render custom elements. Shadow DOM is imperative; you code statements that tell the browser to instantiate a new Shadow Root. This Shadow Root is what provides the ability for custom elements to take advantage of CSS scoping, DOM encapsulation, and composability. While the Shadow DOM specification is powerful, due to its imperative nature, Shadow DOM isn’t immediately server-side renderable. Browser specifications aren’t natively available in server environments like Node.js. Node.js is built on the V8 JavaScript engine that originated in the Chrome browser, but Node.js lacks browser-specific specifications like the Document Object Model (DOM). If you were going to try to instantiate the class that extends HTMLElement in a Node.js environment, there would be an error because HTMLElement doesn’t exist in the context of Node.js, for instance.

The lack of the DOM in Node.js presents an interesting problem when server-side rendering custom elements. All the necessary browser specifications would need to be “shimmed” or “polyfilled” before the custom element class could instantiate, then custom logic on the server would need to parse and output a server-side generated template. An npm package that did just that is @skatejs/ssr, a package currently in maintenance mode, which was created by Github user @treshugart. @skatejs/ssr extended undom and brought support for Custom Elements v1 to Node.js. You could use this package to server-side render custom elements built with Skate, or with some configuration, custom elements coded directly with browser specifications. This tool generated templates server-side that enabled sites built with custom elements to be SEO friendly and highly performant. @skatejs/ssr worked for static-site generation, but it lacked the ability to “hydrate” components. It became apparent to the web development community a specification that enabled server-side rendering was needed. Enter Declarative Shadow DOM.

Declarative Shadow DOM

Declarative Shadow DOM is a browser specification that enables Shadow Root to be declaratively instantiated in HTML. Looking at the AppHeader component you developed in the last chapter, let’s see how Declarative Shadow DOM differs. Instead of imperatively declaring a Shadow Root, you can declare the Shadow Root directly on a HTML template using the shadowroot HTML attribute. In the example below that abbreviates the necessary styling and HTML template, <app-header> tag name is included in a template. Using Declarative Shadow DOM, the direct child of the AppHeader is a HTML template. The HTML template includes a Shadow Root with the HTML attribute shadowroot set to the mode that would have otherwise been imperatively defined via a call to attachShadow on the AppHeader class. The template includes the CSS styling and HTML for the component.

In the below example, you can compare the Declarative Shadow DOM example above to the imperative style of declaring a Shadow Root you’ve used to define the template for each component developed in this book.

Declarative Shadow DOM enables server-side rendering because a template is expressed as a String. Strings can be manipulated in any JavaScript environment. In the browser, HTML is parsed by the user agent which isn’t present in the Node.js environment. If you attempted to use methods that create HTML like document.createElement on the server, that method would fail because it doesn’t exist. By expressing the template as a String, you can pass the template in the HTTP response from the server to the client: a browser that can parse the HTML template as DOM.

Once the browser receives a HTML response with elements that use Declarative Shadow DOM, the user agent parses the HTML template with the shadowroot attribute much like it would when calling attachShadow. Components that have registered their ES2015 class with the CustomElementRegistry and rendered with Declarative Shadow DOM don’t have to call attachShadow any longer in the class constructor. This presents a problem for components that imperatively declare their Shadow Root, and components that need to “hydrate” their template during instantiation. If a component imperatively calls attachShadow that also has its template defined declaratively, the component will render duplicates of the same template in the browser window.

To prevent this phenomenon, you can check if a Declarative Shadow Root exists prior to imperatively declaring a template for each component. This is possible because any custom element using Declarative Shadow DOM is already upgraded and will already have attached the Shadow Root prior to the constructor being called.

When developing custom elements that can be rendered with Declarative Shadow DOM, it’s important to separate the logic for template instantiation and component hydration. This allows for easier maintenance of custom elements and makes their instantiation more predictable.

@lit-labs/ssr

@lit-labs/ssr is an npm package distributed by Lit at Google for server-side rendering Lit templates and components. While developing with Storybook, you used Lit templates when writing each story. Storybook is dependent on story templates being wrapped in the Lit html function. Throughout the course of this book, we opted to code custom elements using just browser specifications and didn’t adopt a library like Lit to develop UI components. Had we done so, those LitElement would be directly compatible with @lit-labs/ssr and benefit from everything that package has to offer. Lit is built on top of web standards, much like the @in/common micro-library you coded, although Lit is way more powerful, at the cost of performance. By developing with web standards, we helped ensure the UI components perform as close to the custom element spec itself, which is as performant as you can get in the browser, short of ahead-of-time compilation. The benefits of using a library like Lit can outweigh those performance concerns. The reactive properties and declarative templates alone make Lit an alluring choice for developing UI components.

Using @lit-labs/ssr in Node.js, we can opt to use Lit only in the context of declaring the server-side renderable template for each component, keeping our existing UI component library intact. @lit-labs/ssr works with vanilla custom elements.

Challenges

In this chapter, you’ll refactor each component from Chapters Eight and Nine to provide Declarative Shadow DOM templates that will be server-side rendered with @lit-labs/ssr. You’ll use ES2015 template strings to define Declarative Shadow DOM templates in a composable fashion so you can reuse the same template in both imperative and declarative contexts. To help with composability, you’ll use another npm package named es6-template-strings that resolves interpolated template strings. es6-template-strings allows any HTML response that includes Declarative Shadow DOM templates to resolve as String, as opposed to function references embedded in an ES2015 template string.

You’ll import the same JavaScript used to declare each view in the application into the context of Node.js, where @lit-labs/ssr renders the template. When the web browser requests the HTML document, Node.js will respond with a server-side rendered template.

@lit-labs/ssr does a decent job at shimming the browser specifications needed for autonomous custom elements to work in Node.js, although the class names customized built-in elements extend from are not there by default. You’ll use tooling provided by @lit-labs/ssr to shim any missing specifications needed to render some of the customized built-in elements exported from @in/ui.

At the time of writing this, Declarative Shadow DOM isn’t available in every browser. Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge have support for Declarative Shadow DOM. Browsers that lack the specification require a “ponyfill” that parses Shadow Roots in a similar way.

By moving to server-side rendering, you’ll no longer need the client-side router developed in Chapter Nine. Each route of the application will be handled by the server instead of the SPA in Chapter 10. You will be able to reuse the configuration for the router server-side in Node.js. In this chapter, you’ll provide the route configuration to map a specific route to the view component. This view component will when be server-side rendered by @lit-labs/ssr and returned in the HTTP response.

After you’ve declared Declarative Shadow DOM templates, deprecated the client-side router, and shimmed DOM specifications in Node.js, you’ll develop Express middleware that server-side renders each template with @lit-labs/ssr. If you’ve never coded in Node.js, have no worries. You’ll develop the Express server with JavaScript to reduce some complexity from compiling TypeScript, while completing tasks in this chapter using step-by-step instructions.

What you will build

  • Declarative Shadow DOM templates for server-side rendering
  • Express middleware that server-side renders custom element templates with @lit-labs/ssr
  • Router schema to support client and server implementations

What you will learn

  • What is Declarative Shadow DOM?
  • How to server-side render web components with @lit-labs/ssr and Express
  • How to shim Web Component specifications in Node.js
  • How to reuse client custom element templates server-side
  • Best Practices for server-side rendering that impact performance and SEO

Acceptance criteria

  • Each route is server-side rendered

Declarative Shadow DOM Templates

Declarative Shadow DOM templates aren’t much different from the HTML templates you’ve been coding with all along. The same rules apply. Global CSS styling still can’t cross the Shadow boundary. If a customized built-in element is found in the template, you’ll need to provide the styles for that component in the template as well. The imperative logic you coded in previous chapters that includes the appropriate <style> tag via the @Component decorator won’t be available server-side, where these Declarative Shadow DOM templates will be used to server-side render the template of each route in the application.

The only real difference is that any custom element declared in a Declarative Shadow DOM template is represented by its tag name. When imperatively creating templates, you didn’t need to encapsulate the template with the tag name of the custom element. That was assumed.

To provide Declarative Shadow DOM templates for each of the components in the app, you’ll export a new const named template in each of the component files you coded in Chapters Eight and Nine. This const will equal a function that returns a template string. This format has two main advantages: a data model could be passed through the function arguments and passed to the template, hydrating the template with content on the server. Secondly, we can reuse existing const for CSS styles and HTML template that were originally passed to the @Component decorator.

This approach will only get you so far. Unfortunataly, the above example won’t fully resolve the interpolated strings (${styles} or ${data.label}) found in the template string. For that, we’ll need to use a second package named es6-template-strings. The resolve function exported from the es6-template-strings will print the content of each interpolated string.

After importing resolve we can ensure each interpolated string prints the necessary content server-side.

Several of the components you’ll server-side render have a child ButtonComponent customized built-in element. If the styling for that custom element will also be server-side rendered, you’ll need to find a way to import the styling from the @in/ui package.

Open packages/component/src/button/Button.ts and export the buttonStyles from the file.

Follow up by exporting the same buttonStyles from packages/component/src/button/index.ts.

If you have already started the application server, stop and restart the development server.

We’re going to start refactoring each component from the ground up. That means beginning with CookieFooter and AppHeader before moving onto MainView, LoginView, and DashboardView. We don’t have to be so concerned with Background, which lazyloads a rasterized image and can’t be easily server-side rendered. We can however server-side render all vector-based SVG elements because those are declared like any other DOM element.

Begin in packages/client/src/component/footer/CookieFooter.ts by importing buttonStyles from @in/ui and resolve from es6-template-stings.

At the bottom of the file, declare and export a new const named template, making it equal to a function that returns a template string. This will be the format for all server-side rendered templates. In the template string, wrap the entire template in a <cookie-footer> tag. Declare a new HTML template as the direct child of CookieFooter, adding the shadowroot attribute and making it equal to open to establish this template uses the Declarative Shadow DOM spec.

Add a <style> tag and using string interpolation with resolve, pass the styles used by CookieFooter and the buttonStyles into the <style> tag. This will eventually have the effect of printing the entire CSS styling needed for CookieFooter to display properly. Next, after the <style> tag, use string interpolation and resolve again to provide the template of CookieFooter stored in shadowTemplate.

At this point, we can’t test server-side rendering of this or any template developed in this section, but you could log the output of template() and observe how the template would be rendered server-side in Chrome Dev Tools.

AppHeader

Repeat the same steps in packages/client/src/component/header/Header.ts. Import buttonStyles and resolve.

Export a new const named template that returns the template for the AppHeader, being sure to declare the <app-header> tag, a HTML template that uses Declarative Shadow DOM. Provide the styling and template needed for the component to display.

Now both of the reusable components have server-side renderable templates. You’ll reference those templates in the context of the view layer. You’ll use the template exported from Header.ts and CookieFooter.ts to compose the layout in a Declarative Shadow DOM HTML template.

MainView

We’ll need to address the same concerns in theMainView template found in packages/client/src/view/main/MainView.ts. MainView takes care of its own template’s styling, but to style the AppHeader and CookieFooter, you’ll need to reuse the templates from those two component implementations. Just like in AppHeader.ts and CookieFooter.ts, import resolve into MainView.ts from the es6-template-strings package.

Another problem we need to take care of in the view layer is how to provide all the code for the components in each view. Right now all the components are bundled in one JavaScript file in packages/client/src/index.ts but that should change if we want to optimize each route, only bundling the components needed for that view. To help with the transition to multiple bundles that are server-side rendered, import all the necessary dependencies of MainView in MainView.ts (AppHeader, CookieFooter, and Background). Import the template exported from Header.ts and CookieFooter.ts, but since they are named the same, use as to rename the exports HeaderTemplate and FooterTemplate.

There’s a precarious problem to solve with the MainView template. We want to reuse the HeaderTemplate and FooterTemplate functions for server-side rendering but those elements are referenced in shadowTemplate. The content in between the header and footer could be reused between the client-side and server-side template as well, so extract the two marketing sections into another template string stored in a const named contentTemplate.

Reference contentTemplate in the necessary part of shadowTemplate, the content area of the <div id="content-root">.

Near the end of MainView.ts, export a const named template that is a function where the Declarative Shadow DOM HTML template is returned. Inject the styles of MainView into the template, along with HeaderTemplate, contentTemplate, and FooterTemplate using resolve.

Export all the necessary components that should be bundled with this view, including children of AppHeader and CookieFooter like ButtonComponent.

LoginView

Repeat the same steps for LoginView. Import resolve and the necessary dependencies from Header.ts.

Extract the content from the shadowTemplate in a new const named contentTemplate that can be reused on the client and server.

Inject the new contentTemplate into the appropriate part of shadowTemplate.

Export a new template that injects styles, HeaderTemplate, and contentTemplate with resolve.

Ensure all components needed for this view are exported from the bundle.

DashboardView

Repeat the same steps in DashboardView.ts. Import any needed dependencies at the top of the file.

Extract the content into a separate template that can be referenced in the Declarative Shadow DOM HTML template. Notice how we’re not trying to server-side render the entire table in this example, but that could be possible with some additional effort.

Inject the contentTemplate into the existing shadowTemplate.

Export a template that returns the Declarative Shadow DOM template for DashboardView.

Export all the necessary components to display DashboardView.

That’s it for refactoring each application custom element to be server-side renderable. We didn’t touch every component in the @in/ui library, although those components that use Shadow DOM could also expose a Declarative Shadow DOM template. Customized built-in elements just need to export the styling for the component so the CSS styles can be server-side rendered.

Webpack

To complete the setup needed for each route to be bundled separately for each server-side rendered route, modify the webpack.config.js at packages/client/webpack.config.js to bundle additional entry points, one for each view.

Routing

For server-side rendering, we no longer need the entry point of the client application at packages/client/src/index.ts to export components. The custom elements that make up each view are available in each bundle built by Webpack. The responsibility of routing will also shift from client to server, so we can deprecate the client-side router, but opt to keep the same route configuration stored in routes to configure routing server-side instead. Modify packages/client/src/index.ts so index.ts only exports routes.

In this section, you exported Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates that will be imported into the context of Node.js later in this chapter. These changes have the undesireable effect of taking the client offline. Custom elements will no longer appear for each route in the browser until you complete the Express middleware that renders each route. Before you even tackle that challenge, you’ll need to provide a shim for custom element specificiations that are not available in Node.js.

Shim

In the last section, you exported three new JavaScript bundles corresponding to each route of the application (/, /login, and /dashboard). If we’re going to import client-side bundles in Node.js to get their exported Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates, Node.js will attempt to parse the JavaScript in the bundle. Declarative Shadow DOM, along with all custom element specifications, is still a browser-based technology, no way around it. Node.js runs on a server that lacks browser specific DOM specifications. You’ll need to provide mocked implementations of the custom elements v1 specification so the components you’ve coded in this book can be interpreted by the Node.js runtime.

@lit-labs/ssr, the package you’ll use to server-side render the Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates exports a function named installWindowOnGlobal. When executed in Node.js, installWindowOnGlobal provides coverage for autonomous custom elements portion of the Custom Elements v1 specification, but lacks support for the customized built-ins several components from the @in/ui package and Background in the client package rely on. If the application just included autonomous custom elements, we could import installWindowOnGlobal, call the function and have complete coverage for running custom element code in Node.js.

The shim is stored in a separate package in the repository named @in/dom-shim at packages/shim. In this section, you’ll code the shim, build the @in/dom-shim package, so that in the next section you can import the shim and use it.

In packages/shim/index.ts import the installWindowOnGlobal method from @lit-labs/ssr.

Since you need to support customized built-ins as well, you’ll need to mock portions of custom elements specification. This includes HTMLElement and several of its class methods, including attributes, setAttribute, removeAttribute, hasAttribute, attachShadow, and getAttribute. Using code from the @lit-labs/ssr package, mock the HTMLElement class so we can run custom elements in the context of Node.js. Starting with the attributes of a HTMLElement, create a new WeakMap() and reusable function named attributesForElement that will help mock each of the necessary methods on the HTMLElement class.

Declare a new class named Element, leaving it empty. HTMLElement actually extends from the Element class in the browser, so you’ll mock that same behavior here, only that Element doesn’t exist in Node.js. Define the HTMLElement class and establish the first getter named attributes, which calls the attributesForElement function you defined earlier and returns an Array of attribute names and values.

Define the remaining methods on HTMLElement that need to be mocked for HTMLElement class to instantiate properly in Node.js.

Now that HTMLElement is mocked, define class for each of the customized built-in elements that extend from a class available in the browser, but not Node.js. For example, ButtonComponent extends HTMLButtonElement, but HTMLButtonElement is undefined in Node.js. Declare HTMLButtonElement here, along with HTMLTableElement, HTMLTableCellElement, HTMLTableRowElement and HTMLDivElement.

Internally, installWindowOnGlobal mocks HTMLElement for us, but doesn’t expose that class as an export for you to extend other class from it. That’s why we needed to duplicate the HTMLElement mock in index.ts. installWindowOnGlobal does allow us to add mocks when the shim executes, by calling the function with an Object where each of the class is stored as a property on that Object. So we can execute installWindowOnGlobal in the context of the Express application, wrap the call to installWindowOnGlobal in another function named installShimOnGlobal and export that function. Call the installShimOnGlobal function so it executes very early in the Node.js environment.

In the next section, while developing the Express middleware that server-side renders custom elements, you’ll import the installShimOnGlobal function from @in/dom-shim and call it prior to other code running, effectively polyfilling portions of the custom elements v1 specification required for browser-based code to run on a server. Go ahead and build the @in/dom-shim package so it’s possible to import the function in the next section.

Ponyfill

In Node.js you needed to polyfill the custom elements v1 specification just enough so the JavaScript exported from client bundles can run in Node.js. Similarly, we need to ensure Declarative Shadow DOM templates are parsed properly by browsers that don’t support that specification yet. At the time of writing this, Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge are the only two browsers that natively support Declarative Shadow DOM. To provide support for Declarative Shadow DOM in other browsers, we can’t use a polyfill. The entire Document Object Model (DOM) needs to be fully loaded before any code can begin to interpret the HTML document, parsing Declarative Shadow DOM Shadow Roots. A package exists that does just that named @webcomponents/template-shadowroot, but in the form of a ponyfill. Ponyfills execute at the end of the document.body, while polyfills are typically found in the document.head, so code in the polyfill can execute prior to any DOM loading or other JavaScript being parsed. Ponyfills typically execute after JavaScript in the document.head and the document.body has loaded. While developing the HTML template that is server-side rendered, you’ll need to inject the polyfill at the end of the document.body before the template is sent to the browser client.

Store the ponyfill for now in packages/client/src/ponyfill.ts. In the next section, you’ll find a way to import this code into the server-side rendered template.

Now that you’ve shimmed the custom elements v1 specification in Node.js and provided a ponyfill to Declarative Shadow DOM for browsers that don’t support the specification yet, move onto developing the Express middleware responsible for server-side rendering custom element templates.

Express Middleware

Express.js is a popular Node.js framework that handles common use cases for server-side web development like handling http requests, routing, templating, and debugging. This project uses Express.js to provide backend API services for the web application. When the web application made HTTP requests to /api/login for instance, Express handled that request, checked the username and password against a database, then sent a response depending on the validity of the username and password. Express uses middleware to achieve this. API middleware defined in the file packages/server/src/middleware/api.js handles multiple types of HTTP requests following REST API design guidelines. That middleware is then imported and injected into the Express application in the entry point (packages/server/src/index.js).

In the above example, the instance of express.Router defined in packages/server/src/middleware/api.js is imported into the entry point of the Express application. The application is instantiated by calling express(). Afterward, middleware can be declared for the Express application. Whenever a HTTP request is made at /api, the apiRouter will handle the request.

Most of the development of the Express server was handled for you. This was done so you could concentrate on coding custom elements, with one notable exception: Express middleware that handles server-side rendering Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates. To achieve this, you’ll develop the Express middleware that handles server-side rendered HTML responses at the following routes:

  • /
  • /login
  • /dashboard

Right now, every request by default loads the index.html of the client-side application. This was necessary because in the previous chapter you were dealing with a single-page application.

Later in this chapter, you’ll deprecate that handling of the SPA. After importing the ssr middleware, you’ll map the HTTP requests for the three routes to the middleware.

Development in this section is done like any other before it. You may continue by running the command yarn start:app which starts both the client and server development environments.

Client

Before working on the Express middleware, there’s still a bit of preparation work that needs to be done on the client. You recently deprecated the client-side SPA router, but left the routes around to use them in the context of the server-side renderer. It wasn’t made apparant at the time, but this change was necessary to expose the Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates somewhere that mapped each template to a given route.

The Route configuration already defines the route of each view, but you’ll need to add the template for each Route to the configuration, so later you can use this configuration in the Express middleware. In packages/client/src/routes.ts, import all three of the templates from their respective files.

Add a new property to each Route called template, specifying the HTML template for each view to the route it should map to. For instance, mainTemplate is the Declarate Shadow DOM HTML template that should render at /, while dashboardTemplate should display when the user navigates to /dashboard.

With that configuration complete on the client, it’s time to code the Express middleware.

Server

To get started coding the Express middleware that will server-side render each view, make a new file named ssr.js in the packages/server/src/middleware directory.

Import the routes you just exported from the client application using a relative path for now. This could very well be done using the package name @in/client, assuming that package is built.

In this first part of the ssr.js, you’ll have to wrangle paths to different files. You’re going to write some code that reads the content of several .html, .css, and .js files and then prints the content of those files to a server-side rendered template. To deal with the paths to those files in the local filesystem, import resolve from path.

Import readFileSync from fs, which will be used to read the content of a file at a given path on the local filesystem.

If you haven’t already, build the project before proceeding to ensure all packages are built property and their distributed files can be read by the Express server.

Read Client Bundles

Most of the files that should be returned in the response of the HTML document are found in one of two locations: @in/client and @in/style package’s dist directories. Code two reusable functions that return the path of a file from either of these two directories. Inject the filename into the first argument of the function. Use resolve to return the path of the file, relative to where the script is run. process.cwd() returns the path where the server is run (packages/server). Use a relative path to find the dist directories of the @in/client and @in/style packages, passing the filename argument to the end of the path, so the function returns a path to the filename.

Declare two similar function that return the content of the file at the path returned by either clientPath or stylePath. readFileSync will read the content of the file synchronously. By calling toString you can easily convert the file contents to a string.

In the next part you’ll read the content of files in the @in/client and @in/style packages, then minify the content for performance reasons, before inserting the content into the HTML document.

Minify CSS and HTML

Before handling the Declarative Shadow DOM templates, we need to figure out a way to render the global CSS styling that contains CSS variables used in every component and the HTML templates that can be referenced by any component. The CSS styles are available in the file at packages/style/dist/style.css and the HTML templates are in packages/client/dist/template.html. You just coded two functions that can read the content of files in these directories, although there’s still some processing of these files that needs to happen. Minifying the content of style.css and template.html will help reduce the size of the overall HTML document, making it faster for browsers to request the document. To minify the content of both files, import minify from the html-minifier-terser package.

Make a new const named styles. Using top-level await, call minify, passing in the file content returned by readStyleFile("style.css"). Configure minify so that CSS is optimized, all comments are removed, and whitespace is removed, ensuring the most optimal global CSS possible.

Do the same for the HTML templates stored in template.html.

Both styles and htmlTemplates return string you’ll be able to inject directly into the HTML document which will be sent in the initial response from the server.

SSR

The @lit-labs/ssr package provides tools for rendering Lit templates that use the html function exported from the lit package. The Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates exported in each of the application components don’t use Lit, instead preferring to export string including HTML templates coded entirely with browser specifications. Because of that architectural design, you’ll need to wrap each template in a call to unsafeHTML which tells Lit to render HTML instead of just a string. The render function exported from @lit-labs/ssr accepts a LitTemplate. Import both render and html into ssr.js.

Make a new function named sanitizeTemplate that accepts one argument: the template exported from each view bundle. sanitizeTemplate returns an asynchronous function that calls html with a template string, where the template is processed by unsafeHTML.

Export the middleware from the file with export default. All Express middleware are asynchronous, formatted as a function with three arguments: the request and response represented by Object, and next (denoting the “next” middleware to be called).

The first thing you’ll need to do in this function is use the current request URL found at req.url to match the request against an available route in the configuration. To parse the URL at req.url you’ll need another tool named url imported from url.

Loop over the routes Array, using find to return a match where the route’s path equals the pathname returned by url.parse.

If the route is not found with find, route will be undefined. Detect this use case and using res.redirect, rediect the request to a special route at /404 that handles requests that do not exist.

Finally, create a new const named template. Calling sanitizeTemplate with await, pass in the template string returned by route.template(), the template exported by the bundle at that route.

Now that you have the template that should appaer in the document.body, build out the rest of the document using a JavaScript Generator. This is the preferred style for generating a server-side rendered document with @lit-labs/ssr, so we’re not only sticking to convention by using a generator, but also coding with an extremely powerful and performant way to iterate over the template and produce an HTML document.

Declare a new Generator named renderApp, denoted by the * after the function keyword. renderApp takes two arguments, the route Object and the template returned from sanitizedTemplate. Using yield statements, build out the necessary parts of the HTML document, being sure to call render in between a containing HTMLDivElement with id attribute set to root, like you had done for the client.

Declare a new const named ssrResult and make it equal to what the generator returns, passing in the route and template to the renderApp function.

The generator will return a stream of data, so you need another function that handles that stream and concatenates the output of the stream to a string. Declare a new function named streamToString that does exactly that. Import Buffer to handle the stream.

Import Readable for the next part so you can read the output of renderApp.

Make another function named renderStream that takes the stream as an argument and returns the synchronous streamToString. Use Readable to read the content of the stream as a Buffer.

Add a new const named stream, passing in the ssrResult to renderStream.

Handle the response, sending a positive “200 Success” code, along with the contents of the stream.

At this point, any route that uses this middleware should return a proper HTML document with a server-side rendered view.

Entry Point

To attach the middleware to specific routes, import ssr into packages/server/src/index.js.

Deprecate the existing middleware that returns the client-side SPA either by deleting or commenting out the following lines.

Add handlers for each route that map requests to /, /login, and /dashboard to the ssr middleware.

After the development environment refreshes, you should observe the following in the browser window at http://localhost:4443/.

The output of the middleware is working. You can tell by inspecting the network response and observing that the template for each route is server-side rendered. You’re still missing some styling and client-side logic, but you’ve done it! Let’s fill in some of the missing pieces before finishing the application.

Filling In Gaps

If you inspect the document closely, it appears @lit-labs/ssr is printing empty Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates for some reason. In ssr.js, remove empty templates by postprocessing the stream with a RegExp that finds all instances of empty templates and replaces them with empty string.

Turning your attention to the document.head, provide the title for the document in the <title> tag, sourcing the title from the route. Build tooling deploys the fonts with the server in a directory that is accessible by browser requests at /style/font/. Use a <style> tag to inject the fonts for the application with @import statements that point to the necessary files. Finally, inject the server-side optimized global styles in another <style> tag. This should provide more styling in the view.

Still in the document.head, provide the ncessary polyfills for browsers that don’t support all of the Web Components specifications, reading the content of polyfill.js and injecting the content of the file into a <script> tag.

Add the HTML templates referenced by several components after the starting <body> tag.

Inject the contents of ponyfill.js near the closing </body> tag. Similarly, inject the bundle for each route by referencing the name of the bundle on route.component and reading the file from the client dist directory.

Congratulations! You’ve server-side rendered the application using @lit-labs/ssr. Let’s wrap up development with what you learned in this chapter.

Summary

Declarative Shadow DOM provides the ability to encapsulate custom elements with Shadow DOM in a declarative, template-based approach that allows custom elements to be server-side rendered. In this chapter, you provided Declarative Shadow DOM HTML templates for each of the autonomous custom elements in the application and refactored the client application by deprecating the router. After providing the templates on the Route configuration, you shimmed the necessary browser specifications so client-side custom element implementations could be interpreted in the context of Node.js. You developed Express middleware using @lit-labs/ssr that used the same route configuration to server-side render custom element templates with Declarative Shadow DOM.

By finishing the content of Chapter Ten you’ve completed all the exercises available in Fullstack Web Components.

Fullstack Web Components

Conclusion

Congratulations! You’ve completed the exercises included in Fullstack Web Components. You coded several UI components using the set of specifications known as Custom Elements v1. You used Shadow DOM to encapsulate a component’s HTML template and CSS styling. Upon further investigation of custom elements v1, you found that only autonomous and form-associated custom elements can leverage Shadow DOM. Customized built-in elements lack this capability due to how built-ins extend from common HTML elements, some of which either lack the ability to employ Shadow DOM, or in the case of HTMLVideoElement, already utilize Shadow DOM and cannot be overwritten. While this may diminish the use-value of customized built-ins, you developed against this specification with some novel use cases: ButtonComponent and TableComponent to name a couple. While autonomous custom elements enable the creation of fully custom user interfaces, customized built-ins allow engineers to inherit the accessibility and other user experience characteristics from HTML elements. Through the use of ElementInternals, form-associated custom elements enable engineers to develop feature-rich custom implementations of elements that can participate in HTML forms. In the final chapter, you used Declarative Shadow DOM to server-side render custom elements. Declarative Shadow DOM allows Shadow DOM to be declared entirely in a HTML template, opening up the possibility for custom elements to be statically rendered.

Specification

One of the potential hazards developing against browser specifications like custom elements v1 is that modern browsers implement specifications at different times, or potentially not at all. Such is the case with the customized built-in elements specification which the WebKit team has vehemently rejected. While customized built-ins may never be included in Apple Safari, a polyfill exists that brings the specification to the Safari browser. Polyfills patch functionality that doesn’t exist in a web browser yet, while ponyfills provides that functionality in a module that usually executes after DOM has loaded. A ponyfill needs to statically analyze DOM to function, while a polyfill grants the functionality to the browser before DOM is parsed. Both ponyfills and polyfills are useful for custom element development as different specifications are introduced in web browsers over time.

Specifications can come and go. As browser vendors and members of the community propose new specifications, a browser may introduce a specification while others linger. One of the critiques of Web Components has been that specifications are unstable. While that may have been true during custom elements v0, a legacy specification that is not covered in this book, custom elements v1 is here to stay. The specifications engineers should be concerned with moving forward are those that augment the experience of developing custom elements. To illustrate how to navigate this terrain of web specifications, let’s look at how CSS specifications have either been successful or failed to catch on.

As we observed in the exercises of this book, CSS variables can pierce the shadow boundary and help style custom elements. It would be rather limiting if CSS variables were the only tool for styling custom elements. Early in the development of the custom elements specifications, other CSS selectors were proposed that pierced the shadow boundary (>>>, /deep/, and ::shadow), but they failed to gain traction as a standard. These selectors would have enabled a custom element to style slotted descendants through a special CSS selector. CSS Shadow Parts were designed, in part, to address the concerns over implementing these aforementioned selectors in various browsers. CSS Shadow Parts allow engineers to declare parts of a HTML template that can be styled outside of the custom element’s shadow boundary. While CSS Shadow Parts help CSS authors style a component from the outside, which could be useful for theming or styling a child element from a parent, this specification still doesn’t address a problem with styling custom elements: the duplication of CSS styles throughout the codebase. Another specification named Constructable Stylesheets aims to solve this problem by giving engineers a way to compose CSS for a custom element without the need to create a CSS stylesheet. At the time of writing this, CSS variables and CSS Shadow Parts are available in every mainstream browser, while Constructable Stylesheets are only found in Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and behind a flag in Mozilla Firefox. This bodes well for the specification. Most browsers have signaled Constructable Stylesheets will be implemented and for those browsers which lag, a polyfill exists that brings the functionality to that browser. Over time, the specifications that support styling custom elements have evolved, giving engineers greater flexibility when authoring elements that employ Shadow DOM.

It can often be confusing determining if a particular specification can be used in a specific browser. The Web Platform Incubator Community Group provides a spreadsheet with the status of each specification. Chrome Platform Status is also a useful tool for determining the viability of a particular specification. One source of confusion happens when a browser fails to signal if they intend to implement a specification, as is often the case with Apple Safari. Searching for a particular specification’s polyfill may also yield information as the maintainers of the polyfill or ponyfill are keenly aware of browser support.

Another promising specification includes the HTML Template Instantiation Proposal which brings data binding to HTML templates. A polyfill exists to support these “Template Parts”. The Context API Proposal serves to provide a means to pass data between components. If adopted by mainstream browsers, this specification would replace the need for BroadcastChannel which we used in this book for the same purpose. The Pending Task Protocol Proposal would alleviate issues with custom elements that have asynchronous dependencies. While a pattern for hydration exists as part of the implementation of Declarative Shadow DOM, Partial Hydration would provide finer grained control over what should trigger hydration of a custom element. All of these specifications are indeed very promising. While some enterprising engineers may develop a polyfill when it doesn’t exist yet, the rest of us should check the status of a specification, if a polyfill or ponyfill exists before developing against the specification.

Benefits

While navigating the browser landscape can be daunting, it shouldn’t stop anyone from coding with custom elements today. The benefits of coding with browser specifications far outweigh the potential negatives. By developing a UI library with custom elements, you can ensure the components have a long lifespan. Custom elements v1 will remain in the browser without breaking changes for the foreseeable future. Unlike framework-based UI components, custom elements don’t incur the cost of dependency management. This can be a boon for large enterprise organizations that can struggle to maintain dependencies across disparate teams. When developing a UI library with React, for instance, teams must maintain the version of react and react-dom packages, along with any CSS-in-JS library. This can be disruptive at large corporations. When a corporate UI library upgrades various dependencies, teams using that library for use in their respective applications must upgrade as well. When Web Components are distributed in a fashion that requires zero dependencies, it can reduce the churn around maintaining dependencies at large enterprise organizations.

When UI libraries are distributed with Web Components, it allows a large corporation to scale. Web Components are interoperable with any JavaScript framework. Components that are interoperable can have a farther reach than components built with a JavaScript framework. Teams in large enterprise organizations adopt different JavaScript frameworks, having competing priorities which makes front end architectures difficult to maintain. If a UI library were distributed with framework-based UI components, it could be a blocker for teams. Angular components aren’t compatible with React, for instance. If a UI library is distributed with Web Components, it removes barriers for adoption.

One benefit of Web Components we didn’t explore in this book is how custom elements are composable. Custom elements are ES2015 classes that extend either from HTMLElement, or in the case of customized built-ins, the element that you wish to replicate some behavior. Once you’ve declared functionality in a component class, you could further extend that class and compose further functionality. With the micro-library you developed in this book, you could even override the template or styling.

If the long lifespan, reusability, interoperability, and composability of custom elements weren’t enough of a benefit, consider the performance implications. Custom elements have zero dependency, meaning no JavaScript is blocking the page from loading. Unlike most JavaScript frameworks which have to parse the DOM tree, custom elements are parsed directly by the browser. Declarative Shadow DOM allows custom elements to be statically rendered server-side, allowing blazingly fast page loads.

The future is bright

I wrote this book to help anyone who wants to learn the fundamentals of web development. At the component level that fundamental knowledge resides in the set of specifications known as Web Components. By engaging with the exercises in this book, I hope you’ve learned how to develop with custom elements in a meaningful way. Take what you’ve learned and apply it to developing a UI library where you work or if you want, follow the best practices you’ve learned for personal use.

Over the time I’ve been a software engineer, I’ve watched large enterprises both benefit and struggle with the adoption of JavaScript frameworks. The benefit of JavaScript frameworks is undeniable when developing an application, however; frameworks can fall short in certain ways when corporations need to scale their product. UI libraries help organizations scale since engineers across the company can reuse the UI components. JavaScript frameworks can’t guarantee components built with the framework are interoperable with other JavaScript frameworks. Custom elements are interoperable, giving them a clear advantage over framework-based UI components. With additional specifications becoming available for custom element development sometime in the future, software engineers will gain browser specifications that provide features once only available in JavaScript frameworks.

Custom elements don’t just help large corporations scale, but they also help solve another problem in the web development community. Over the past few years, web development education has often focused on teaching software engineers the most popular JavaScript library: jQuery and then React. If higher education bypasses the fundamentals of web development: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and teaches about frameworks instead, software engineers often don’t fully understand how the web works “under the hood”. When custom elements are developed using browser specifications, software engineers are immersed in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. By learning these fundamental technologies before a framework, it enables software engineers to diagnose problems and innovate new tools for web development. Web Components have emerged as a fundamental part of the web developer’s toolkit and should be included in any web development curricula.

Web Components have been growing in popularity among web developers ever since Custom Elements v1 became available in every evergreen browser: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Edge. According to Google, in 2019 “> 5% of page loads use a Web Component”. Chrome Platform Status in 2022 revealed ~18% of page loads tracked by Google contain a Web Component. There is no better time than now to implement custom elements. I can’t wait to see what you make with Web Components. Mention me in a tweet or post in the Web Components Community on Twitter and I’ll take a look.
